| $\,-0.7\,$ | $\,0.2206\,$ | $\,0.2177\,$ | $\,0.2148\,$ |

The probability that a randomly selected student scores less than $68$ is approximately
{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the exam score. Then we have $X∼N(75,{8}^{2}).$

We want to find $P(X<68).$ First, we write this as a cumulative probability:

$$
P(X<68)=P(X\le 68)
$$

Then, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 68) & =P(Z\le \frac{68-75}{8}) \\  & ≈P(Z\le -0.88) \\  & =Φ(-0.88)\end{aligned}
$$

From the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(-0.88)=0.1894≈0.19.
$$

Therefore, the probability that a randomly selected student scores less than $68$ is approximately $0.19.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-07bafdfe-77c0-5c1b-9c62-90a031acb268"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-07bafdfe-77c0-5c1b-9c62-90a031acb268" :answer-field/id #uuid "07bafdfe-77c0-5c1b-9c62-90a031acb268" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-2c059257-dee3-5562-812a-d0dc9d6f5f02" :answer-field/choices ["answer-2c059257-dee3-5562-812a-d0dc9d6f5f02"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2c059257-dee3-5562-812a-d0dc9d6f5f02" :answer/id #uuid "2c059257-dee3-5562-812a-d0dc9d6f5f02" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.19" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-e312f711-a596-58e6-bba4-4f3bc71c5f9f" :question/id #uuid "e312f711-a596-58e6-bba4-4f3bc71c5f9f" :question/math-academy-id "q-132434" :question/problem "The volume of soda in cans filled at a particular factory is normally distributed with a mean of $12$ ounces and a standard deviation of $0.1$ ounces. What is the probability that a randomly selected soda can contains more than $12.2$ ounces? Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,2.0\,$ | $\,0.9772\,$ | $\,0.9778\,$ | $\,0.9783\,$ |
| $\,2.1\,$ | $\,0.9821\,$ | $\,0.9826\,$ | $\,0.9830\,$ |
| $\,2.2\,$ | $\,0.9861\,$ | $\,0.9864\,$ | $\,0.9868\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the volume (in ounces) of soda in a randomly selected can. Then we have $X∼N(12,{0.1}^{2}).$

We want to find $P(X>12.2).$ Thus, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>12.2) & =P(Z>\frac{12.2-12}{0.1}) \\  & =P(Z>2) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 2) \\  & =1-Φ(2)\end{aligned}
$$

From the $z$-table, we see that

$$
1-Φ(2)=1-0.9772≈0.02.
$$

Therefore, the probability that a randomly selected soda can contains more than $12.2$ ounces is approximately $0.02.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c5d04840-0a76-5834-bd32-257991f12cc2"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-c5d04840-0a76-5834-bd32-257991f12cc2" :answer-field/id #uuid "c5d04840-0a76-5834-bd32-257991f12cc2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-ad72aa07-660d-51b0-afc8-b41ca13de413" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b79552a7-3376-5da8-91ca-17bece0d388e" "answer-7f62054b-c721-5065-baa7-a2e088063d8b" "answer-ad72aa07-660d-51b0-afc8-b41ca13de413" "answer-ae4692a1-b2be-56d2-9388-d0e19d2609ff" "answer-7836d0df-6d0e-53c1-9b87-066f993123a0"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b79552a7-3376-5da8-91ca-17bece0d388e" :answer/id #uuid "b79552a7-3376-5da8-91ca-17bece0d388e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.00" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7f62054b-c721-5065-baa7-a2e088063d8b" :answer/id #uuid "7f62054b-c721-5065-baa7-a2e088063d8b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.01" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ad72aa07-660d-51b0-afc8-b41ca13de413" :answer/id #uuid "ad72aa07-660d-51b0-afc8-b41ca13de413" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.02" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ae4692a1-b2be-56d2-9388-d0e19d2609ff" :answer/id #uuid "ae4692a1-b2be-56d2-9388-d0e19d2609ff" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.03" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7836d0df-6d0e-53c1-9b87-066f993123a0" :answer/id #uuid "7836d0df-6d0e-53c1-9b87-066f993123a0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.04" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186302160 :question/problem "The durations of direct flights on a certain route are normally distributed with a mean of $180$ minutes and a standard deviation of $20$ minutes. </tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the diastolic blood pressure of the selected person. Then we have $X∼N(85,{14}^{2}).$

We want to find $P(77<X<86).$ First, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(77<X<86) & =P(\frac{77-85}{14}<Z<\frac{86-85}{14}) \\  & =P(-0.57<Z<0.07)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we express the required probability in terms of $Φ(z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-0.57<Z<0.07) & =P(Z<0.07)-P(Z\le -0.57) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.07)-P(Z\le -0.57) \\  & =Φ(0.07)-Φ(-0.57)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.07) & =0.5279 \\ Φ(-0.57) & =0.2843\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-0.57<Z<0.07) & =Φ(0.07)-Φ(-0.57) \\  & =0.5279-0.2843 \\  & =0.2436.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that the randomly selected person from the group has a diastolic blood pressure greater than $77\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}$ and less than $86\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}$ is approximately $0.24.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-044df1b7-c311-5b38-a151-6ea7331c7eee"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083973 :question/problem "In a factory, soda cans are filled with a mean volume of $12$ ounces of soda. However, $1%$ of cans contain no more than $11.5$ ounces of soda. Assuming that the volume of soda in each can is normally distributed, find the standard deviation of the volume of soda in a can, rounded to $2$ decimal places.

*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $p$ | $\,0.900\,$ | $\,0.950\,$ | $\,0.975\,$ | $\,0.990\,$ | $\,0.995\,$ | $\,0.999\,$ | $\,0.9995\,$ |

| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,1.2816\,$ | $\,1.6449\,$ | $\,1.9600\,$ | $\,2.3263\,$ | $\,2.5758\,$ | $\,3.0902\,$ | $\,3.2905\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the volume (in ounces) of soda in a can. Then we have $X∼N(12,{\sigma }^{2}),$ and we want to find the standard deviation $\sigma .$ 

We know that $P(X\le 11.5)=0.01.$ Converting $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 11.5) & =0.01 \\ P(Z\le \frac{11.5-12}{\sigma }) & =0.01 \\ Φ(-\frac{0.5}{\sigma }) & =0.01 \\ -\frac{0.5}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.01).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.99)=2.3263,
$$

and therefore by symmetry, we have

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(1-0.99)={Φ}^{-1}(0.01)=-2.3263.
$$

Finally then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{0.5}{\sigma } & =-2.3263 \\ \frac{1}{\sigma } & =4.6524 \\ \sigma  & =\frac{1}{4.6524} \\  & ≈0.21.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186082769 :answer-field/correct 17592186082773 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-d916a01a-c116-520b-be92-bf93eddd6997" :question/id #uuid "d916a01a-c116-520b-be92-bf93eddd6997" :question/math-academy-id "q-95126" :question/problem "The lengths of babies at birth in a given population are normally distributed with a mean of $\mu \,\text{cm}$ and a standard deviation of $6\,\text{cm}.$ Additionally, the length of $60%$ of the newborns falls between $0.9\mu \,\text{cm}$ and $1.1\mu \,\text{cm}.$ Find the mean $\mu $ rounded to $2$ decimal places.

*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $p$ | $\,0.75\,$ | $\,0.80\,$ | $\,0.85\,$ | $\,0.90\,$ | $\,0.95\,$ | $\,0.97\,$ | $\,0.99\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,0.6745\,$ | $\,0.8416\,$ | $\,1.0364\,$ | $\,1.2816\,$ | $\,1.6449\,$ | $\,1.8808\,$ | $\,2.3263\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the length of a randomly selected newborn. Then we have $X∼N(\mu ,{6}^{2}),$ and we want to find the mean $\mu .$ 

We know that $P(0.9\mu <X<1.1\mu )=0.6.$ First, we convert this to a cumulative probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.9\mu <X<1.1\mu ) & =0.6 \\ 2P(\mu <X<1.1\mu ) & =0.6 \\ P(\mu <X<1.1\mu ) & =0.3 \\ P(X<\mu )+P(\mu <X<1.1\mu ) & =0.5+0.3 \\ P(X<1.1\mu ) & =0.8\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<1.1\mu ) & =0.8 \\ P(Z<\frac{0.1\mu }{6}) & =0.8 \\ Φ(\frac{0.1\mu }{6}) & =0.8 \\ \frac{0.1\mu }{6} & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.8)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.8)≈0.8416.
$$

Finally then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{0.1\mu }{6} & =0.8416 \\ 0.1\mu  & =5.0496 \\ \mu  & =\frac{5.0496}{0.1} \\  & ≈50.50\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7782954d-0945-5a09-a4ad-d4eaf2acb6cc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 2.3) & =0.20 \\ P(Z\le \frac{2.3-2.5}{\sigma }) & =0.20 \\ Φ(-\frac{0.2}{\sigma }) & =0.20 \\ -\frac{0.2}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.20).\end{aligned}

*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

We know that $P(X<59)=0.20.$ Converting $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<59) & =0.20 \\ P(Z\le \frac{59-\mu }{5}) & =0.20 \\ Φ(\frac{59-\mu }{5}) & =0.20 \\ \frac{59-\mu }{5} & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.20).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.20)=-0.8416.
$$

Finally then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{59-\mu }{5} & =-0.8416 \\ 59-\mu  & =-4.208 \\ \mu  & ≈63\,\text{days.}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186082793 :answer-field/correct 17592186082795 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-1e826c15-fd0c-50c0-b8b3-b16460ce62c6" :question/id #uuid "1e826c15-fd0c-50c0-b8b3-b16460ce62c6" :question/math-academy-id "q-95073" :question/problem "A group of students took a test and got an average score of $81.$ Additionally, $5%$ of the students scored greater than $91.$ Assuming that the students' scores are normally distributed, find the percent of students with a score lower than $70,$ rounded to $1$ decimal place.

*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

We know that $P(X>91)=0.05.$ First, we convert this to a cumulative probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 91) & =1-P(X>91) \\  & =1-0.05 \\  & =0.95\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 91) & =0.95 \\ P(Z\le \frac{91-81}{\sigma }) & =0.95 \\ Φ(\frac{10}{\sigma }) & =0.95 \\ \frac{10}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.95)\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{10}{\sigma } & =1.6449 \\ \frac{1}{\sigma } & =0.16449 \\ \sigma  & =\frac{1}{0.16449} \\  & ≈6.0794.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<70) & =P(X\le 70) \\  & =P(Z\le \frac{70-81}{6.0794}) \\  & ≈P(Z\le -1.81) \\  & =Φ(-1.81) \\  & =0.0351 \\  & ≈3.5%\end{aligned}
$$

| $\,0.6\,$ | $\,0.7422\,$ | $\,0.7454\,$ | $\,0.7486\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the time a full charge lasts. Then we have $X∼N(26,{\sigma }^{2}),$ and we want to find $P(X>30).$ But first, we need to find the standard deviation $\sigma .$ 

We know that $P(X<20)=0.20.$ First, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<20) & =0.20 \\ P(Z\le \frac{20-26}{\sigma }) & =0.20 \\ Φ(\frac{-6}{\sigma }) & =0.20 \\ \frac{-6}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.20)\end{aligned}

Finally, we can solve for $P(30<X)$ as follows:

$$

Therefore, approximately $28.8%$ of the times the battery lasts more than $30$ hours." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186082787 :answer-field/correct 17592186082792 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083466 :activity/expected-seconds 1380.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166848 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-39f657eb-aa97-5394-b0e6-ecba3bf80018" "question-deb0627a-b1f4-5ecd-95e2-372ffa642f2c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167117 :question/problem "The students in a particular school are split among three classes, class $1,$ class $2,$ and class $3.$

- Class $1$ contains $25%$ of the students in the school, and $55%$ of those students take biology.

- Class $2$ contains $35%$ of the students in the school, and $40%$ of those students take biology.

- Class $3$ contains $40%$ of the students in the school.

If $45%$ of students in the entire school are female, $80%$ of female students take biology, and $70%$ of biology students are female, what is the probability that a randomly selected student from class $3$ takes biology? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let $F$ be the event that a student is female, $B$ be the event that a student takes biology, and ${C}_{1},{C}_{2},{C}_{3}$ be the event that a student is in class $1,$ $2,$ or $3,$ respectively. 

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P({C}_{1})=0.25 &  & P(B|{C}_{1})=0.55 \\  & P({C}_{2})=0.35 &  & P(B|{C}_{2})=0.4 \\  & P({C}_{3})=0.4\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${C}_{1}⊔{C}_{2}⊔{C}_{3}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$
P({C}_{1})+P({C}_{2})+P({C}_{3})=0.25+0.35+0.4=1.
$$

- Since $45%$ of students in the entire school are female, we have

$$
P(F)=0.45.
$$

- Since $80%$ of females take biology, we have

$$
P(B|F)=0.8.
$$

- Since $70%$ of biology students are female, we have

$$
P(F|B)=0.7.
$$

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen student from class $3$ takes biology, which is represented as $P(B|{C}_{3}).$ 

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(F|B) & =\frac{P(B|F)P(F)}{P(B)} \\ P(F|B) & =\frac{P(B|F)P(F)}{P(B|{C}_{1})P({C}_{1})+P(B|{C}_{2})P({C}_{2})+P(B|{C}_{3})P({C}_{3})} \\ 0.7 & =\frac{(0.8)(0.45)}{(0.55)(0.25)+(0.4)(0.35)+P(B|{C}_{3})(0.4)} \\ 0.7 & =\frac{0.36}{0.2775+0.4P(B|{C}_{3})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $P(B|{C}_{3}),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0.7(0.2775+0.4P(B|{C}_{3})) & =0.36 \\ 0.2775+0.4P(B|{C}_{3}) & =\frac{0.36}{0.7} \\ 0.2775+0.4P(B|{C}_{3}) & =\frac{18}{35} \\ 0.4P(B|{C}_{3}) & =\frac{18}{35}-0.2775 \\ P(B|{C}_{3}) & =\frac{1}{0.4}(\frac{18}{35}-0.2775) \\ P(B|{C}_{3}) & ≈0.592\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163780 :answer-field/correct 17592186163785 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-39f657eb-aa97-5394-b0e6-ecba3bf80018" :question/id #uuid "39f657eb-aa97-5394-b0e6-ecba3bf80018" :question/math-academy-id "q-148666" :question/problem "A manufacturing company has three sites, factory $1,$ factory $2,$ and factory $3.$ They all produce two types of light bulbs: A and B.

Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the event that a light bulb is of type A, $D$ be the event that a light bulb is defective, and ${F}_{1},{F}_{2},{F}_{3}$ be the event that a light bulb is produced in factory $1,$ $2,$ or $3,$ respectively. 

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P({F}_{1})=0.45 &  & P(D|{F}_{1})=0.05 \\  & P({F}_{2})=0.45 \\  & P({F}_{3})=0.1 &  & P(D|{F}_{3})=0.01\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${F}_{1}⊔{F}_{2}⊔{F}_{3}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$
P({F}_{1})+P({F}_{2})+P({F}_{3})=0.45+0.45+0.1=1.
$$

- Since $57%$ of all light bulbs are of type A, we have

$$
P(A)=0.57.
$$

- Since $3%$ of type A light bulbs are defective, we have

$$
P(D|A)=0.03.
$$

- Since $41%$ of defective light bulbs are of type A, we have

$$
P(A|D)=0.41
$$

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen light bulb from factory $2$ is defective, which is represented as $P(D|{F}_{2}).$ 

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A|D) & =\frac{P(D|A)P(A)}{P(D)} \\ P(A|D) & =\frac{P(D|A)P(A)}{P(D|{F}_{1})P({F}_{1})+P(D|{F}_{2})P({F}_{2})+P(D|{F}_{3})P({F}_{3})} \\ 0.41 & =\frac{(0.03)(0.57)}{(0.05)(0.45)+P(D|{F}_{2})(0.45)+(0.01)(0.1)} \\ 0.41 & =\frac{0.0171}{0.0235+0.45P(D|{F}_{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $P(D|{F}_{2}),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0.41(0.0235+0.45P(D|{F}_{2})) & =0.0171 \\ 0.0235+0.45P(D|{F}_{2}) & =\frac{0.0171}{0.41} \\ 0.0235+0.45P(D|{F}_{2}) & =\frac{171}{4100} \\ 0.45P(D|{F}_{2}) & =\frac{171}{4100}-0.0235 \\ P(D|{F}_{2}) & =\frac{1}{0.45}(\frac{171}{4100}-0.0235) \\ P(D|{F}_{2}) & ≈0.040\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f3f4b001-3f5d-563e-a82a-efaf92b09aad"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166877 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-2ad5265b-a872-53d0-b3f1-65585e111dd6"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167118 :question/problem "Arthur and Sara are finding the best recipe for chocolate muffins, and they test three different oven cooking modes, mode $1,$ mode $2,$ and mode $3.$ They also try two types of yeast, A and B.

- They use mode $1$ to cook the $30%$ of their muffins, and $90%$ of those muffins turn out well.

- They use mode $2$ to cook the $40%$ of their muffins, and $85%$ of those muffins turn out well.

- They use mode $3$ to cook the $30%$ of their muffins, and $88%$ of those muffins turn out well.

If $20%$ of all muffins was prepared with yeast A, and $87%$ of yeast A muffins turn out well, what is the probability that a randomly chosen good muffin is done with yeast A? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the event that a muffin is made with yeast A, $G$ be the event that a muffin turns out well, and ${M}_{1},{M}_{2},{M}_{3}$ be the event that a muffin is cooked with mode $1,$ $2,$ or $3,$ respectively. 

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P({M}_{1})=0.3 &  & P(G|{M}_{1})=0.9 \\  & P({M}_{2})=0.4 &  & P(G|{M}_{2})=0.85 \\  & P({M}_{3})=0.3 &  & P(G|{M}_{3})=0.88\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${M}_{1}⊔{M}_{2}⊔{M}_{3}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$
P({M}_{1})+P({M}_{2})+P({M}_{3})=0.3+0.4+0.3=1.
$$

- Since $20%$ of muffins are made with yeast A, we have

$$
P(A)=0.2.
$$

- Since $87%$ of muffins made with yeast A turn out well, we have

$$
P(G|A)=0.87.
$$

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen good muffin is made with yeast A, which is represented as $P(A|G).$ 

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A|G) & =\frac{P(G|A)P(A)}{P(G)} \\  & =\frac{P(G|A)P(A)}{P(G|{M}_{1})P({M}_{1})+P(G|{M}_{2})P({M}_{2})+P(G|{M}_{3})P({M}_{3})} \\  & =\frac{(0.87)(0.2)}{(0.9)(0.3)+(0.85)(0.4)+(0.88)(0.3)} \\  & =\frac{0.174}{0.874} \\  & ≈0.199,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163786 :answer-field/correct 17592186163788 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-deb0627a-b1f4-5ecd-95e2-372ffa642f2c" :question/id #uuid "deb0627a-b1f4-5ecd-95e2-372ffa642f2c" :question/math-academy-id "q-149493" :question/problem "A volleyball school for children splits the players into three teams, team $1$, team $2,$ and team $3.$ 

- $44%$ of children are in team $1,$ and $23%$ of children in this team have been playing for over two years.

- $32%$ of children are in team $2,$ and $26%$ of children in this team have been playing for over two years.

- $24%$ of children are in team $3.$

If $7%$ of all children can play in the blocker position, $40%$ of children who can play as blockers have been playing for over two years, and $10%$ of children who have been playing for over two years can play as blockers, what is the probability that a randomly chosen child in team $3$ has been playing for over two years? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let $B$ be the event that a child can play in the blocker position, $I$ be the event that a child has been playing for over two years, and ${T}_{1},{T}_{2},{T}_{3}$ be the events that a child is in team $1,$ $2,$ or $3,$ respectively. 

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P({T}_{1})=0.44 &  & P(I|{T}_{1})=0.23 \\  & P({T}_{2})=0.32 &  & P(I|{T}_{2})=0.26 \\  & P({T}_{3})=0.24\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${T}_{1}⊔{T}_{2}⊔{T}_{3}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$
P({T}_{1})+P({T}_{2})+P({T}_{3})=0.44+0.32+0.24=1.
$$

- Since $7%$ of children can play in the blocker position, we have

$$
P(B)=0.07.
$$

- Since $40%$ of children who can play as blockers have been playing for over two years, we have

$$
P(I|B)=0.4.
$$

- Since $10%$ of children who have been playing for over two years can play as blockers, we have

$$
P(B|I)=0.1.
$$

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen child in team 3 has been playing for over two years, which is represented as $P(I|{T}_{3}).$

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(B|I) & =\frac{P(I|B)P(B)}{P(I)} \\ P(B|I) & =\frac{P(I|B)P(B)}{P(I|{T}_{1})P({T}_{1})+P(I|{T}_{2})P({T}_{2})+P(I|{T}_{3})P({T}_{3})} \\ 0.1 & =\frac{(0.4)(0.07)}{(0.23)(0.44)+(0.26)(0.32)+P(I|{T}_{3})(0.24)} \\ 0.1 & =\frac{0.028}{0.1844+0.24P(I|{T}_{3})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $P(I|{T}_{3}),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0.1(0.1844+0.24P(I|{T}_{3})) & =0.028 \\ 0.1844+0.24P(I|{T}_{3}) & =\frac{0.028}{0.1} \\ 0.1844+0.24P(I|{T}_{3}) & =\frac{7}{25} \\ 0.24P(I|{T}_{3}) & =\frac{7}{25}-0.1844 \\ P(I|{T}_{3}) & =\frac{1}{0.24}(\frac{7}{25}-0.1844) \\ P(I|{T}_{3}) & ≈0.398\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b2b5eda7-fc54-5354-9c43-01751b2546c8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b2b5eda7-fc54-5354-9c43-01751b2546c8" :answer-field/id #uuid "b2b5eda7-fc54-5354-9c43-01751b2546c8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-e44bfd71-59f5-5456-8e29-b331fc4b994f" :answer-field/choices ["answer-db3514aa-7da2-58cd-a765-4883b4c73d8a" "answer-e5ca70ca-440e-5d09-bd91-1a12c84d2bf9" "answer-aad9a2ec-8c38-50c5-a148-e148cf1a201f" "answer-e44bfd71-59f5-5456-8e29-b331fc4b994f" "answer-cb08ac4c-bcdb-5bf3-803d-48abd3c44b23"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-db3514aa-7da2-58cd-a765-4883b4c73d8a" :answer/id #uuid "db3514aa-7da2-58cd-a765-4883b4c73d8a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.135" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e5ca70ca-440e-5d09-bd91-1a12c84d2bf9" :answer/id #uuid "e5ca70ca-440e-5d09-bd91-1a12c84d2bf9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.252" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-aad9a2ec-8c38-50c5-a148-e148cf1a201f" :answer/id #uuid "aad9a2ec-8c38-50c5-a148-e148cf1a201f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.307" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e44bfd71-59f5-5456-8e29-b331fc4b994f" :answer/id #uuid "e44bfd71-59f5-5456-8e29-b331fc4b994f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.398" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cb08ac4c-bcdb-5bf3-803d-48abd3c44b23" :answer/id #uuid "cb08ac4c-bcdb-5bf3-803d-48abd3c44b23" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.546" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-2ad5265b-a872-53d0-b3f1-65585e111dd6" :question/id #uuid "2ad5265b-a872-53d0-b3f1-65585e111dd6" :question/math-academy-id "q-149494" :question/problem "In a nature park, there are $4$ species of squirrels, each with the same population.

- Among the squirrels of species $1,$ $12%$ are born in captivity.

- Among the squirrels of species $2,$ $5%$ are born in captivity.

- Among the squirrels of species $3,$ $6%$ are born in captivity.

- Among the squirrels of species $4,$ $3%$ are born in captivity.

If $35%$ of the squirrels are adult females, and $8%$ of the adult female squirrels are born in captivity, what is the probability that a randomly chosen squirrel born in captivity is an adult female? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let $F$ be the event that a squirrel is an adult female, $C$ be the event that a squirrel is born in captivity, and ${S}_{1},{S}_{2},{S}_{3},{S}_{4}$ be the event that a squirrel is of species $1,$ $2,$ $3,$ or $4,$ respectively. 

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- Each species has the same number of squirrels, so we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned}P({S}_{1})=P({S}_{2})=P({S}_{3})=P({S}_{4})=0.25\end{aligned}
$$

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P(C|{S}_{1})=0.12 \\  & P(C|{S}_{2})=0.05 \\  & P(C|{S}_{3})=0.06 \\  & P(C|{S}_{4})=0.03\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${S}_{1}⊔{S}_{2}⊔{S}_{3}⊔{S}_{4}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$
P({S}_{1})+P({S}_{2})+P({S}_{3})+P({S}_{4})=0.25+0.25+0.25+0.25=1.
$$

- Since $35%$ of the squirrels are adult females, we have

$$
P(F)=0.35.
$$

- Since $8%$ of adult females are born in captivity, we have

$$
P(C|F)=0.08.
$$

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen squirrel born in captivity is an adult female, which is represented as $P(F|C).$ 

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(F|C) & =\frac{P(C|F)P(F)}{P(C)} \\  & =\frac{P(C|F)P(F)}{P(C|{S}_{1})P({S}_{1})+P(C|{S}_{2})P({S}_{2})+P(C|{S}_{3})P({S}_{3})+P(C|{S}_{3})P({S}_{3})} \\  & =\frac{(0.08)(0.35)}{(0.12)(0.25)+(0.05)(0.25)+(0.06)(0.25)+(0.03)(0.25)} \\  & =\frac{0.028}{0.065} \\  & ≈0.431,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ae7e24b9-313e-560b-9e0c-e4316aa55761"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083132 :question/problem "Calculate $\textrm{LCM}(120, 90).$" :question/worked-solution "To find the lowest common multiple of two numbers, we first find the prime factorization of both numbers. 

- We start by finding the prime factorization of $120\mathbin{:}$ 

![](images/fb/fb213f6ac09abbf31aacfdbfbd08b76dbea4199528abeb1c8041a73f0d7780ed.png)

Therefore, $120 = 2^3 \cdot 3 \cdot 5.$

- Next, we find the prime factorization of $90\mathbin{:}$

![](images/03/034b3fe25edb2741abb035b8ca71a3c499fe6fae1a5975b4241d6379b819f19e.png)

Therefore, $90 = 2 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5.$

So, we have the following prime factorizations:

$$
\begin{aligned}120 & ={2}^{3}\cdot 3\cdot 5 \\ 90 & =2\cdot {3}^{2}\cdot 5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we write down every prime factor that is shown above, and we raise each prime factor to the highest power given in either factorization:

- the highest power of $2$ is $3$

- the highest power of $3$ is $2$

- the highest power of $5$ is $1$

Therefore, the lowest common multiple of $120$ and $90$ is 

$$
\textrm{LCM}(120, 90) = 2^3 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5  = 360.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083332 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-4dbbbcc8-62df-5e8e-bfa9-1313bcce5620" "question-ca4901aa-e3e7-56b2-8843-d65effed5ee5" "question-42ddf56f-a8d0-56db-815a-a130a857fd56" "question-02c3ac78-aa7f-5ad9-a0fe-7e15cb1f374c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083134 :question/problem "Calculate $\textrm{LCM}(30, 33, 20).$" :question/worked-solution "To find the lowest common multiple of three numbers, we first find their prime factorizations. 

- We start by finding the prime factorization of $30\mathbin{:}$

![](images/31/312d8c33355fb36260cce172ab20bf907637528d0a5d04dc4dd1eceb59d765dd.png)

Therefore, $30 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5.$

- Next, we find the prime factorization of $33.$ We easily deduce that $33 = 3 \cdot 11.$

- Then, we find the prime factorization of $20{:}$

![](images/7e/7e03a139fc3afa7df4d7f32ecf42f8f30d19bfe0415725f47fe5be63301899b5.png)

Therefore, $20=2^2 \cdot 5 .$

So, we have the following prime factorizations:

$$
\begin{aligned}30 & =2\cdot 3\cdot 5 \\ 33 & =3\cdot 11 \\ 20 & ={2}^{2}\cdot 5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we write down every prime factor that is shown above, and we raise each prime factor to the highest power given in any of the factorizations:

- the highest power of $2$ is $2$

- the highest power of $3$ is $1$

- the highest power of $5$ is $1$

- the highest power of $11$ is $1$

Therefore, the lowest  common multiple of $30$, $33,$ and $20$ is 

$$
\textrm{LCM}(30,  33, 20) = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 11  = 660.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083331 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-dc2e2da4-0526-5cbb-b99c-ff4e18d482b4" "question-2e11aa68-986c-58e0-bcdf-2852036febc7"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083133 :question/problem "Find the lowest common denominator of $\dfrac{4}{45}$ and $\dfrac{7}{48}.$" :question/worked-solution "The lowest common denominator of two fractions is the least common multiple of the denominators.

So, to find the lowest common denominator of two fractions, we first find the prime factorization of both denominators.

- We start by finding the prime factorization of $45\mathbin{:}$

![](images/5e/5e53857c25c4b7fd8dd1897dcd1b0608e48512d5a61a200a11a3f8a0ca92fcd2.png)

Therefore, $45= 3^2 \cdot 5.$

- Next, we find the prime factorization of $48{:}$

![](images/e2/e21d5cf36f2f08fbbb46e1d923d84e0b02f10531c42c590ab7d3a813f34009dc.png)

Therefore, $48 = 2^4 \cdot 3.$

So, we have the following prime factorizations:

$$
\begin{aligned}45 & ={3}^{2}\cdot 5 \\ 48 & ={2}^{4}\cdot 3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we write down every prime factor that is shown above, and we raise each prime factor to the highest power given in either factorization:

- the highest power of $2$ is $4$

- the highest power of $3$ is $2$

- the highest power of $5$ is $1$

Therefore, the lowest common denominator is $2^4\cdot 3^2 \cdot 5 = 720.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083690 :question/problem "$\text{LCM}(98,175)=$" :question/worked-solution "To find the lowest common multiple of two numbers, we first find the prime factorization of both numbers. 

- We start by finding the prime factorization of $98:$ 

![](images/c7/c74979d4af6e34328dca1fab75fbf07c138c28ec8b93d5462d889f08ac6ea6c0.png)

Therefore, $98=2\cdot {7}^{2}.$

- Next, we find the prime factorization of $175:$

![](images/56/56e885903dd09097a256b6740f7f6307ba2af3c0e43f32bb6456745acfb3e777.png)

 
Therefore, $175=7\cdot {5}^{2}.$

So, we have the following prime factorizations:

$$
\begin{aligned}98 & =2\cdot {7}^{2} \\ 175 & =7\cdot {5}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we write down every prime factor that is shown above, and we raise each prime factor to the highest power given in either factorization:

- the highest power of $2$ is $1$

- the highest power of $7$ is $2$

- the highest power of $5$ is $2$

Therefore, the lowest common multiple of $98$ and $175$ is

To find the lowest common multiple of two small numbers, we can list all multiples of the two numbers and identify the smallest multiple that they have in common.

For example, let's find the lowest common multiple of $4$ and $6.$ We start by listing all multiples of $4$ and $6\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & \,\to \,4,\,8,\,\boxed{\text{[math]12[/math]}},\,16,\,20,\,24,\,… \\ 6 & \,\to \,6,\,\boxed{\text{[math]12[/math]}},\,18,\,24,\,30,\,36,\,…\end{aligned}
$$

The smallest multiple in both lists is ![](images/92/9285d37c7b455395acb42a54f78348bedfd8c9a72ad63d6e6ab7c2426148ea0d.svg) So $12$ is our answer, and we can write

$$
\textrm{LCM}(4,6)= 12.
$$

**Note:** The lowest common multiple is also sometimes called the *least* common multiple." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186084485 :tutorial/content "Now suppose that we want to find the lowest common multiple of two larger numbers. It would take a while to make long lists of multiples. Luckily, there is a faster method. 

Let's demonstrate by finding $\textrm{LCM}(10,12).$ We start by writing the prime factorization of $10$ and $12$, writing any repeating factors as powers:

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =2\cdot 5={2}^{1}\cdot {5}^{1} \\ 12 & =2\cdot 2\cdot 3={2}^{2}\cdot {3}^{1}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we write down each unique prime factor that appears in either of our decompositions. In our case, the unique prime factors are 

$$
{\color{red}2}, \qquad {\color{red}3}, \qquad {\color{red}5}.
$$

Now, for each number in our list, we look at *both* prime factorizations and we take the *largest* power shown for each prime factor:

- The factors corresponding to ${\color{red}2}$ are ${\color{red}2}^{\color{blue}1}$ and ${\color{red}2}^{\color{blue}2}.$ Of these, the larger power is ${\color{red}2}^{\color{blue}2}.$

- There is only one factor corresponding to ${\color{red}3}.$ It is ${\color{red}3}^{\color{blue}1}.$

- There is only one factor corresponding to ${\color{red}5}.$ It is ${\color{red}5}^{\color{blue}1}.$

Finally, we multiply the largest powers of each factor together, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{LCM}(10,12) & ={2}^{2}\cdot {3}^{1}\cdot {5}^{1} \\  & =4\cdot 3\cdot 5 \\  & =60.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083445 :activity/expected-seconds 480.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [[17592186389804 :question/problem "Let $I=[0,1]⊂R$ and ${X}_{i}=[0,i]\times \{i\}.$ Which of the following represents ${⋃}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}?$"] [17592186389804 :question/worked-solution "Recall that the union of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *at least one* set:

["question-39aef628-7059-5436-8f38-6e05c93c2909" :question/problem "A $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$

Since the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ is $13,$ we obtain

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}=13\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=\sqrt{13}.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sqrt{13}.$"] ["question-39aef628-7059-5436-8f38-6e05c93c2909" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] :question/problem "Find $k$ given that the vectors $x=⟨1,k,2⟩$, $y=⟨5,-2,3⟩$, and $z=⟨-4,k,1⟩$ are coplanar.

$k=${{field-1}}"] ["question-b407ea24-4cac-5cb8-bbfb-b1a7b706dc73" :question/worked-solution "Computing the triple product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (y\times z) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & k & 2 \\ 5 & -2 & 3 \\ -4 & k & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ k & 1\end{aligned}|-k\cdot |\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}|+2\cdot |\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ -4 & k\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(-2\cdot 1-3\cdot k)-k(5\cdot 1-3\cdot -4)+2(5k-(-2)(-4)) \\  & =-2-3k-k(5+12)+2(5k-8) \\  & =-2-3k-17k+10k-16 \\  & =-10k-18\end{aligned}
$$

Three vectors are coplanar if and only if their triple product is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (y\times z) & =0 \\ -10k-18 & =0 \\ k & =-\frac{9}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the three vectors are coplanar if and only if $k=-\frac{9}{5}.$"] ["question-b407ea24-4cac-5cb8-bbfb-b1a7b706dc73" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] - a **null** angle has a measure of $0^\circ,$

- an **acute** angle has a measure between $0^\circ$ and $90^\circ,$

- a **right** angle has a measure of $90^\circ,$

- an **obtuse** angle has a measure between $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ,$

- a **straight** angle has a measure of $180^\circ,$

- a **reflex** angle has a measure between $180^\circ$ and $360^\circ,$ and

- a **full** angle has a measure of $360^\circ.$

It is also helpful to remember that when two lines meet at a point, the opposite angles are called **vertical angles**. Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.

["question-4a6f2377-d91b-5967-99d3-f6f62abbce5f" :question/math-academy-id "q-152221"] ["question-4a6f2377-d91b-5967-99d3-f6f62abbce5f" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true? 

I. The sum of $4{x}^{2}+1$ and $2{x}^{2}$ is a binomial.

II. The sum of $3{x}^{2}-2x$ and $5$ is a binomial.

III. The sum of a binomial and a monomial is **sometimes** a binomial."] ["question-4a6f2377-d91b-5967-99d3-f6f62abbce5f" :question/worked-solution "Let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
(4{x}^{2}+1)+(2{x}^{2})=6{x}^{2}+1,
$$

which is a binomial.

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
(3{x}^{2}-2x)+(5)=3{x}^{2}-2x+5,
$$

which is *not* a binomial (it's a trinomial).

- Statement III is true. The sum of a binomial and a monomial *could be* a binomial (see, for example, statement I). 

 However, the sum of a binomial and a monomial is *not always* a binomial (see, for example, statement II). 

 So, the sum of a binomial and a monomial is *sometimes* binomial.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""] ["question-4a6f2377-d91b-5967-99d3-f6f62abbce5f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] I. Any $6\times 5$ matrix $A$ has at most $6$ distinct singular values.

II. Any $8\times 9$ matrix $A$ has at most $9$ distinct singular values.

III. The matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]$ has at most two non-negative distinct singular values."] ["question-dfba6eb1-d0b6-5cbc-ac16-d682a2e1cc93" :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $A$ is a $6\times 5$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $5\times 6$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $5\times 5$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{5\times 6}\times {A}_{6\times 5}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{5\times 5}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $8\times 9$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $9\times 8$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $9\times 9$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{9\times 8}\times {A}_{8\times 9}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{9\times 9}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $9$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is true.  Indeed, all singular values of any matrix are non-negative.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""] ["question-dfba6eb1-d0b6-5cbc-ac16-d682a2e1cc93" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] We begin by moving all of the variables to the left-hand side and all of the constants to the right-hand side. This gives

$$
-\frac{2}{5}x+y=-3
$$

Now, we multiply both sides of the equation by $-1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{5}x+y & =-3 \\ (-1)\cdot (-\frac{2}{5}x+y) & =(-1)\cdot (-3) \\ \frac{2}{5}x-y & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we multiply both sides of the equation by $5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{5}x-y & =3 \\ 5\cdot (\frac{2}{5}x-y) & =5\cdot (3) \\ 2x-5y & =15\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors, and $a\ge 0.$ So we are done!

The standard form of the line is 

$$
2x-5y=15.
$$"] ["question-8d0eef6f-b433-56d1-a89d-4aab29bca392" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-2578c7dc-df07-5c9f-9883-dccf1b4fa276" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-62452c7f-a9e2-5c51-81ef-baa2650df43c" :question/worked-solution "Our goal is to write the equation in the form $ax+by=c,$ where $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors and $a\ge $$
\begin{aligned}3y+3x+3 & =0 \\ 3x+3y & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+3y & =-3 \\ \frac{3x+3y}{3} & =\frac{-3}{3} \\ x+y & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors, and $a\ge 0.$ So we are done!

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-4 & =3(x-(-1)) \\ y-4 & =3(x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Finally, we multiply by $-1$ to make the $x$-coefficient positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x+y & =7 \\ (-1)\cdot (-3x+y) & =(-1)\cdot 7 \\ 3x-y & =-7\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$"] [17592186088066 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-ccfc196e-d2b9-5e51-b03e-0879a7618102" :answer/id #uuid "ccfc196e-d2b9-5e51-b03e-0879a7618102"] ["answer-ccfc196e-d2b9-5e51-b03e-0879a7618102" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-ccfc196e-d2b9-5e51-b03e-0879a7618102" :answer/value "3x-y"] [17592186085127 :answer-field/correct "answer-ccfc196e-d2b9-5e51-b03e-0879a7618102"] [17592186085127 :answer-field/choices "answer-ccfc196e-d2b9-5e51-b03e-0879a7618102"] ["answer-592087b3-94fc-571b-8975-e20b1af01fdd" :answer/id #uuid "592087b3-94fc-571b-8975-e20b1af01fdd"] ["answer-592087b3-94fc-571b-8975-e20b1af01fdd" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-592087b3-94fc-571b-8975-e20b1af01fdd" :answer/value "-7"] [17592186085126 :answer-field/correct "answer-592087b3-94fc-571b-8975-e20b1af01fdd"] [17592186085126 :answer-field/choices "answer-592087b3-94fc-571b-8975-e20b1af01fdd"] [17592186088991 :tutorial/content "The **standard form** equation of a line is 

$$
ax+by=c,
$$

where

- $a,b,$ and $c$ are all integers,

- $a \geq 0,$ and

- $a,b,$ and $c$ have no common factors.

Note that we always write $x$ *before* $y$ on the left-hand side!

Let's see some examples:

- The equation $2x - y= -5$ is in standard form. Indeed, the variables are on the left-hand side, while the constant term is on the right-hand side:

$$
\underbrace{2x - y}_{\textrm{variables}} \quad = \underbrace{-5\phantom{y}}_{\textrm{constant}}
$$

 
All coefficients are integers (namely, $2,$ $-1,$ and $-5$) and don't have common factors greater than $1.$ Also, the coefficient of $x$ is non-negative ($2$).

- The equation $-3x + y = 1$ is *not* in standard form because the coefficient of $x$ is negative ($-3$).

- The equation $2x+4y = -10$ is *not* in standard form because the coefficients $(2,4,$ and $-10)$ have a common factor of $2.$

- The equation $\dfrac12x+\dfrac13y = 6$ is *not* in standard form because the coefficients of $x$ and $y$ are not integers."] [17592186088993 :tutorial/content "Let's now discuss how to convert the equation of a line to standard form.

To illustrate, we will take the line $y = 2x-1$ and convert it into standard form. We begin by moving all of the variables to the left-hand side and all of the constants to the right-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2x-1 \\ y-2x & =-1 \\ -2x+y & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now the equation is in the form $ax+by=c.$ However, it violates the rule $a \geq 0.$ We can fix this by multiplying the equation by $-1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+y & =-1 \\ (-1)\cdot (-2x+y) & =(-1)\cdot (-1) \\ 2x-y & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors, and $a \geq 0.$ So, we are done!

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{5}\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-\sqrt{5}\text{i} & 3 \\ -3 & -2-\sqrt{5}\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(2-\sqrt{5}\text{i}){x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0 \\ -3{x}_{1}+(-2-\sqrt{5}\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-\sqrt{5}\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{3}(2+\sqrt{5}\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3}(2+\sqrt{5}\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}2+\sqrt{5}\text{i} \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $C$ is closed under matrix addition

II. $C$ is closed under scalar multiplication

III. $C$ is a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$

IV. $C$ is **not** a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$"] [17592186125154 :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. If ${A}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ and ${A}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ are two matrices from $C,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}+{a}_{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which is a matrix from $C.$ So, $C$ is closed under addition.

- Statement II is true. If $A=[\begin{aligned}a & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ is an element of $C$ and $k\in R,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}kA & =k[\begin{aligned}a & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}ka & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which is a matrix from $C.$ So, $C$ is closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is true, while statement IV is false. $C$ is a subspace because it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only.""] [17592186125154 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] [17592186123524 :answer-field/correct 17592186123528] ["question-3ec301c4-26d6-5f2a-9132-b21928f5ee67" :question/id #uuid "3ec301c4-26d6-5f2a-9132-b21928f5ee67"] ["question-3ec301c4-26d6-5f2a-9132-b21928f5ee67" :question/math-academy-id "q-94638"] ["question-3ec301c4-26d6-5f2a-9132-b21928f5ee67" :question/problem "Consider the vector space $C[0,3]$ of all continuous functions $f:[0,3]\to R$ and its subset $N$ containing all functions that return a nonzero value at exactly one point in $[0,3].$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $N$ is closed under function addition

II. $N$ is closed under scalar multiplication

III. $N$ is a subspace of $C[0,3]$

IV. $N$ is **not** a subspace of $C[0,3]$

*Hint: Different functions from $N$ might give a nonzero value at different points in $[0,3].$*"] ["question-3ec301c4-26d6-5f2a-9132-b21928f5ee67" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. For example, if $f({a}_{1})\ne 0$ and $g({a}_{2})\ne 0,$ where ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ are distinct points in $[0,3],$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}f({a}_{1})+g({a}_{1}) & \ne 0 \\ f({a}_{2})+g({a}_{2}) & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)+g(x)\ne 0$ at two distinct points. So, $N$ is *not* closed under addition.

- Statement II is false. For example, if $f(a)\ne 0$ for some $a\in [0,3],$ and $k=0,$ then

$$
kf(x)=0
$$

 
for any $x\in [0,3].$ So, $N$ is *not* closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is false, while statement IV is true. $N$ is *not* a subspace because it's not closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

"970e7795-a408-5210-80aa-25f375509b0b"] ["question-970e7795-a408-5210-80aa-25f375509b0b" :question/math-academy-id "q-65263"] ["question-970e7795-a408-5210-80aa-25f375509b0b" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}?$

I. The partial derivative with respect to $x$ is defined at $(1,-1,-1)$

II. ${f}_{y}(-1,1,1)$ is defined

III. ${f}_{z}(1,1,0)$ is defined"] ["question-970e7795-a408-5210-80aa-25f375509b0b" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{yz}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\  & =\frac{yz{e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{xz}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\  & =\frac{xz{e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{xy}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\  & =\frac{xy{e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}}{2\sqrt{xyz}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one. 

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,-1,-1)$, where we have 

$$
f(1,-1,-1)={e}^{\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{1}}=e,
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,-1,-1) & =\frac{(-1)(-1){e}^{\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}}{2\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}=\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{1}}}{2\sqrt{1}}=\frac{e}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(-1,1,1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(-1,1,1)={e}^{\sqrt{(-1)(1)(1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{-1}},
$$

which is undefined since we have a negative number under the radical. Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

- Statement III is false. If we substitute $(1,1,0)$ into ${f}_{z}$, we get

$$
{f}_{z}(1,1,0)=\frac{1\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{\sqrt{1\cdot 1\cdot 0}}}{2\sqrt{1\cdot 1\cdot 0}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I  only'."] ["question-970e7795-a408-5210-80aa-25f375509b0b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-8c27c81b-25fa-5185-a05b-37e0f78454cf" "question-970e7795-a408-5210-80aa-25f375509b0b"] [17592186268903 :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $g(x,y,z)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{z}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1>0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of $g$ is 

$$
{D}_{g}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${g}_{x}(x,y,z)=\frac{2x}{z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1\ne 0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

- Similarly, the domain of ${g}_{y}(x,y,z)$ is the same: 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{y}}={D}_{{g}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

- The function ${g}_{z}(x,y,z)=-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{{z}^{2}}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1>0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{z}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $g$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{g}\cap {D}_{{g}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{z}} & ={D}_{g}\cap {D}_{{g}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{z}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\} \\  & \,\,\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\} \\  & \,\,\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["answer-ee12a67f-64f9-5a94-956a-3d8cefbc2906" :answer/id #uuid "ee12a67f-64f9-5a94-956a-3d8cefbc2906"] ["answer-ee12a67f-64f9-5a94-956a-3d8cefbc2906" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["question-4227b37a-8e18-5afd-83bf-26143e32cd4d" :question/problem "$2÷\frac{2}{5}\times 4=$"] ["question-4227b37a-8e18-5afd-83bf-26143e32cd4d" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate this expression, $$
\begin{aligned}7|2x-5|+1 & =15 \\ 7|2x-5| & =14 \\ |2x-5| & =2\end{aligned}
$$

- If $|2x-5|=2x-5,$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|2x-5| & =2 \\ 2x-5 & =2 \\ 2x & =7 \\ x & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $|2x-5|=-(2x-5),$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|2x-5| & =2 \\ -(2x-5) & =2 \\ -2x+5 & =2 \\ -2x & =-3 \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

III. $|5z+1|=-6$"] ["question-2e7c0ce7-7ffd-571f-9543-de7ea37af680" :question/worked-solution "An absolute value equation has no solution if, when the absolute value is isolated on the left side, the right-hand side is negative.

With that in mind, let's look at each equation in turn:

- Equation I has a solution. The absolute value is already isolated on the left-hand side, and the right-hand side is non-negative.

- Equation II has a solution. To see this, we first isolate the absolute value on the left-hand side as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|5z+1|-3 & =-1 \\ |5z+1| & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Since the right-hand side is non-negative, this equation has a solution.

- Equation III *has no solution*. The absolute value is already isolated on the left-hand side, and the right-hand side is *negative*.

Therefore, the answer is "III only.""] ["question-2e7c0ce7-7ffd-571f-9543-de7ea37af680" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-09294ff2-d9d6-52b7-9077-c43a5e430b15" equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(1,1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}-z)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}-z)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{e}^{y}-z)\text{ }k \\  & ={e}^{y}\text{ }i+x{e}^{y}\text{ }j-k \\ ∇\,f(1,1,e) & ={e}^{1}\text{ }i+(1){e}^{1}\text{ }j-k \\  & =e\,i+e\,j-k \\  & =⟨e,e,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,1,e)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-e⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨e,e,-1⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-e⟩ & =0\end{aligned}

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.

[17592186097276 :question/worked-solution "From the identity $1+{cot}^{2}⁡\theta ={csc}^{2}⁡\theta $ with $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}-x,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}1+{cot}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x) & ={csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x) \\ {cot}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x) & ={csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {cot}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)\text{d}x & =\int ({csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)-1)\text{d}x \\  & =\int {csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)\text{d}x-\int 1\cdot \text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)-x+C.\end{aligned}

{{field-1}}"] ["question-d59d88c8-9c62-51d9-bd12-48f5c362cc67" :question/worked-solution "In this case, we have to use the identity  $1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x.$ Substituting this into our integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x+1}{{sec}^{3}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡x}{{sec}^{3}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-0 \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}

$$
1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Rearranging the above identity gives

$$
{sec}^{2}⁡x-1={tan}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Using the above, we compute the given integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3/2}\frac{3{x}^{2}{tan}^{2}⁡x}{{sec}^{2}⁡x-1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{3/2}\frac{3{x}^{2}{tan}^{2}⁡x}{{tan}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3/2}3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{3}\,{|}_{1}^{3/2} \\  & ={(\frac{3}{2})}^{\,3}-{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{27}{8}-1 \\  & =\frac{19}{8}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-43534459-b512-57ce-a24a-a07661c93918" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-f5f4070c-c95c-5ed1-901f-4528153978ca" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-2dd7bee1-71b3-5685-9b9f-df2041d5d283" :question/math-academy-id "q-79732"] ["question-2dd7bee1-71b3-5685-9b9f-df2041d5d283" :question/problem "Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix with eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1$ corresponding to the eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ respectively, where

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Solve the following initial value problem:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]
$$"] ["question-2dd7bee1-71b3-5685-9b9f-df2041d5d283" :question/worked-solution "Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),
$$

where $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2}$ with corresponding eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2},$ the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our matrix differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$, we substitute $t=0$ in the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}5{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}5{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=2 \\ {c}_{1}=6.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{c}_{1}=6.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
5\cdot 6+{c}_{2}=2\,⟹\,{c}_{2}=-28.
$$

 

Therefore, the solution for the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =6\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+(-28)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}30 \\ 6\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+[\begin{aligned}-28 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-2dd7bee1-71b3-5685-9b9f-df2041d5d283" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-8bc94f58-c888-5f48-8bc9-61a9a2954b43" :answer-field/id #uuid Find $‖Q(x)‖$, where $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 5\end{aligned}].$"] ["question-dfb0578c-1343-53e2-a376-085feaa6ce26" :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

In this case, since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Q(x)‖ & =‖x‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{5}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{30}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-dfb0578c-1343-53e2-a376-085feaa6ce26" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-131118e0-de48-5f9d-ada7-20da3689be40" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-c7e0b385-be5e-5415-b9aa-b210f7036677" :question/math-academy-id "q-161046"] ["question-c7e0b385-be5e-5415-b9aa-b210f7036677" :question/problem "$$
r(z,\theta )=⟨\text{__________},\,\sqrt{z-1}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩
$$

The vector-valued function $r(z,\theta )$ above parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=\sqrt{z-1}$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $z$-axis for $z\in [1,10].$ What is the first component of $r?$"] ["question-c7e0b385-be5e-5415-b9aa-b210f7036677" :question/worked-solution "![](images/04/04de4ea7dc617be1429c596812ce4f450c2cdaafd8d94d86f75e68a6743acba9.png)

 

A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $y=f(z)$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $z$-axis has the position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(z)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f(z)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,z\in [a,b],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that $y=f(z)=\sqrt{z-1}\ge 0$ for all $z\in [1,10].$ 

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
r(z,\theta )=⟨\sqrt{z-1}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\sqrt{z-1}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,z\in [1,10],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Therefore, the first component of $r$ is $\sqrt{z-1}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$"] ["question-c7e0b385-be5e-5415-b9aa-b210f7036677" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["activity-bf53dea8-f555-5d67-8b1f-60c3c23bf32f" :activity/first-step "step-1c778fa9-95bd-5205-85c3-55aecdf8bb5a"] [17592186110297 :question/problem "Calculate $\left(\dfrac{2x}{3}\right)^4.$"] [17592186110297 :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the power of quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{2x}{3})}^{4}=\frac{(2x)^{4}}{{3}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the power rule and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(2x)^{4}}{{3}^{4}} & = \\ \frac{{2}^{4}{x}^{4}}{{3}^{4}} & = \\ \frac{16{x}^{4}}{81} & \end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186110298 :question/problem "Simplify $\left(\dfrac{y}{2}\right)^3 \left(\dfrac{2y}{3}\right)^2.$"] [17592186110298 :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the power of quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{y}{2})}^{3}{(\frac{2y}{3})}^{2}=\frac{{y}^{3}}{{2}^{3}}\cdot \frac{(2y)^{2}}{{3}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we apply the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{3}}{{2}^{3}}\cdot \frac{(2y)^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & = \\ \frac{{y}^{3}}{8}\cdot \frac{{2}^{2}{y}^{2}}{9} & = \\ \frac{{y}^{3}}{8}\cdot \frac{4{y}^{2}}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we apply the product rule and simplify:

quotient rule** states that if we want to raise the quotient $\dfrac{x}{y}$ to some power $n,$ we must raise the numerator and denominator to the power $n$ as follows:

$$
\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)^n=\dfrac{x^n}{y^n}
$$

For example,

$$
\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)^4=\dfrac{x^4}{y^4}.
$$

To see why the power of quotient rule is true, let's take the above example and work it out again the long way. We get the same result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{x}{y})}^{4} & = \\ \frac{x}{y}\cdot \frac{x}{y}\cdot \frac{x}{y}\cdot \frac{x}{y} & = \\ \frac{x\cdot x\cdot x\cdot x}{y\cdot y\cdot y\cdot y} & = \\ \frac{{x}^{4}}{{y}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

The power of quotient rule is just a shortcut for the process above."] [17592186110819 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] ["question-e9c37ee3-304c-5283-97a5-75391f3d1e94" :question/id #uuid "e9c37ee3-304c-5283-97a5-75391f3d1e94"] ["question-e9c37ee3-304c-5283-97a5-75391f3d1e94" :question/math-academy-id "q-82985"] ["question-e9c37ee3-304c-5283-97a5-75391f3d1e94" :question/problem "Using the change of variables $u=x+3y$ and $v=x+2y,$ evaluate the double integral

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{x+3y}{x+2y}\,dx\,dy,
$$

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x+3y\le 2,\,2\le x+2y\le 4\}.$"] ["question-e9c37ee3-304c-5283-97a5-75391f3d1e94" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=x+3y,\,v=x+2y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,2\le v\le 4\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & \text{ }\text{ }2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{x+3y}{x+2y}\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{u}{v}\cdot |\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{u}{v}\cdot |-1|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{u}{v}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}u[{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{1}{v}\,dv]du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}u[\operatorname{ln}⁡v]_{2}^{4}\,du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}u(\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\,du \\  & =(2\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡2){\int }_{0}^{2}u\,du \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2[\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2\cdot (2-0) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-e9c37ee3-304c-5283-97a5-75391f3d1e94" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-b260735c-8ce2-5820-82bd-e9db5e7533a8" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Using the change of variables $u=\frac{y}{x}$ and $v=xy,$ evaluate the double integral

$$
{∬}_{D}{e}^{-xy/2}\,dx\,dy,
$$

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,\frac{x}{4}\le y\le 2x,\,1\le xy\le 4\}.$"] ["question-c5c02db8-6f5e-5ac6-a24e-9e9016b1082e" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{y}{x},\,v=xy
$$

 
gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,\frac{1}{4}\le u\le 2,\,1\le v\le 4\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x} \\ y & \text{ }\text{ }x\end{aligned}| \\  & =-\frac{2y}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{(-\frac{2y}{x})}=-\frac{1}{2u}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{e}^{-xy/2}\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}{e}^{-v/2}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{e}^{-v/2}\cdot |-\frac{1}{2u}|\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{1/4}^{2}\frac{{e}^{-v/2}}{u}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{e}^{-v/2}[{\int }_{1/4}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u]\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{e}^{-v/2}[\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|\,{|}_{1/4}^{2}]du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{e}^{-v/2}[\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{1}{4}]\,du \\  & =\frac{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{e}^{-v/2}\,du \\  & =\frac{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{2}\cdot {[-2{e}^{-v/2}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =-3\operatorname{ln}⁡2\cdot ({e}^{-2}-{e}^{-1/2}) \\  & =3({e}^{-1/2}-{e}^{-2})\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-c5c02db8-6f5e-5ac6-a24e-9e9016b1082e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-15ea503e-c96f-567a-8f89-cf26cc3e1193" :answer-field/id #uuid To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

subject to the constraints 

$$
g(x,y,z)=x+y+z=2, \qquad h(x,y,z)=x^2 + z^2 = 4.
$$

Since $f(x,y,z)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y,z)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ g(x,y,z)=2 \\ h(x,y,z)=4\end{aligned}
$$

We start by expanding the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x},{f}_{y},{f}_{z}⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x},{g}_{y},{g}_{z}⟩+\mu ⟨{h}_{x},{h}_{y},{h}_{z}⟩ \\ ⟨1,-1,-1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨1,1,1⟩+\mu ⟨2x,0,2z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we have the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}1=\lambda +2\mu x \\ -1=\lambda  \\ -1=\lambda +2\mu z\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{1}{\mu } \\ \lambda =-1 \\ \mu z=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\mu$ can't be zero since this leads to a contradiction. So, from the third equation above, we must have $z=0.$

Next, we substitute $z=0$  into the second constraint:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =4 \\ {x}^{2} & =4 \\ x & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we substitute $x$ and $z$ into the first constraint:

- If $x=2$ and $z= 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+z & =2 \\ 2+y+0 & =2 \\ 2+y & =2 \\ y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x=-2$ and $z=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+z & =2 \\ -2+y+0 & =2 \\ -2+y & =2 \\ y & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(2, 0, 0), \qquad (-2, 4, 0).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y,z)$ | $(2, 0, 0 )$ | $(-2, 4, 0)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y,z)$ | $2$ | $-6$ |

$4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1.$"] ["question-4d8f93db-ca73-5128-94a3-1e0c56cdcf95" :question/worked-solution "We need to find the maximum value of 

$$
f(x,y,z)=x+2y+3z
$$

subject to the constraints 

$$
g(x,y,z)=x-y-z=0,\,h(x,y,z)=4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

Since $f(x,y,z)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y,z)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ g(x,y,z)=0 \\ h(x,y,z)=1\end{aligned}
$$

We start by expanding the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x},{f}_{y},{f}_{z}⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x},{g}_{y},{g}_{z}⟩+\mu ⟨{h}_{x},{h}_{y},{h}_{z}⟩ \\ ⟨1,2,3⟩ & =\lambda ⟨1,-1,-1⟩+\mu ⟨8x,2y,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we have the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}1=\lambda +8\mu x \\ 2=-\lambda +2\mu y \\ 3=-\lambda \end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{1}{2\mu } \\ y=-\frac{1}{2\mu } \\ \lambda =-3\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\mu $ can't be zero since this leads to a contradiction.

Next, we substitute our expressions for $x$ and $y$ into the second constraint:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ \frac{1}{{\mu }^{2}}+\frac{1}{4{\mu }^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{5}{4{\mu }^{2}} & =1 \\ {\mu }^{2} & =\frac{5}{4} \\ \mu  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, 

$$
x=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},\,y=∓\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}.
$$

Finally, we substitute $x$ and $y$ into the first constraint:

- If $x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$ and $y=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y-z & =0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}-(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}})-z & =0 \\ z & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$ and $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y-z & =0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}-(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}})-z & =0 \\ z & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}),\,(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}})
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y,z)$ | $(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}})$ | $(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}})$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y,z)$ | $\sqrt{5}$ | $-\sqrt{5}$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at $(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}),$ and its   maximum value is $\sqrt{5}.$"] Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ g(x,y,z)=1 \\ h(x,y,z)=2\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x},{f}_{y},{f}_{z}⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x},{g}_{y},{g}_{z}⟩+\mu ⟨{h}_{x},{h}_{y},{h}_{z}⟩ \\ ⟨2,-2,1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨1,-1,1⟩+\mu ⟨2x,2y,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}2=\lambda +2\mu x \\ -2=-\lambda +2\mu y \\ 1=\lambda \end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{1}{2\mu } \\ y=-\frac{1}{2\mu } \\ \lambda =1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2 \\ \frac{1}{4{\mu }^{2}}+\frac{1}{4{\mu }^{2}} & =2 \\ \frac{1}{2{\mu }^{2}} & =2 \\ {\mu }^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ \mu  & =\pm \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, 

$$
x=\pm 1,\,y=∓1.
$$

Finally, we substitute $x$ and $y$ into the first constraint:

- If $x=1$ and $y=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y+z & =1 \\ 1-(-1)+z & =1 \\ 2+z & =1 \\ z & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x=-1$ and $y=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y+z & =1 \\ -1-1+z & =1 \\ -2+z & =1 \\ z & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(1,-1,-1),\,(-1,1,3).
$$

| $(x,y,z)$ | $(1,-1,-1)$ | $(-1,1,3)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y,z)$ | $3$ | $-1$ |

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+z & =0 \\ -2+1+z & =0 \\ -1+z & =0 \\ z & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(2,-1,-1),\,(-2,1,1).
$$

| $(x,y,z)$ | $(2,-1,-1)$ | $(-2,1,1)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |

$$
\{\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ g(x,y,z)=1 \\ h(x,y,z)=2\end{aligned}

$$

Therefore, we have the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}2=2\lambda +2\mu x \\ 4=-4\lambda  \\ -2=-2\lambda +2\mu z\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{2}{\mu } \\ \lambda =-1 \\ z=-\frac{2}{\mu }\end{aligned}\end{aligned}

$$

As a result, 

$$
x=\pm 1,\,z=∓1.
$$

$$

$$

- If $x=-1$ and $z=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-4y-2z & =1 \\ 2(-1)-4y-2(1) & =1 \\ -4y & =5 \\ y & =-\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
(1,\frac{3}{4},-1),\,(-1,-\frac{5}{4},1).

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at $(1,1,-2),$ and its maximum value is $8.$"] ["question-e3b568f7-cd27-5a4c-97e4-f5b7033e39b7" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard]
