If $f(x),g(x)\\in B,$ then\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}(f+g)(1) & =f(1)+g(1) \\\\  & =f(-1)+g(-1) \\\\  & =(f+g)(-1).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, $B$ is closed under addition.\n\n- Statement II is true. If $f(x)\\in B$ and $k\\in R,$ then \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}(kf)(1) & =kf(1) \\\\  & =kf(-1) \\\\  & =(kf)(-1).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, $B$ is closed under scalar multiplication.\n\n- Statement III is true, while statement IV is false. $B$ is a subspace because it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I, II, and III only.\""} {:db/id :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.\n\nWith that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.\n\n- Statement I is true. If ${A}_{1}={\\alpha }_{1}A$ and ${A}_{2}={\\alpha }_{2}A$ are two matrices from $E,$ then\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} & ={\\alpha }_{1}A+{\\alpha }_{2}A=({\\alpha }_{1}+{\\alpha }_{2})A,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhich is a matrix from $E.$ So, $E$ is closed under addition.\n\n- Statement II is true. space, is called a **subspace** of $V$. \n\nFortunately, we do not need to check all vector space axioms to determine whether a subset of some vector space is a subspace. Instead, we only need to check the **subspace criterion**, which states the following:\n\n*A subset $H$ of a vector space $V$ is a subspace of $V$ if and only if $H$ is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication. That is to say, both of the following conditions hold:*\n\n- *If $\\mathbf{u}$ and $\\mathbf{v}$ lie in $H$, then their sum $\\mathbf{u}+\\mathbf{v}$ also lies in $H$. Formally,*\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{u},\\mathbf{v} \\in H \\quad\\Rightarrow\\quad  \\mathbf{u}+\\mathbf{v} \\in H.\n$$\n\n- *If $\\mathbf{u}$ lies in $H$, then $k \\cdot \\mathbf{u}$ also lies in $H$ for any scalar  $k$. Formally,* \n\n$$\nk \\in \\mathbb{R}, \\,\\mathbf{u} \\in H \\quad\\Rightarrow\\quad  k\\cdot\\mathbf{u} \\in H.\n$$\n\nFor example, consider the vector space $\\mathbb{R}_3[t]$ containing all polynomials of degree at most $3,$ along with the subset \n\n$$\nA = \\{ at^2 \\:|\\: a \\in \\mathbb{R} \\}.\n$$\n\nIs $A$ a subspace? Let's check the two subspace criterion conditions: \n\n- Suppose $p_1(t)=a_1 t^2$ and $p_2(t)=a_2 t^2$ are two polynomials from $A$. Summing the two polynomials, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{p}_{1}(t)+{p}_{2}(t) & =({a}_{1}{t}^{2})+({a}_{2}{t}^{2}) \\\\  & ={{({a}_{1}+{a}_{2})}_{⏟}}_{a\\in R}{t}^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \nThus, $p_1(t)+p_2(t)$ is a polynomial of the form $at^2,$ which belongs to $A$.\n\n- If $p_1(t)=a_1 t^2 \\in A$ and $k \\in \\mathbb{R},$ then \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}k{p}_{1}(t) & =k({a}_{1}{t}^{2}) \\\\  & ={{(k{a}_{1})}_{⏟}}_{a\\in R}{t}^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \nThus, $kp_1(t)$ is a polynomial of the form $at^2,$ which belongs to $A$.\n\nSince both conditions hold, we conclude that $A$ is a subspace $\\mathbb{R}_3[t].$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4274a05d-d402-5dfc-a339-e5a6b5a8e5b0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3205 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid $f(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)) \\\\  & =x\\cdot \\frac{x}{xy} \\\\  & =\\frac{x}{y}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe function ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ is defined only for\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}y\\ne 0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is\n\n$$\n{D}_{{f}_{y}}=\\{(x,y)\\,:\\,y\\ne 0\\}.\n$$\n\nFinally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ exists on the set\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}} & =\\{(x,y)\\,:\\,xy>0\\}\\cap \\{(x,y)\\,:\\,y\\ne 0\\} \\\\  & =\\{(x,y)\\,:\\,xy>0\\}.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186436747 :question/id #uuid "5c311fab-0276-5890-a0ca-a5fc54209d6b" :question/math-academy-id "q-132642"} {:db/id 17592186436748 :question/id that apply.\n\n- **I.** Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(1,1)$\n- **II.** ${f}_{x}(0,1)$ is defined\n- **III.** ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that $f$ is defined only when\n\n$$\n\\frac{x}{x+y}>0.\n$$\n\nAt points in the domain of $f,$ we can compute the partial derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\\frac{∂}{∂x}\\operatorname{ln}⁡(\\frac{x}{x+y}) \\\\  & =\\frac{x+y}{x}\\cdot \\frac{∂}{∂x}(\\frac{x}{x+y}) \\\\  & =\\frac{x+y}{x}\\cdot \\frac{1\\cdot (x+y)-x\\cdot 1}{(x+y)^{2}} \\\\  & =\\frac{x+y}{x}\\cdot \\frac{y}{(x+y)^{2}} \\\\  & =\\frac{y}{x(x+y)} \\\\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\\frac{∂}{∂y}\\operatorname{ln}⁡(\\frac{x}{x+y}) \\\\  & =\\frac{x+y}{x}\\cdot \\frac{∂}{∂y}(\\frac{x}{x+y}) \\\\  & =\\frac{x+y}{x}\\cdot (-\\frac{x}{(x+y)^{2}}) \\\\  & =-\\frac{1}{x+y}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, let's examine the statements one by one.\n\n- Statement I is true. The function is defined at $(1,1),$ since\n\n$$\nf(1,1)=\\operatorname{ln}⁡(\\frac{1}{1+1})=\\operatorname{ln}⁡(\\frac{1}{2}),\n$$\n\nand both partial derivatives are defined there:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =\\frac{1}{1(1+1)}=\\frac{1}{2} \\\\ {f}_{y}(1,1) & =-\\frac{1}{1+1}=-\\frac{1}{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- Statement II is false. At $(0,1),$\n\n$$\n\\frac{x}{x+y}=\\frac{0}{0+1}=0,\n$$\n\nso\n\n$$\nf(0,1)=\\operatorname{ln}⁡(0),\n$$\n\nwhich is undefined. Therefore, ${f}_{x}(0,1)$ is not defined.\n\n- Statement III is false for the same reason. Since $f$ is not defined at $(0,1),$ the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is not defined. The simplified expression $-\\frac{1}{x+y}$ cannot be used to define the partial derivative at a point outside the domain of $f.$\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I only.\""} {:db/id (-\\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\\\  & =\\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\\cdot (-\\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\\\  & =-\\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, let's examine the statements one-by-one.\n\n- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(\\sqrt{3},1)$, where we have \n\n$$\nf(\\sqrt{3},1)=\\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\\frac{\\sqrt{3}}{1})=\\frac{\\pi }{3},\n$$\n\nand both partial derivatives are also defined at $(\\sqrt{3},1):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(\\sqrt{3},1) & =\\frac{1}{(\\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\\frac{1}{4} \\\\ {f}_{y}(\\sqrt{3},1) & =-\\frac{\\sqrt{3}}{(\\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=-\\frac{\\sqrt{3}}{4}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(1,\\sqrt{3})$, where we have \n\n$$\nf(1,\\sqrt{3})=\\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{3}})=\\frac{\\pi }{6},\n$$\n\nand ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,\\sqrt{3}):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\\sqrt{3})=\\frac{\\sqrt{3}}{{1}^{2}+(\\sqrt{3})^{2}}=\\frac{\\sqrt{3}}{4}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- Statement III is also true. :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{\\sqrt{xy}}\\cdot \\frac{y}{2\\sqrt{xy}} \\\\  & =\\frac{y{e}^{\\sqrt{xy}}}{2\\sqrt{xy}} \\\\ \\frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{\\sqrt{xy}}\\cdot \\frac{x}{2\\sqrt{xy}} \\\\  & =\\frac{x{e}^{\\sqrt{xy}}}{2\\sqrt{xy}}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, let's examine the statements one-by-one. \n\n- Statement I is false. If we substitute $(1,-1)$ into $f$, we get\n\n$$\nf(1,-1)={e}^{\\sqrt{(1)(-1)}}=-{e}^{\\sqrt{-1}}\n$$\n\nwhich is undefined since we have a negative number under the radical.\n\n- Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(-1,-1)$, where we have \n\n$$\nf(-1,-1)={e}^{\\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}}={e}^{\\sqrt{1}}={e}^{1}=e,\n$$\n\nand ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(-1,-1):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-1,-1) & =\\frac{(-1){e}^{\\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}}}{2\\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}}=-\\frac{{e}^{\\sqrt{1}}}{2\\sqrt{1}}=-\\frac{e}{2}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- Statement III is false. If we substitute $(0,1)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get\n\n$$\n{f}_{x}(0,1)=1\\cdot \\frac{{e}^{\\sqrt{0\\cdot 1}}}{2\\sqrt{0\\cdot 1}}=\\frac{{e}^{0}}{2\\sqrt{0}}=\\frac{1}{0},\n$$\n\nwhich is undefined since we have division by zero.\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is 'II  only'."} {:db/id 17592186436752 :question/id #uuid "efd3e6cc-b29d-5cd4-ba97-6a3820c7c7c6" :question/math-academy-id "q-132672"} derivatives of $g$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $g(x,y)=x\\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0.$ So, the domain of $g$ is \n\n$$\n{D}_{g}={(x,y)\\,:\\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0}.\n$$\n\nAs for the partial derivatives, we have the following.\n\n- The function ${g}_{x}(x,y)=\\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{x}$ is \n\n$$\n{D}_{{g}_{x}}={(x,y)\\,:\\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0}.\n$$\n\n- The function ${g}_{y}(x,y)=\\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{y}$ is \n\n$$\n{D}_{{g}_{y}}={(x,y)\\,:\\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\\ne 0}.\n$$\n\nFinally, we conclude that the partials of $g$ exist on the set\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{D}_{g}\\cap {D}_{{g}_{x}}\\cap {D}_{{g}_{y}} & ={(x,y)\\,:\\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0}\\cap {(x,y)\\,:\\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0}\\cap {(x,y)\\,:\\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\\ne 0} \\\\  & ={(x,y)\\,:\\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0}.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186339044 ${f}_{x}=\\frac{y{e}^{\\sqrt{xy}}}{2z\\sqrt{xy}}$ is defined only when $xy>0$ and $z\\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is \n\n$$\n{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\\{(x,y,z)\\,:\\,xy>0,z\\ne 0\\}.\n$$\n\n- Similarly, the domain of ${f}_{y}=\\frac{x{e}^{\\sqrt{xy}}}{2z\\sqrt{xy}}$ is the same\n\n$$\n{D}_{{f}_{y}}=\\{(x,y,z)\\,:\\,xy>0,z\\ne 0\\}.\n$$\n\n- The function ${f}_{z}=-\\frac{{e}^{\\sqrt{xy}}}{{z}^{2}}$ is defined only when $xy\\ge 0$ and $z\\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{z}$ is\n\n$$\n{D}_{{f}_{z}}=\\{(x,y,z)\\,:\\,xy\\ge 0,z\\ne 0\\}.\n$$\n\nFinally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\\\  & =\\{(x,y,z)\\,:\\,xy\\ge 0,z\\ne 0\\}\\cap \\{(x,y,z)\\,:\\,xy>0,z\\ne 0\\} \\\\  & =\\{(x,y,z)\\,:\\,xy>0,z\\ne 0\\}.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186409559 :question/id #uuid "5744243e-c58b-5537-916f-bee0cb473253" :question/math-academy-id "q-132654" defined *and* the partial derivative is defined.\n\nFor example, let's consider the function $f(x,y) = \\ln(xy).$ We wish to determine the set of values $(x,y)$ on which the partial derivative $\\dfrac{\\partial f}{\\partial x}$ exists.\n\nFirst, we need to find the domain of $f$ since we cannot differentiate $f$ at any point that lies outside of its domain. The natural logarithm is defined only for positive inputs, so the domain of $f$ is \n\n$$\nD_f = \\{ (x,y)\\, : \\, xy > 0 \\}.\n$$\n\nNext, we compute the partial derivative:\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\partial f}{\\partial x} = \\dfrac{1}{x}\n$$\n\nThe partial derivative $\\dfrac{\\partial f}{\\partial x}$ (also denoted $f_x$) is not defined at $x=0.$ So, the domain of $f_x$ is\n\n$$\nD_{f_x} = \\{ (x,y)\\, : \\, x \\ne 0 \\}.\n$$\n\nTo compute the set where  $\\dfrac{\\partial f}{\\partial x}$ exists, we take the intersection of the domain of the original function $(D_f)$ with the domain of the partial derivative $(D_{f_x})$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} & =\\{(x,y)\\,:\\,xy>0\\}\\cap \\{(x,y)\\,:\\,x\\ne 0\\} \\\\  & =\\{(x,y)\\,:\\,xy>0\\}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we conclude that $\\dfrac{\\partial f}{\\partial x}$ exists on the set $\\{ (x,y)\\, : \\, xy \\gt 0 \\}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f4cc9d43-0b3e-5cd2-8e04-c1f0f43e9e2a" :step/math-academy-id 11429 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125314}} {:db/id 17592186125314 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125742 :tutorial/content "From single-variable calculus, if a function $y=f(x)$ is differentiable at a point, then it is continuous at that point.\n\nBut for a multivariable function, even if all partial derivatives are defined at a certain point, it **does not mean** that the function is continuous at that point!\n\nThe reason why partial differentiability does not imply continuity in the case of a multivariable function is that\n\n- the existence of the partial derivatives $f_x$ and $f_y$ depend only on the behavior of $f$ parallel to the $x$- and $y$-axes, whereas\n\n- the continuity of $f$ depends on its behavior as we approach $(x_0,y_0)$ from any direction.\n\nFor example, let's consider the following multivariable function:\n\n![](images/cb/cb5aad599789d1e317ff3ddc07eaa418e80469307f67e98e2108660fc7d15701.svg)\n\nThe function $f$ is defined at the point $(0,0)\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\nf(0,0)=0\n$$\n\nLikewise, the partial derivatives $f_x$ and $f_y$ are both defined at the point $(0,0).$ We can compute them using the limit definition of the partial derivative, as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,0) & ={lim}_{h\\to 0}\\frac{1}{h}[f(0+h,0)-f(0,0)] \\\\  & ={lim}_{h\\to 0}\\frac{1}{h}[\\frac{(h)(0)}{{h}^{2}+{0}^{2}}-0] \\\\  & ={lim}_{h\\to 0}\\frac{1}{h}[0-0] \\\\  & =0 \\\\ {f}_{y}(0,0) & ={lim}_{h\\to 0}\\frac{1}{h}[f(0,0+h)-f(0,0)] \\\\  & ={lim}_{h\\to 0}\\frac{1}{h}[\\frac{(0)(h)}{{0}^{2}+{h}^{2}}-0] \\\\  & ={lim}_{h\\to 0}\\frac{1}{h}[0-0] \\\\  & =0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo the partial derivatives both exist at $(0,0).$ We will now show that the function is not continuous at $(0,0).$\n\nFor the function $f$ to be continuous at $(0,0),$ the limit of the function must be equal to the function value, regardless of the path taken. So, we must have\n\n$$\n\\lim\\limits_{(x,y) \\to (0,0)}  f(x,y) = f(0,0) =0.\n$$\n\nHowever, this is not the case here. When we evaluate the limit along the path $y=x,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{lim}_{(x,y)\\to (0,0)\\,\\,y=x}f(x,y) & ={lim}_{y\\to 0}\\frac{x\\cdot x}{{x}^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\\\  & ={lim}_{y\\to 0}\\frac{{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}} \\\\  & ={lim}_{y\\to 0}\\frac{1}{2} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2} \\\\  & \\ne 0.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, our function $f(x,y)$ is *not* continuous at the point $(0,0),$ even though both of its partial derivatives exist there." :tutorial/id #uuid "ca47070b-a1d3-53ad-8f57-2dbd4e770dce" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2533 :tutorial/title "Partial Differentiability Does Not statements one-by-one. \n\n- Statement I is false. If we substitute $(1,-1)$ into $f$, we get\n\n$$\nf(1,-1)={e}^{\\sqrt{(1)(-1)}}=-{e}^{\\sqrt{-1}}\n$$\n\nwhich is undefined since we have a negative number under the radical.\n\n- Statement II is true. If we substitute $(0,1)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get\n\n$$\n{f}_{x}(0,1)=1\\cdot \\frac{{e}^{\\sqrt{0\\cdot 1}}}{2\\sqrt{0\\cdot 1}}=\\frac{{e}^{0}}{2\\sqrt{0}}=\\frac{1}{0},\n$$\n\nwhich is undefined (-\\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\\\  & =-\\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, let's examine the statements one-by-one.\n\n- Statement I is true. =\\frac{∂}{∂y}\\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2) \\\\  & =\\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, let's examine the statements one-by-one.\n\n- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(0,2)$, where we have \n\n$$\nf(0,2)=\\operatorname{ln}⁡({0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2)=\\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\n$$\n\nand both partial derivatives are also defined at $(0,2):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,2) & =\\frac{2(0)}{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2}=0 \\\\ {f}_{y}(0,2) & =\\frac{2(2)}{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2}=2\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(1,1)$ into $f$, we get\n\n$$\nf(1,0)=\\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2}+{1}^{2}-2)=\\operatorname{ln}⁡(0)\n$$\n\nwhich is undefined since $\\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$ \\\\  & =\\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2} \\\\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\\frac{∂}{∂y}\\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2) \\\\  & =\\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, let's examine the statements one-by-one.\n\n- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(0,2)$, where we have \n\n$$\nf(0,2)=\\operatorname{ln}⁡({0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2)=\\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\n$$\n\nand both partial derivatives are also defined at $(0,2):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,2) & =\\frac{2(0)}{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2}=0 \\\\ {f}_{y}(0,2) & =\\frac{2(2)}{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2}=2\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(1,0)$ into $f$, we get\n\n$$\nf(1,0)=\\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2}+{0}^{2}-2)=\\operatorname{ln}⁡(-1)\n$$\n\nwhich is undefined since $\\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$ Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.\n\n- Statement III is also false. If we substitute $(1,1)$ into $f$, we get\n\n$$\nf(1,0)=\\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2}+{1}^{2}-2)=\\operatorname{ln}⁡(0)\n$$\n\nwhich is undefined since $\\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$ \\frac{1}{2\\sqrt{x}} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2{y}^{2}\\sqrt{x}} \\\\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\\frac{∂}{∂y}(\\frac{\\sqrt{x}}{{y}^{2}}) \\\\  & =\\sqrt{x}\\cdot \\frac{∂}{∂y}(\\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}) \\\\  & =\\sqrt{x}\\cdot (-\\frac{2}{{y}^{3}}) \\\\  & =-\\frac{2\\sqrt{x}}{{y}^{3}}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, let's examine the statements one-by-one.\n\n- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(4,2)$, where we have \n\n$$\nf(4,2)=\\frac{\\sqrt{4}}{{2}^{2}}=\\frac{1}{2},\n$$\n\nand both partial derivatives are also defined at $(4,2):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(4,2) & =\\frac{1}{2({2}^{2})\\sqrt{4}}=\\frac{1}{16} \\\\ {f}_{y}(4,2) & =-\\frac{2\\sqrt{4}}{{2}^{3}}=-\\frac{1}{2}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(0,2)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get\n\n$$\n{f}_{x}(0,2)=\\frac{1}{2({2}^{2})\\sqrt{0}}=\\frac{1}{0},\n$$\n\nwhich is undefined since we have division by zero.\n\n- Statement III is true. :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}xy{z}^{2} & =6-z \\\\ xy{z}^{2}+z & =6\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nIf we set $f(x,y,z)=xy{z}^{2}+z$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=6.$ \n\nRecall that the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as\n\n$$\n∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\\,y-{y}_{0},\\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.\n$$\n\nNow, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(1,1,2):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}∇\\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\\,k \\\\  & =\\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy{z}^{2}+z)\\text{ }i+\\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy{z}^{2}+z)\\text{ }j+\\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy{z}^{2}+z)\\text{ }k \\\\  & =(y{z}^{2})\\text{ }i+(x{z}^{2})\\text{ }j+(2xyz+1)\\text{ }k \\\\ ∇\\,f(1,1,2) & =(1)(2)^{2}\\text{ }i+(1)(2)^{2}\\text{ }j+(2(1)(1)(2)+1)\\text{ }k \\\\  & =4\\,i+4j+5\\,k \\\\  & =⟨4,4,5⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\\,y-{y}_{0},\\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\\\ ∇f(1,1,2)\\cdot ⟨x-1,\\,y-1,\\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\\\ ⟨4,4,5⟩\\cdot ⟨x-1,\\,y-1,\\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\\\ 4(x-1)+4(y-1)+5(z-2) & =0 \\\\ 4x+4y+5z-18 & =0\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186237933 :question/id #uuid "1ad56de2-2034-5a41-8c24-d9e39c97ae51" :question/math-academy-id "q-102718"} {:db/id 17592186323850 :question/id #uuid as\n\n$$\n∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\\,y-{y}_{0},\\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.\n$$\n\n \n\nNow, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(4,2,-2):$ =\\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xyz)\\text{ }i+\\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xyz)\\text{ }j+\\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+xyz)\\text{ }k \\\\  & =(2x+yz)\\text{ }i+xz\\text{ }j+xy\\text{ }k \\\\ ∇\\,f(4,2,-2) & =(2(4)+2(-2))\\text{ }i+4(-2)\\text{ }j+4(2)\\text{ }k \\\\  & =4\\,i-8j+8\\,k \\\\  & =⟨4,-8,8⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nFinally, we can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to surface $f (x, y, z) = k,$ where $k$ is a constant, at some point $\\mathbf x_0 = (x_0, y_0, z_0).$ \n\nAs an example, consider the function\n\n$$\nf(x,y,z) = x^2 +y^2+z.\n$$\n\n \n\nSuppose that we wish to find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=  (1,1, 2).$ \n\nEvaluating $f$ at the point $(1,1,2),$ we get\n\n$$\nf(x,y,z) = (1)^2 +(1)^2+2 = 4.\n$$\n\n \n\nSo, the equation of our level surface is\n\n$$\nx^2 +y^2+z = 4.\n$$\n\nNow, to find the equation of the tangent plane to this surface at $(1,1,2),$ we can use the following result:\n\n  *Given a hypersurface $w = f(x,y,z)$ and a point $\\mathbf x_0 = (x_0,y_0,z_0)$ that lies in the domain of $f$, the gradient $\\nabla \\! f (\\mathbf x_0)$ is normal to the tangent plane of the level surface $f (x, y, z) = k$ at the point $\\mathbf x_0$*. \n\n![](images/11/1140e80fbb2efd684311cb7625e5b0be361d6fb951036253f57b9e51234de3ee.png)\n\n       \n\nWe can now find the equation of the tangent plane to our level surface.\n\nFirst, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $\\mathbf x_0 = (1,1,2)\\mathbin{:}$ \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}∇\\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}\\,i+{f}_{y}\\,j+{f}_{z}\\,k \\\\  & =\\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+z)\\text{ }i+\\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+z)\\text{ }j+\\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+z)\\text{ }k \\\\  & =2x\\text{ }i+2y\\text{ }j+k \\\\ ∇f(1,1,2) & =2(1)\\text{ }i+2(1)\\text{ }j+k \\\\  & =2\\text{ }i+2\\text{ }j+k \\\\  & =⟨2,\\,2,1⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nFinally,  we write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane:\n\n$$\n\\eqalign{\n\\nabla f(x_0,y_0,z_0) \\cdot \\langle x-x_0, \\: y-y_0, \\: z-z_0 \\rangle & = 0 \\[3pt]\n\\nabla f(1,1,2) \\cdot \\langle x-1, \\: y-1, \\: z-2 \\rangle & = 0 \\[3pt]\n\\langle 2,\\:2,\\:1\\rangle\\cdot \\langle x-1, y-1, z-2\\rangle &= 0\\[3pt]\n      2(x-1)+ 2(y-1) + (z-2) & =0\\\n      2x +2y +z -6&=0   \n}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=1$ and $y=1$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}-2x+2y+z & =6 \\\\ -2(1)+2(1)+z & =6 \\\\ z & =6.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, we get the point $Q(1,1,6)$ which lies on the plane.\n\nComputing $\\overset{\\to }{PQ},$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\overset{\\to }{PQ} & =⟨1,1,6⟩-⟨-1,4,-5⟩ \\\\  & =⟨2,-3,11⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe also need a normal vector to the plane. :question/math-academy-id "q-129166" :question/problem "Find the shortest distance between the point $P(-2,3,-6)$ and the plane $Π$ with equation $-x+2y+2z=8.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=-2$ and $y=1$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}-x+2y+2z & =8 \\\\ -1(-2)+2(1)+2z & =8 \\\\ 2z & =4 \\\\ z & =2.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, we get the point $Q(-2,1,2)$ which lies on the plane.\n\nComputing $\\overset{\\to }{PQ},$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\overset{\\to }{PQ} & =⟨-2,1,2⟩-⟨-2,3,-6⟩ \\\\  & =⟨0,-2,8⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨-1,2,2⟩.$ \n\nFinally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\\overset{\\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}d & =|{\\text{comp}}_{n}\\,\\overset{\\to }{PQ}| \\\\  & =\\frac{|\\overset{\\to }{PQ}\\cdot n|}{|n|} \\\\  & =\\frac{|0\\cdot (-1)+(-2)\\cdot 2+8\\cdot 2|}{\\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\\\  & =\\frac{|0-4+16|}{\\sqrt{1+4+4}} \\\\  & denominator of $9.$\n\nFirst, we write $3$ as an improper fraction:\n\n$$\n\\frac{3}{1}\n$$\n\nThen we put this fraction over a denominator of $9$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $9:$\n\n$$\n\\frac{3\\times 9}{1\\times 9}=\\frac{27}{9}\n$$\n\nSo now, we have to find:\n\n$$\n\\frac{27}{9}+\\frac{17}{9}\n$$\n\nTo add two fractions with like denominators, we add the numerators and keep the denominators the same:\n\n$$\n\\frac{27}{9}+\\frac{17}{9}=\\frac{27+17}{9}=\\frac{44}{9}\n$$\n\nExpressing our answer as a mixed number, we multiply two-digit numbers.\n\nTo illustrate, let's use the standard algorithm to compute $12\\times 13$.\n\nRecall that ${\\color{blue}1}{\\color{red}3}$ in expanded form is ${\\color{blue}10} + {\\color{red}3}$. The idea is to first multiply $12$ by ${\\color{red}3}$, then by ${\\color{blue}10}$, and add the results.\n\nWe write one number above the other as follows:\n\n$$\n1\\begin{vmatrix}2 \\\\ \\cdot\\end{vmatrix}0\\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 & 3\\end{vmatrix}36 + 120 = 156\n$$\n\nFirst, we multiply the top number ($12$) by the value in the ones place of the second number ($\\bbox[2px, lightgray]{3}$), writing the result under the line:\n\n$$\n1\\begin{vmatrix}2 \\\\ \\cdot\\end{vmatrix}0\\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1\\end{vmatrix}3; 3 \\mid 6 \\mid 12 \\cdot 3 = 36000\n$$\n\nNext, we multiply $12$ by $\\bbox[2px, lightgray]{1}0$. :step/math-academy-id 45216} {:db/id 17592186199367 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199497 :tutorial/content "We saw how to compare fraction models using common denominators in a previous lesson. In this lesson, we'll learn how to carry out these processes without models.\n\nFor example, suppose we have the following two fractions:\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{1}{\\color{blue}3} \\qquad \\dfrac{4}{\\color{red}6}\n$$\n\nWhich of them is larger?\n\nAt the moment, it's difficult to compare them as they don't have a common denominator. Therefore, we must *create* a common denominator.\n\nNotice that our denominators are ${\\color{blue}3}$ and ${\\color{red}{6}}$, and ${\\color{red}{6}}$ is a multiple of ${\\color{blue}3}$. In fact,\n\n$$\n{\\color{red}{6}} = {\\color{purple}{2}} \\times {\\color{blue}3}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we can create a common denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of the *first* fraction by ${\\color{purple}{2}}$, as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\frac{1}{3} &= \\frac{1 \\cdot 2}{3 \\cdot 2} = \\frac{2}{6}\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, we now have the following two fractions:\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{2}{\\color{red}6} \\qquad \\dfrac{4}{\\color{red}6}\n$$\n\nFrom here, it's easy to see that the second fraction is larger. If we want the final answer to be an improper fraction, then we can proceed by turning the whole number into an improper fraction.\n\nFor example, let's find\n\n$$\n2+\\dfrac{1}{\\color{blue}5}\n$$\n\nas an improper fraction.\n\nWe start by writing $2$ as an improper fraction with $1$ in the denominator:\n\n$$\n2 =\\dfrac{2}{1}\n$$\n\nThen, we put this fraction over a denominator of $\\color{blue}5$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by ${\\color{blue}5}$:\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{2\\times {\\color{blue}{5}}}{1\\times {\\color{blue}{5}}} = \\dfrac{10}{\\color{blue}5}\n$$\n\nNow, we can add the two numbers:\n\n$$\n2 + \\frac{1}{5} = \\frac{10}{5}_(⏟)_(2) + \\frac{1}{5} = \\frac{11}{5}\n$$\n\nAnd we're done!\n\nTo use some math jargon, we put the numbers $2$ and\n\n$$\n\\dfrac 1{\\color{blue}5}\n$$\n\nover a **common denominator** of ${\\color{blue}5}$ before adding them.\n\nNotice that this process is very similar to using fraction models.\n\n![](images/cb/cbe49aa64f7d53911592001c5d93e8cde826ac46dabf2ba9c5e9579738ce6ebd.png)\n\nTo add $2$ to\n\n$$\n\\dfrac 1{\\color{blue}5}\n$$\n\nusing a model, we split each whole into ${\\color{blue}5}$ equal parts. When we do, we see that there are $11$ shaded parts in total. So we arrive at the same answer:\n\n$$\n2 +\\dfrac{1}{\\color{blue}5} = \\dfrac{11}{{\\color{blue}5}}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "cf351f38-5bcb-5302-93d1-22730dbb7ef1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8974 :tutorial/title "Adding Proper Fractions and Whole Numbers"} :step/id #uuid "ea2f4743-4aac-5c5c-9b9b-7bd499491aaa" :step/math-academy-id 116991 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074574}} {:db/id 17592186074574 :step/content {:db/id 17592186073697 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073502 :question/id #uuid "ba9e10b8-4601-5f2a-8681-0ab478bdb081" :question/math-academy-id "e-14511"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "aa913057-6bdb-5708-b094-da7880696db4" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050311}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186073993} {:db/id 17592186074302}] :knowledge-point/title "Expressing a Sum as an Improper Fraction"} :step/id #uuid "4252d06c-1791-5c1d-a068-07b9fbfc75c7" :step/math-academy-id 116992 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074575}} {:db/id 17592186074575 :step/content {:db/id 17592186075058 :tutorial/content "How do we write\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{7}{\\color{blue}4} + 5\n$$\n\nas a mixed number?\n\nNotice that we cannot write\n\n$$\n5\\,\\dfrac 7 4\n$$\n\nbecause\n\n$$\n\\dfrac 7 4\n$$\n\nis an improper fraction. to find the following sum:\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{7}{4} + \\dfrac{20}{4}\n$$\n\nTo add two fractions with like denominators, we add the numerators and keep the denominators the same:\n\n$$\n\\frac{7}{4} + \\frac{20}{4} = \\frac{7 + 20}{4} = \\frac{27}{4}\n$$\n\nFinally, we convert this to a mixed number:\n\n$$\n27 \\div 4 = 6 \\, \\textrm{R} \\, 3 = 6 \\, \\dfrac{3}{4}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid **III.** $⟨a,b⟩\\in R$ for any $a,b\\in {C}^{n}$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties:\n\n- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\\alpha \\in C,$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\\,$ and $\\,⟨\\alpha a,b⟩=\\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$\n\n- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\\alpha \\in C,$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\\,$ and $\\,⟨a,\\alpha b⟩=\\overset{―}{\\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$\n\n- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\\in {C}^{n},$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$\n\n- It is positive-definite. Indeed, the inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry.\n\n- Statement II is false. To factor out a constant multiple from the second argument, we must change it to its complex conjugate.\n\n- Statement III is false. The inner product over $C$ is a complex number in general.\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I only.\""} {:db/id 17592186134552 :question/id #uuid "f527ee5b-22e1-5696-9bd4-0e444190bb44" {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Given that $⟨\\,\\cdot \\,,\\,\\cdot \\,⟩$ is the standard Hermitian inner product over $C,$ find $⟨a,\\,b-(1+3\\text{i})c⟩$ if \n\n$\\,$ $⟨b,a⟩=1+\\text{i}\\,$ and $\\,⟨a,c⟩=2.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties. \n\n- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\\alpha \\in C,$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\\,$ and $\\,⟨\\alpha a,b⟩=\\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$\n\n- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\\alpha \\in C,$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\\,$ and $\\,⟨a,\\alpha b⟩=\\overset{―}{\\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$\n\n- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\\in {C}^{n},$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$\n\n- It is positive-definite. For any $a\\in {C}^{n},$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$\n\nFirst, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ is antilinear in the second argument:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}⟨a,\\,b-(1+3\\text{i})c⟩ & =⟨a,b⟩-⟨a,(1+3\\text{i})c⟩ \\\\  & =⟨a,b⟩-(\\overset{―}{1+3\\text{i}})⟨a,c⟩ \\\\  & =⟨a,b⟩-(1-3\\text{i})⟨a,c⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}⟨a,b⟩-(1-3\\text{i})⟨a,c⟩ & =\\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}-(1-3\\text{i})⟨a,c⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we substitute the values for $⟨b,a⟩$ and $⟨a,c⟩:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}-(1-3\\text{i})⟨a,c⟩ & =\\overset{―}{1+\\text{i}}-(1-3\\text{i})\\cdot 2 \\\\  & =1-\\text{i}-2+6\\text{i} \\\\  & =-1+5\\text{i}\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186272228 :question/id #uuid $⟨a,\\,(4-\\text{i})b+c⟩$ if  \n\n$\\,$ $⟨b,a⟩=-1-\\text{i}\\,$ and $\\,⟨a,c⟩=5.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties. \n\n- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\\alpha \\in C,$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\\,$ and $\\,⟨\\alpha a,b⟩=\\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$\n\n- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\\alpha \\in C,$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\\,$ and $\\,⟨a,\\alpha b⟩=\\overset{―}{\\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$\n\n- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\\in {C}^{n},$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$\n\n- It is positive-definite. For any $a\\in {C}^{n},$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$\n\nFirst, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ is antilinear in the second argument:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}⟨a,\\,(4-\\text{i})b+c⟩ & =⟨a,(4-\\text{i})b⟩+⟨a,c⟩ \\\\  & =(\\overset{―}{4-\\text{i}})⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩ \\\\  & =(4+\\text{i})⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}(4+\\text{i})⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c\\text{ }⟩ & =(4+\\text{i})\\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}+⟨a,c⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we substitute the values for $⟨b,a⟩$ and $⟨a,c⟩:$  \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}(4+\\text{i})\\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}+⟨a,c⟩ & =(4+\\text{i})\\cdot (\\overset{―}{-1-\\text{i}})+5 \\\\  & =(4+\\text{i})\\cdot (-1+\\text{i})+5 \\\\  & =-5+3\\text{i}+5 \\\\  & =3\\text{i}\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186360769 :question/id #uuid "57383a07-e3d6-5131-921a-e0eecd15115d" :question/math-academy-id "q-97200"} {:db/id 17592186360770 :question/id #uuid "0821bac1-cf18-5c7e-985e-332add7238bf" :question/math-academy-id "q-97209"} {:db/id 17592186360771 :question/id #uuid "589fd79e-dcf6-5066-9979-9da6a025b573" :question/math-academy-id "q-97215"} {:db/id 17592186049306} {:db/id 17592186428650 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. $V:$\n\n$$\n{f}_{1}(t)=\\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\\,{f}_{2}(t)=\\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\\,g(t)={sin}^{2}⁡t-\\operatorname{cos}⁡t\n$$\n\nFind the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $S=\\text{Span}{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)}$ given that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\\text{Span}{{f}_{2}(t)}$ equals $-\\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$" :question/worked-solution "Since the set ${{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by\n\n$$\n{\\text{proj}}_{S}\\,g(t)={\\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\\,g(t)+{\\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\\,g(t).\n$$\n\nWe are given that ${\\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\\,g(t)=-\\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\\text{Span}{{f}_{1}(t)}.$ This can be computed as\n\n$$\n{\\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\\,g(t)=\\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}\\,{f}_{1}(t).\n$$\n\n \n\nIn our case, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩ & ={\\int }_{-\\pi }^{\\pi }g(t){f}_{1}(t)\\,\\text{d}t \\\\  & ={\\int }_{-\\pi }^{\\pi }({sin}^{2}⁡t-\\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\\cdot \\operatorname{sin}⁡t\\,\\text{d}t \\\\  & ={\\int }_{-\\pi }^{\\pi }\\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\\,\\text{d}t\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNotice that $\\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ is an odd function, while ${sin}^{2}⁡t-\\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is even. Hence, their product $\\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\\operatorname{cos}⁡t)$ must be an odd function. Now, since we have an integral over the interval $[-\\pi ,\\pi ],$ which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that\n\n$$\n{\\int }_{-\\pi }^{\\pi }\\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\\,\\text{d}t=0.\n$$\n\n  \n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n{\\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\\,g(t)=\\frac{0}{⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}\\cdot \\operatorname{sin}⁡t=0.\n$$\n\nFinally,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\text{proj}}_{S}\\,g(t) & ={\\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\\,g(t)+{\\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\\,g(t) \\\\  & =0-\\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\\\  & =-\\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186134562 :question/id #uuid "2b04e926-3f28-54fc-a52b-7c1f046fb290" :question/math-academy-id "q-98689"} {:db/id 17592186240950 :question/problem "$$\n⟨\\text{_______}\\,,\\,-\\operatorname{sin}⁡x\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,\\,-\\operatorname{sin}⁡x\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ⟩\n$$\n\nThe fundamental vector product of the What is the $1$st component of the product?" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $y=\\operatorname{sin}⁡x\\ge 0$ for all $x\\in [0,\\pi ].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}r=⟨x,f(x)\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,\\,f(x)\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ⟩,\\,(x,\\theta )\\in D\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhere $f(x)=\\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ and\n\n$$\nD={(x,\\theta )\\,:\\,0\\le x\\le \\pi ,\\,0\\le \\theta <2\\pi }.\n$$\n\nWe now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨\\frac{∂x}{∂x},\\,\\frac{∂y}{∂x},\\,\\frac{∂z}{∂x}⟩=⟨1,\\,{f}^{′}\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,\\,{f}^{′}\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ⟩ \\\\ {r}_{\\theta }^{′} & =⟨\\frac{∂x}{∂\\theta },\\,\\frac{∂y}{∂\\theta },\\,\\frac{∂z}{∂\\theta }⟩=⟨0,\\,-f\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ,\\,f\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, the fundamental vector product is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\\times {r}_{\\theta }^{′} & =|\\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\\\ 1 & {f}^{′}\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  & {f}^{′}\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  \\\\ 0 & -f\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  & f\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =⟨|\\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  & {f}^{′}\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  \\\\ -f\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  & f\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\end{aligned}|,\\,-|\\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  \\\\ 0 & f\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\end{aligned}|,\\,|\\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  \\\\ 0 & -f\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\end{aligned}|⟩ \\\\  & =⟨f{f}^{′}{cos}^{2}⁡\\theta +f{f}^{′}{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta ,\\,-f\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,\\,-f\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ⟩ \\\\  & =⟨f{f}^{′},\\,-f\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,\\,-f\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince $f=\\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ we obtain ${f}^{′}=\\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\\times {r}_{\\theta }^{′}=⟨\\operatorname{sin}⁡x\\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\\,-\\operatorname{sin}⁡x\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,\\,-\\operatorname{sin}⁡x\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id )\\,:\\,1\\le z\\le 10,\\,0\\le \\theta <2\\pi }.\n$$\n\nWe now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′} & },\\,\\frac{∂y}{∂\\theta },\\,\\frac{∂z}{∂\\theta }⟩=⟨f\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,\\,-f\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ,\\,0⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, the fundamental vector product f\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  & -f\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  & 0\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =⟨|\\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  & 1 \\\\ -f\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  & {f}^{′}\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  \\\\ f\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  & -f\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\end{aligned}|⟩ \\\\  & =⟨f\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ,\\,f\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,\\,-{f}^{′}f{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta -{f}^{′}f{cos}^{2}⁡\\theta ⟩ \\\\  & =⟨f\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ,\\,f\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,\\,-{f}^{′}f⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince $f=\\sqrt{z-1},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}=\\frac{1}{2\\sqrt{z-1}}.$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′}\\times {r}_{\\theta [{:db/id 17592186172933 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173175 :tutorial/content "Consider the planar curve $y=e^{-x}$ defined on the interval $x \\in [0,2],$ as shown below.\n\n![](images/a8/a8ce2449af085548fecc543fbd5ccfec0e8024344547b2a7825f3a6e9ccf63d4.png)\n\nBy rotating this curve $2\\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis, we get a **surface of revolution**:\n\n![](images/88/88c9c1ec629ab9967cc011aaadafebea255cd50abee9c3730bed4f53f671c71b.png)\n\nWe can parametrize this surface in the following way:\n\n- We take a point $P$ on the surface with $x$-coordinate equal to $x_0$ for some fixed $x_0 \\in [0,2].$\n\n- Now, by taking the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=x_0,$ we get a circle of radius $e^{-x_0}.$\n\n![](images/f1/f1e2cf1c571a21e06f1b25f99a64b5529fea8c65c897b3f225cfd0d307d725d7.png)\n\n \nThis circle can be parameterized as follows:\n\n$$\n\\mathbf r(x_0, \\theta) = \\big\\langle {\\color{black}x_0}, \\: e^{-x_0} \\, \\cos{\\theta}, \\: e^{-x_0} \\, \\sin{\\theta} \\big\\rangle,\n\\quad  \\theta \\in [0,2\\pi).\n$$\n\n- Finally, by allowing $x_0$ to vary over the interval $[0, 2],$ these circles will trace out the surface of revolution. Therefore, our parameterization is\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{r}(x,\\theta) = \\big\\langle x, \\: e^{-x} \\cos{\\theta}, \\: e^{-x}\\sin{\\theta} \\big\\rangle,\n\\quad \nx \\in [0,2], \n\\quad\n\\theta \\in [0,2\\pi).\n$$\n\nLet's now describe some general formulas for parametrizing surfaces of revolution." :tutorial/id #uuid "9bd13796-1bf7-5a1b-a9f4-87567fd6998c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5305 17592186173186 :tutorial/content "Consider the point $(x(y),y,0)$ that lies on the curve $x=x(y)\\geq 0$ for $y\\in [a,b]$ in the $xy$-plane. Rotating this point by $2\\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis generates a circle, as shown below.\n\n![](images/98/981ed341198c54e5dffeae770d13b3d46222ad429d0315ecd057b43995b4c0d6.png)\n\nThe pair $(\\textrm{circle}_1,\\textrm{circle}_2)$ denotes any parametrization of a circle of radius $x(y)$ with parameter $y.$\n\nUsing arguments similar to those seen earlier, the corresponding surface of revolution can be parametrized as\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{r} = \\big\\langle x(y) \\cos\\theta, \\: y, \\: x(y) \\sin\\theta \\big\\rangle, \\quad y\\in[a,b], \\quad \\theta\\in [0,2\\pi).\n$$\n\n**Note:** Since a parametrization of a circle is not unique, we can obtain different parameterizations of our surface of revolution. For example, the following is also a valid parameterization:\n\\[ \n\\mathbf{r} = \\big\\langle x(y) \\sin\\theta, \\: y, \\: x(y) \\cos\\theta \\big\\rangle, \\quad y\\in[a,b], \\quad \\theta\\in [0,2\\pi). \n\\]\n\nSimilarly, the rotation of a point $(0,y,z(y))$ on the curve $z=z(y)\\geq 0$ in the $yz$-plane about the $y$-axis can be visualized as follows:\n\n![](images/59/5936d54e55c151ec2d9786a3ce2bd807970a71c10a21974562fd601bf50dfd37.png)\n\nThe corresponding surface of revolution can be parametrized as\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{r} = \\big\\langle z(y) \\cos\\theta, \\: y, \\: z(y) \\sin\\theta \\big\\rangle, \\quad y\\in[a,b], \\quad \\theta\\in [0,2\\pi).\n$$\n\nAs mentioned previously, neither of these parameterizations is unique.\n\n**Note:** Since a parametrization of a circle is not unique, we can obtain different parameterizations of our surface of revolution. For example, the following is also a valid parameterization:\n\\[\n\\mathbf{r} = \\big\\langle z(y) \\sin\\theta, \\: y, \\: z(y) \\cos\\theta \\big\\rangle, \\quad y\\in[a,b], \\quad \\theta\\in [0,2\\pi). \n\\]" :tutorial/id #uuid "ae882ec8-1ebd-5277-8224-b440b433c8ee" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5507 :tutorial/title "Formulas for Rotation About the y-Axis"} :step/id #uuid "Recall that if $S$ is a surface parametrized by a differentiable vector-valued function\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \\big\\langle x(u,v), \\: y(u,v), \\: z(u,v) \\big\\rangle\n$$\n\ndefined over a region $D$ in the $uv$-plane, then the surface area of $S$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\iint\\limits_{S} \\: \\textrm{d}S =  \\iint\\limits_{D} \\| \\mathbf{r}'_ u \\times \\mathbf{r}'_v  \\| \\: \\textrm{d}A,\n$$\n\nwhere $\\mathbf{r}'_ u \\times \\mathbf{r}'_v$ is the fundamental vector product of the surface.\n\nLet's apply this formula to find the surface area generated by a surface of revolution.\n\nSuppose that the curve [math]y=f(x)[/math] for [math]x \\in [a,b][/math] is rotated [math]2\\pi[/math] radians about the [math]x[/math]-axis. The corresponding surface of revolution can be parametrized as\n\n\\begin{align*}\n\\mathbf{r} = \\big\\langle x, \\: f(x) \\cos\\theta, \\: f(x) \\sin\\theta \\big\\rangle, \\quad (x,\\theta) \\in D, \n\\end{align*}\n\nwhere [math]D= \\big\\{ (x,\\theta) \\: : \\: x \\in[a,b], \\: \\theta \\in [0,2\\pi) \\big\\}.[/math] How can we find the area of this surface?\n\nFirst, we now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:\n\n\\begin{align*}\n\\mathbf{r}'_x \n&= \\bigg\\langle \\dfrac{\\partial x}{\\partial x}, \\: \\dfrac{\\partial y}{\\partial x}, \\: \\dfrac{\\partial z}{\\partial x} \\bigg\\rangle \n= \\big\\langle 1, \\:f'(x) \\cos\\theta, \\: f'(x) \\sin\\theta \\big\\rangle \\\\[10pt]\n\n\\mathbf{r}'_\\theta \n&= \\bigg\\langle \\dfrac{\\partial x}{\\partial \\theta}, \\: \\dfrac{\\partial y}{\\partial \\theta}, \\: \\dfrac{\\partial z}{\\partial \\theta} \\bigg\\rangle \n= \\big\\langle 0, \\: -f(x) \\sin\\theta, \\: f(x) \\cos\\theta \\big\\rangle\n\\end{align*}\n\nNext, the fundamental vector product is\n\n\\begin{align*}\n\\mathbf{r}'_x \\times \\mathbf{r}'_\\theta \n&= \n\\begin{vmatrix}\n\\mathbf{i} & \\mathbf{j} & \\mathbf{k} \\\\\n1 & f'(x) \\cos\\theta & f'(x) \\sin\\theta \\\\\n0 & -f(x) \\sin\\theta & f(x) \\cos\\theta\n\\end{vmatrix} \\\\[5pt]\n&= \\bigg\\langle \\begin{vmatrix} f'(x) \\cos\\theta & f'(x) \\sin\\theta \\\\ -f(x) \\sin\\theta & f(x) \\cos\\theta \\end{vmatrix}, \\: -\\begin{vmatrix} 1 & f'(x) \\sin\\theta \\\\ 0  & f(x) \\cos\\theta \\end{vmatrix}, \\: \\begin{vmatrix} 1 & f'(x) \\cos\\theta \\\\ 0 & -f(x) \\sin\\theta  \\end{vmatrix} \\bigg\\rangle \\\\[5pt]\n&= \\big\\langle f(x)f'(x)\\cos^2\\theta+f(x)f'(x)\\sin^2\\theta, \\: -f(x) \\cos\\theta, \\: -f(x)\\sin\\theta \\big\\rangle \\\\[5pt]\n&= \\big\\langle f(x)f'(x), \\: -f(x) \\cos\\theta, \\:- f(x)\\sin\\theta \\big\\rangle\n\\end{align*}\n\nand\n\n\\begin{align*}\n\\left\\|  \\mathbf{r}'_y \\times \\mathbf{r}'_\\theta \\right\\|\n&= \\sqrt{\\big( f(x)f'(x) \\big)^2 + \\big( -f(x) \\cos\\theta \\big)^2 + \\big( -f(x)\\sin\\theta \\big)^2 } \\\\[3pt]\n&= \\sqrt{\\big(f(x)\\big)^2\\big(f'(x)\\big)^2 + \\big(f(x)\\big)^2 \\big( \\cos^2\\theta + \\sin^2\\theta \\big) } \\\\[3pt]\n&= \\sqrt{\\big(f(x)\\big)^2\\big(f'(x)\\big)^2 + \\big(f(x)\\big)^2 } \\\\[3pt]\n&= f(x) \\sqrt{1 + \\big(f'(x)\\big)^2 }.\n\\end{align*}\n\nTherefore, the surface area is\n\n\\begin{align*}\nA \n&= \\iint\\limits_S \\,  \\text{d}S \\\\[5pt]\n&= \\iint\\limits_D  \\left\\|  \\mathbf{r}'_y \\times \\mathbf{r}'_\\theta \\right\\|  \\text{d}x\\text{d}\\theta \\\\[5pt]\n&= \\int_{a}^{b} \\int_{0}^{2\\pi} f(x) \\sqrt{1 + \\big(f'(x)\\big)^2 } \\: \\text{d}\\theta \\: \\text{d}x \\\\[5pt]\n&= \\int_{a}^{b} f(x) \\sqrt{1 + \\big(f'(x)\\big)^2} \\: \\text{d}x \\cdot \\int_{0}^{2\\pi}  \\text{d}\\theta \\\\[5pt]\n&= \\int_{a}^{b} f(x) \\sqrt{1 + \\big(f'(x)\\big)^2} \\: \\text{d}x \\cdot \\big[ \\theta \\big]_{0}^{2\\pi}  \\\\[5pt]\n&= 2\\pi \\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\\sqrt{1 + \\big(f'(x)\\big)^2 } \\: \\text{d}x.\n\\end{align*}" :tutorial/id #uuid "79f42de8-4cc4-576a-b367-c08bd87f8bcd" Rotating this point by $2\\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis generates a circle, as shown below.\n\n![](images/86/86cbc06bd3730430665744216a702ed29cc75acae33a569e00636ee53149065d.png)\n\nIn the diagram above, the pair $(\\textrm{circle}_1,\\textrm{circle}_2)$ denotes any parametrization of a circle of radius $y(x)$ with parameter $x.$\n\nIn general, given a curve $y=y(x)\\geq 0$ for $x \\in [a,b]$ that is rotated $2\\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis, the corresponding surface of revolution can be parametrized as\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{r} = \\big\\langle x, \\: y(x) \\cos\\theta, \\: y(x) \\sin\\theta \\big\\rangle, \\quad x\\in[a,b], \\quad \\theta\\in [0,2\\pi).\n$$\n\nSince a parametrization of a circle is not unique, we can obtain different parameterizations of our surface of revolution. For example, the following is also a valid parameterization:\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{r} = \\big\\langle x, \\: y(x) \\sin\\theta, \\: y(x) \\cos\\theta \\big\\rangle, \\quad x\\in[a,b], \\quad \\theta\\in [0,2\\pi)\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3148fb53-9ae7-5747-aa63-b79dd1bc224f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7648 :tutorial/title "Parametrizing a Surface Generated by Rotating y=y(x) About the x-Axis"} :step/id #uuid "93cfa70b-b133-5659-9bce-ab370759c49e" :step/math-academy-id 44408 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173089}} {:db/id 17592186173087 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173255 :tutorial/content "Now consider the point $(x(z),0,z)$ on the curve $x=x(z)\\geq 0$ for $z\\in [a,b]$ in the $xz$-plane. An alternative parametrization is\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{r} = \\big\\langle x, \\: z(x) \\sin\\theta, \\: z(x) \\cos\\theta \\big\\rangle, \\quad z\\in[a,b], \\quad \\theta\\in [0,2\\pi).\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c06437e5-d847-5d03-aac0-497649901444" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7714 :tutorial/title "Parametrizing a Surface Generated by Rotating z=z(x) About the x-Axis"} :step/id #uuid "3100ec93-73c0-5fba-bebc-ee40c07ece7d" :step/math-academy-id 44739 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172934}}] :activity/title "Surfaces of Revolution" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186172185} {:db/id 17592186172933 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173175 :tutorial/content "Consider the planar curve $y=e^{-x}$ defined on the interval $x \\in [0,2],$ as shown below.\n\n![](images/a8/a8ce2449af085548fecc543fbd5ccfec0e8024344547b2a7825f3a6e9ccf63d4.png)\n\nBy rotating this curve $2\\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis, we get a **surface of revolution**:\n\n![](images/88/88c9c1ec629ab9967cc011aaadafebea255cd50abee9c3730bed4f53f671c71b.png)\n\nWe can parametrize this surface in the following way:\n\n- We take a point $P$ on the surface with $x$-coordinate equal to $x_0$ for some fixed $x_0 \\in [0,2].$\n\n- Now, by taking the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=x_0,$ we get a circle of radius $e^{-x_0}.$\n\n![](images/f1/f1e2cf1c571a21e06f1b25f99a64b5529fea8c65c897b3f225cfd0d307d725d7.png)\n\n \nThis circle can be parameterized as follows:\n\n$$\n\\mathbf r(x_0, \\theta) = \\big\\langle {\\color{black}x_0}, \\: e^{-x_0} \\, \\cos{\\theta}, \\: e^{-x_0} \\, \\sin{\\theta} \\big\\rangle,\n\\quad  \\theta \\in [0,2\\pi).\n$$\n\n- Finally, by allowing $x_0$ to vary over the interval $[0, 2],$ these circles will trace out the surface of revolution. Therefore, our parameterization is\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{r}(x,\\theta) = \\big\\langle x, \\: e^{-x} \\cos{\\theta}, \\: e^{-x}\\sin{\\theta} \\big\\rangle,\n\\quad \nx \\in [0,2], \n\\quad\n\\theta \\in [0,2\\pi).\n$$\n\nLet's now describe some general formulas for parametrizing surfaces of revolution." :tutorial/id #uuid "9bd13796-1bf7-5a1b-a9f4-87567fd6998c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5305 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1d490ab1-06f7-5e16-b643-b1b0d8fab4fe" :step/math-academy-id 33155 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173086}} {:db/id 17592186173175 :tutorial/content "Consider the planar curve $y=e^{-x}$ defined on the interval $x \\in [0,2],$ as shown below.\n\n![](images/a8/a8ce2449af085548fecc543fbd5ccfec0e8024344547b2a7825f3a6e9ccf63d4.png)\n\nBy rotating this curve $2\\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis, we get a **surface of revolution**:\n\n![](images/88/88c9c1ec629ab9967cc011aaadafebea255cd50abee9c3730bed4f53f671c71b.png)\n\nWe can parametrize this surface in the following way:\n\n- We take a point $P$ on the surface with $x$-coordinate equal to $x_0$ for some fixed $x_0 \\in [0,2].$\n\n- Now, by taking the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=x_0,$ we get a circle of radius $e^{-x_0}.$\n\n![](images/f1/f1e2cf1c571a21e06f1b25f99a64b5529fea8c65c897b3f225cfd0d307d725d7.png)\n\n \nThis circle can be parameterized as follows:\n\n$$\n\\mathbf r(x_0, \\theta) = \\big\\langle {\\color{black}x_0}, \\: e^{-x_0} \\, \\cos{\\theta}, \\: e^{-x_0} \\, \\sin{\\theta} \\big\\rangle,\n\\quad  \\theta \\in [0,2\\pi).\n$$\n\n- Finally, by allowing $x_0$ to vary over the interval $[0, 2],$ these circles will trace out the surface of revolution. Rotating this point by $2\\pi$ radians about the $z$-axis generates a circle, as shown below.\n\n![](images/50/50473a5407143c7ec49ce8c192c256bbc184703010209767507e4b922e9f4c7b.png)\n\nThe corresponding surface of revolution can be parametrized as\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{r} = \\big\\langle x(z) \\cos\\theta, \\: x(z) \\sin\\theta, \\: z \\big\\rangle, \\quad z\\in[a,b], \\quad \\theta\\in [0,2\\pi).\n$$\n\nFinally, the rotation of a point $(0,y(z),z)$ on a curve $y=y(z)\\geq 0$ in the $yz$-plane about the $z$-axis can be visualized as follows:\n\n![](images/5f/5ff1574db4d105e7d69cc12ed609898d626b4977902f98dbcbcac6633ad56d2b.png)\n\nThe corresponding surface of revolution can be parametrized as\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{r} = \\big\\langle y(z) \\cos\\theta, \\: y(z) \\sin\\theta, \\: z \\big\\rangle, \\quad z\\in[a,b], \\quad \\theta\\in [0,2\\pi).\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9e8a0947-f30a-5da6-9c3b-7b93bdba56bf" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7649 :tutorial/title "Formulas for Rotation About the z-Axis"} :step/id #uuid "6100252f-8102-5700-8f5a-11a2b77335a0" :step/math-academy-id 44409 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172935}} {:db/id 17592186173084 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173253 :tutorial/content "Recall that if $S$ is a surface parametrized by a differentiable vector-valued function\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \\big\\langle x(u,v), \\: y(u,v), \\: z(u,v) \\big\\rangle\n$$\n\ndefined over a region $D$ in the $uv$-plane, then the surface area of $S$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\iint\\limits_{S} \\: \\textrm{d}S =  \\iint\\limits_{D} \\| \\mathbf{r}'_ u \\times \\mathbf{r}'_v  \\| \\: \\textrm{d}A,\n$$\n\nwhere $\\mathbf{r}'_ u \\times \\mathbf{r}'_v$ is the fundamental vector product of the surface.\n\nLet's apply this formula to find the surface area generated by a surface of revolution.\n\nSuppose that the curve [math]y=f(x)[/math] for [math]x \\in [a,b][/math] is rotated [math]2\\pi[/math] radians about the [math]x[/math]-axis. The corresponding surface of revolution can be parametrized as\n\n\\begin{align*}\n\\mathbf{r} = \\big\\langle x, \\: f(x) \\cos\\theta, \\: f(x) \\sin\\theta \\big\\rangle, \\quad (x,\\theta) \\in D, \n\\end{align*}\n\nwhere [math]D= \\big\\{ (x,\\theta) \\: : \\: x \\in[a,b], \\: \\theta \\in [0,2\\pi) \\big\\}.[/math] How can we find the area of this surface?\n\nFirst, we now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:\n\n\\begin{align*}\n\\mathbf{r}'_x \n&= \\bigg\\langle \\dfrac{\\partial x}{\\partial x}, \\: \\dfrac{\\partial y}{\\partial x}, \\: \\dfrac{\\partial z}{\\partial x} \\bigg\\rangle \n= \\big\\langle 1, \\:f'(x) \\cos\\theta, \\: f'(x) \\sin\\theta \\big\\rangle \\\\[10pt]\n\n\\mathbf{r}'_\\theta \n&= \\bigg\\langle \\dfrac{\\partial x}{\\partial \\theta}, \\: \\dfrac{\\partial y}{\\partial \\theta}, \\: \\dfrac{\\partial z}{\\partial \\theta} \\bigg\\rangle \n= \\big\\langle 0, \\: -f(x) \\sin\\theta, \\: f(x) \\cos\\theta \\big\\rangle\n\\end{align*}\n\nNext, the fundamental vector product is\n\n\\begin{align*}\n\\mathbf{r}'_x \\times \\mathbf{r}'_\\theta \n&= \n\\begin{vmatrix}\n\\mathbf{i} & \\mathbf{j} & \\mathbf{k} \\\\\n1 & f'(x) \\cos\\theta & f'(x) \\sin\\theta \\\\\n0 & -f(x) \\sin\\theta & f(x) \\cos\\theta\n\\end{vmatrix} \\\\[5pt]\n&= \\bigg\\langle \\begin{vmatrix} f'(x) \\cos\\theta & f'(x) \\sin\\theta \\\\ -f(x) \\sin\\theta & f(x) \\cos\\theta \\end{vmatrix}, \\: -\\begin{vmatrix} 1 & f'(x) \\sin\\theta \\\\ 0  & f(x) \\cos\\theta \\end{vmatrix}, \\: \\begin{vmatrix} 1 & f'(x) \\cos\\theta \\\\ 0 & -f(x) \\sin\\theta  \\end{vmatrix} \\bigg\\rangle \\\\[5pt]\n&= \\big\\langle f(x)f'(x)\\cos^2\\theta+f(x)f'(x)\\sin^2\\theta, \\: -f(x) \\cos\\theta, \\: -f(x)\\sin\\theta \\big\\rangle \\\\[5pt]\n&= \\big\\langle f(x)f'(x), \\: -f(x) \\cos\\theta, \\:- f(x)\\sin\\theta \\big\\rangle\n\\end{align*}\n\nand\n\n\\begin{align*}\n\\left\\|  \\mathbf{r}'_y \\times \\mathbf{r}'_\\theta \\right\\|\n&= \\sqrt{\\big( f(x)f'(x) \\big)^2 + \\big( -f(x) \\cos\\theta \\big)^2 + \\big( -f(x)\\sin\\theta \\big)^2 } \\\\[3pt]\n&= \\sqrt{\\big(f(x)\\big)^2\\big(f'(x)\\big)^2 + \\big(f(x)\\big)^2 \\big( \\cos^2\\theta + \\sin^2\\theta \\big) } \\\\[3pt]\n&= \\sqrt{\\big(f(x)\\big)^2\\big(f'(x)\\big)^2 + \\big(f(x)\\big)^2 } \\\\[3pt]\n&= f(x) \\sqrt{1 + \\big(f'(x)\\big)^2 }.\n\\end{align*}\n\nTherefore, the surface area is\n\n\\begin{align*}\nA \n&= \\iint\\limits_S \\,  \\text{d}S \\\\[5pt]\n&= \\iint\\limits_D  \\left\\|  \\mathbf{r}'_y \\times \\mathbf{r}'_\\theta \\right\\|  \\text{d}x\\text{d}\\theta \\\\[5pt]\n&= \\int_{a}^{b} \\int_{0}^{2\\pi} f(x) \\sqrt{1 + \\big(f'(x)\\big)^2 } \\: \\text{d}\\theta \\: \\text{d}x \\\\[5pt]\n&= \\int_{a}^{b} f(x) \\sqrt{1 + \\big(f'(x)\\big)^2} \\: \\text{d}x \\cdot \\int_{0}^{2\\pi}  \\text{d}\\theta \\\\[5pt]\n&= \\int_{a}^{b} f(x) \\sqrt{1 + \\big(f'(x)\\big)^2} \\: \\text{d}x \\cdot \\big[ \\theta \\big]_{0}^{2\\pi}  \\\\[5pt]\n&= 2\\pi \\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\\sqrt{1 + \\big(f'(x)\\big)^2 } \\: \\text{d}x.\n\\end{align*}" :tutorial/id #uuid "79f42de8-4cc4-576a-b367-c08bd87f8bcd" 17592186173085}} {:db/id 17592186173253 :tutorial/content "Recall that if $S$ is a surface parametrized by a differentiable vector-valued function\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \\big\\langle x(u,v), \\: y(u,v), \\: z(u,v) \\big\\rangle\n$$\n\ndefined over a region $D$ in the $uv$-plane, then the surface area of $S$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\iint\\limits_{S} \\: \\textrm{d}S =  \\iint\\limits_{D} \\| \\mathbf{r}'_ u \\times \\mathbf{r}'_v  \\| \\: \\textrm{d}A,\n$$\n\nwhere $\\mathbf{r}'_ u \\times \\mathbf{r}'_v$ is the fundamental vector product of the surface.\n\nLet's apply this formula to find the surface area generated by a surface of revolution.\n\nSuppose that the curve [math]y=f(x)[/math] for [math]x \\in [a,b][/math] is rotated [math]2\\pi[/math] radians about the [math]x[/math]-axis. The corresponding surface of revolution can be parametrized as\n\n\\begin{align*}\n\\mathbf{r} = \\big\\langle x, \\: f(x) \\cos\\theta, \\: f(x) \\sin\\theta \\big\\rangle, \\quad (x,\\theta) \\in D, \n\\end{align*}\n\nwhere [math]D= \\big\\{ (x,\\theta) \\: : \\: x \\in[a,b], \\: \\theta \\in [0,2\\pi) \\big\\}.[/math] How can we find the area of this surface?\n\nFirst, we now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:\n\n\\begin{align*}\n\\mathbf{r}'_x \n&= \\bigg\\langle \\dfrac{\\partial x}{\\partial x}, \\: \\dfrac{\\partial y}{\\partial x}, \\: \\dfrac{\\partial z}{\\partial x} \\bigg\\rangle \n= \\big\\langle 1, \\:f'(x) \\cos\\theta, \\: f'(x) \\sin\\theta \\big\\rangle \\\\[10pt]\n\n\\mathbf{r}'_\\theta \n&= \\bigg\\langle \\dfrac{\\partial x}{\\partial \\theta}, \\: \\dfrac{\\partial y}{\\partial \\theta}, \\: \\dfrac{\\partial z}{\\partial \\theta} \\bigg\\rangle \n= \\big\\langle 0, \\: -f(x) \\sin\\theta, \\: f(x) \\cos\\theta \\big\\rangle\n\\end{align*}\n\nNext, the fundamental vector product is\n\n\\begin{align*}\n\\mathbf{r}'_x \\times \\mathbf{r}'_\\theta \n&= \n\\begin{vmatrix}\n\\mathbf{i} & \\mathbf{j} & \\mathbf{k} \\\\\n1 & f'(x) \\cos\\theta & f'(x) \\sin\\theta \\\\\n0 & -f(x) \\sin\\theta & f(x) \\cos\\theta\n\\end{vmatrix} \\\\[5pt]\n&= \\bigg\\langle \\begin{vmatrix} f'(x) \\cos\\theta & f'(x) \\sin\\theta \\\\ -f(x) \\sin\\theta & f(x) \\cos\\theta \\end{vmatrix}, \\: -\\begin{vmatrix} 1 & f'(x) \\sin\\theta \\\\ 0  & f(x) \\cos\\theta \\end{vmatrix}, \\: \\begin{vmatrix} 1 & f'(x) \\cos\\theta \\\\ 0 & -f(x) \\sin\\theta  \\end{vmatrix} \\bigg\\rangle \\\\[5pt]\n&= \\big\\langle f(x)f'(x)\\cos^2\\theta+f(x)f'(x)\\sin^2\\theta, \\: -f(x) \\cos\\theta, \\: -f(x)\\sin\\theta \\big\\rangle \\\\[5pt]\n&= \\big\\langle f(x)f'(x), \\: -f(x) \\cos\\theta, \\:- f(x)\\sin\\theta \\big\\rangle\n\\end{align*}\n\nand\n\n\\begin{align*}\n\\left\\|  \\mathbf{r}'_y \\times \\mathbf{r}'_\\theta \\right\\|\n&= \\sqrt{\\big( f(x)f'(x) \\big)^2 + \\big( -f(x) \\cos\\theta \\big)^2 + \\big( -f(x)\\sin\\theta \\big)^2 } \\\\[3pt]\n&= \\sqrt{\\big(f(x)\\big)^2\\big(f'(x)\\big)^2 + \\big(f(x)\\big)^2 \\big( \\cos^2\\theta + \\sin^2\\theta \\big) } \\\\[3pt]\n&= \\sqrt{\\big(f(x)\\big)^2\\big(f'(x)\\big)^2 + \\big(f(x)\\big)^2 } \\\\[3pt]\n&= f(x) \\sqrt{1 + \\big(f'(x)\\big)^2 }.\n\\end{align*}\n\nTherefore, the surface area is\n\n\\begin{align*}\nA \n&= \\iint\\limits_S \\,  \\text{d}S \\\\[5pt]\n&= \\iint\\limits_D  \\left\\|  \\mathbf{r}'_y \\times \\mathbf{r}'_\\theta \\right\\|  \\text{d}x\\text{d}\\theta \\\\[5pt]\n&= \\int_{a}^{b} \\int_{0}^{2\\pi} f(x) \\sqrt{1 + \\big(f'(x)\\big)^2 } \\: \\text{d}\\theta \\: \\text{d}x \\\\[5pt]\n&= \\int_{a}^{b} f(x) \\sqrt{1 + \\big(f'(x)\\big)^2} \\: \\text{d}x \\cdot \\int_{0}^{2\\pi}  \\text{d}\\theta \\\\[5pt]\n&= \\int_{a}^{b} f(x) \\sqrt{1 + \\big(f'(x)\\big)^2} \\: \\text{d}x \\cdot \\big[ \\theta \\big]_{0}^{2\\pi}  \\\\[5pt]\n&= 2\\pi \\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\\sqrt{1 + \\big(f'(x)\\big)^2 } \\: \\text{d}x.\n\\end{align*}" :tutorial/id #uuid "79f42de8-4cc4-576a-b367-c08bd87f8bcd" )\\,:\\,1\\le z\\le 10,\\,0\\le \\theta <2\\pi }.\n$$\n\nWe now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′} & =⟨\\frac{∂x}{∂z},\\,\\frac{∂y}{∂z},\\,\\frac{∂z}{∂z}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ,\\,{f}^{′}\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,\\,1⟩ \\\\ {r}_{\\theta }^{′} & =⟨\\frac{∂x}{∂\\theta },\\,\\frac{∂y}{∂\\theta },\\,\\frac{∂z}{∂\\theta }⟩=⟨f\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,\\,-f\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ,\\,0⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, the fundamental vector product f\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  & -f\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  & 0\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =⟨|\\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  & 1 \\\\ -f\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  & 0\\end{aligned}|,\\,-|\\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  & 1 \\\\ f\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  & 0\\end{aligned}|,\\,|\\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  & {f}^{′}\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  \\\\ f\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  & -f\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\end{aligned}|⟩ \\\\  & =⟨f\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ,\\,f\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,\\,-{f}^{′}f{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta -{f}^{′}f{cos}^{2}⁡\\theta ⟩ \\\\  & =⟨f\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ,\\,f\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,\\,-{f}^{′}f⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince $f=\\sqrt{z-1},$ we -f\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  & f\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  & 0\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =⟨|\\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  & 1 \\\\ f\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  & {f}^{′}\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  \\\\ -f\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  & f\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\end{aligned}|⟩ \\\\  & =⟨-f\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,\\,-f\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ,\\,{f}^{′}f{cos}^{2}⁡\\theta +{f}^{′}f{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta ⟩ \\\\  & =⟨-f\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,\\,-f\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ,\\,{f}^{′}f⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n  \n\nand\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{z}^{′}\\times {r}_{\\theta }^{′}‖ & =\\sqrt{(-f\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta )^{2}+(-f\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta )^{2}+({f}^{′}f)^{2}} \\\\  & 17592186158230 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158531 :tutorial/content "In statistics, we often want to use sample data to deduce (or **infer**) the values of various **population parameters**. The two most common population parameters that we wish to find are\n\n- the **population mean** $\\mu,$ and\n\n- the **population variance** $\\sigma^2.$\n\nThe population mean is the mean of the *entire* population. Likewise, the population variance is the variance of the *entire* population. We should consider these values as *fixed* unknowns. \n\nSuppose, for example, we want to find the mean number of pages per book at a particular library. In other words, we wish to find the population mean $\\mu.$ However, it is impractical to count the pages in every book. So, instead, we might approximate $\\mu$ using the following sampling procedure:\n\n1\\. Randomly choose, say, $5$ books off the shelf.\n\n2\\. Count the number of pages in each book.\n\n3\\. Compute the mean of the $5$ observations.\n\nIn this case, the **sample size** $n=5.$\n\nSuppose we follow this procedure and get the following **observations**:\n\n$$\n201, \\qquad 506, \\qquad 58, \\qquad 104, \\qquad 99\n$$\n\nIt's convenient to denote the individual observations as $x_i.$ So, in this case, we have \n\n$$\nx_1 = 201,\\qquad x_2 = 506,\\qquad \\ldots,\\qquad x_5 = 99.\n$$\n\nWe can compute the mean $\\overline{x}$ of our sample as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\overset{―}{x} & =\\frac{1}{n}{\\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{5}(201+506+58+104+99) \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{5}\\cdot 968 \\\\  & =193.6\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n The value $\\bar{x} = 193.6$ is called an **estimate** of the population mean $\\mu.$ We sometimes write $\\hat{\\mu} = 193.6$ to denote that the value $193.6$ is an estimate of $\\mu.$\n\nIt's important to realize that our estimate $\\bar{x}$ depends entirely on this particular sample. We'd get a different estimate for $\\mu$ if we took a different sample." :tutorial/id #uuid "359539bd-254d-5083-aa76-577b8a159438" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4738 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "fab3a24b-2709-54fe-985c-5fe95ec0712c" :step/math-academy-id 29343 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158287}} {:db/id 17592186158231 :step/content {:db/id 17592186157355 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186157172 :question/id #uuid "a485378b-0bce-5576-bcbc-2ef77df2da17" :question/math-academy-id "e-7882"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b60ce582-4127-57b8-bba8-04cf17169ca3" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050862}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186157964} {:db/id 17592186157965} {:db/id 17592186412752} {:db/id 17592186412754} {:db/id 17592186412755} {:db/id 17592186412757} {:db/id 17592186412760} {:db/id 17592186433274} {:db/id 17592186433276} {:db/id 17592186433277} {:db/id 17592186433278} {:db/id 17592186433282}] :knowledge-point/title "Estimating a Population Mean From the Sample Mean"} :step/id #uuid "a21dbb27-5fb2-54ba-a76f-f7231e67b5fd" :step/math-academy-id 29347 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158288}} {:db/id 17592186158287 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158560 :tutorial/content "It is helpful to think of the observations of a particular sample\n\n$$\nx_1,\\quad x_2,\\quad \\ldots,\\quad x_n\n$$\n\nas a particular instance of data generated by a sequence of random variables \n\n$$\nX_1,\\quad X_2,\\quad \\ldots,\\quad X_n.\n$$\n\nLet's make sure we're clear about the notation:\n\n- $X_i$ is a *random variable* that denotes the $i$th observation in a random sample. Its value changes when we conduct a new sample.\n\n- $x_i$ is the value of the $i$th observation in a particular sample.\n\nWe typically assume that our sequence of random variables $X_1, X_2,\\ldots, X_n$ has the following properties:\n\n- They are **independent and identically distributed** (or **I.I.D.**), meaning they are independent and have the same probability distribution. Moreover, they have the same distribution as the population.\n\n- Their mean is equal to the population mean:\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}(X_i) = \\mu, \\qquad 1\\leq i\\leq n\n$$\n\n- Their variance is equal to the population variance:\n\n$$\n\\textrm{Var}(X_i) = \\sigma^2, \\qquad 1\\leq i\\leq n\n$$\n\nWe often refer to a sequence of random variables $X_1, X_2,\\ldots, X_n$ with these properties as a **random sample of size** $\\boldsymbol{n}.$\n\nIn general, if $X_1, X_2, \\ldots, X_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n,$ then the **sample mean** is given by\n\n$$\n\\overline{X} \n= \\dfrac1n\\sum_{i=1}^n X_i .\n$$\n\nWe say that the sample mean $\\overline{X}$ is an **estimator** of the population mean $\\mu.$\n\nSince $X_1, X_2, \\ldots, X_n$ are random variables, so is $\\overline{X}.$ The probability distribution of $\\overline{X}$ is called the **sampling distribution** of $\\overline{X}.$ The sampling distribution of $\\overline{X}$ is an important topic we'll discuss in detail in a future lesson." :tutorial/id #uuid "b79ae73d-8ebe-5dda-916d-6eeb61ce850d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6297 :tutorial/title "The Sample Mean"} :step/id #uuid feature of $\\overline{X}$ is that it's an **unbiased estimator** of $\\mu.$ This means that the expected value of $\\overline{X}$ equals $\\mu,$ that is\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[\\overline{X}] = \\mu.\n$$\n\n \n\nWe can easily show that $\\overline{X}$ is an unbiased estimator of $\\mu$ using the properties of expectation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\text{E}[\\overset{―}{X}] & =\\text{E}[\\frac{1}{n}{\\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{n}\\cdot \\text{E}[{\\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{n}\\cdot \\text{E}[{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{n}] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{n}\\cdot (\\text{E}[{X}_{1}]+\\text{E}[{X}_{2}]+⋯+\\text{E}[{X}_{n}]) \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{n}\\cdot (\\mu +\\mu +⋯+\\mu ) \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{n}\\cdot n\\mu  \\\\  & =\\mu \\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe fact that $\\overline{X}$ is an unbiased estimator of $\\mu$ is a desirable property. We'll meet so-called **biased estimators** in future lessons. \n\nFinally, any estimate $\\bar{x}$ of the population mean $\\mu$ found by computing the mean of a sample is called an **unbiased estimate** of $\\mu.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4c9ca398-f024-59cf-b484-80cf2f43cc8c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6298 :tutorial/title "The Sample Mean as an Unbiased Estimator"} :step/id #uuid "5d85b5ed-e218-547b-81cf-36a60c612b6f" :step/math-academy-id 38137 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158289}} {:db/id 17592186158289 :step/content {:db/id 17592186157392 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186156993 :question/id #uuid "33bedb30-2c99-52e8-a665-e3bddeed7e13" :question/math-academy-id "e-10114"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "38455e74-50c2-5581-b9e1-a8dd0c85f826" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048317} {:db/id 17592186048508}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186157598} {:db/id 17592186157599} {:db/id 17592186412753} {:db/id 17592186412756} {:db/id 17592186412758} {:db/id 17592186412759} {:db/id 17592186433275} {:db/id 17592186433279} {:db/id 17592186433280} {:db/id 17592186433281}] :knowledge-point/title "The Expected Value of the Sample Mean"} :step/id #uuid "2edb1e12-aed2-5310-a098-962a8588a4f0" :step/math-academy-id 38142}] :activity/title "The Sample Mean" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186157528} {:db/id 17592186158230 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158531 :tutorial/content "In statistics, we often want to use sample data to deduce (or **infer**) the values of various **population parameters**. ={x}_{2}-{x}_{1},\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhere $x_1$ and $x_2$ are the $x$-coordinates at the initial and terminal points of $C,$ respectively. is the path along the quarter-circle shown below.\n\n![](images/01/01b5f21b2c778f62f7dd884065ee4ce17dd01bd021063fc7c788f09a89feea86.png)\n\nIf we reverse the orientation of the curve, we get the following path:\n\n![](images/46/469675e85a6ca1d23de6da985d36e8e86c859ceff38ea6849984ea3c2cd34abe.png)\n\nThe initial and terminal points have swapped, and so we now have $x_1 = 2$ and $x_2 = 0.$ Applying our formula, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\int }_{-C}\\,\\text{d}x & ={x}_{2}-{x}_{1} \\\\  & =0-2 \\\\  & =-2.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThis example illustrates an important property of line integrals with respect to $x,$ described in full as follows:\n\n*Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth path in the $xy$-plane, and let $-C$ be the curve consisting of the same points as $C$ but with the opposite orientation. Then,*\n\n$$\n\\displaystyle\\int_{-C} f(x,y)\\,\\textrm d x = -\\int_{C} f(x,y)\\,\\textrm d x.\n$$\n\n*Similarly, *\n\n$$\n\\displaystyle\\int_{-C} f(x,y)\\,\\textrm d y = -\\int_{C} f(x,y)\\,\\textrm d y.\n$$\n\nIn other words, line integrals with respect to $x$ and $y$ are *dependent on orientation*. This is quite different from the case for line integrals with respect to arc length, which are independent of orientation." :tutorial/id #uuid "6fb52502-a498-5599-851c-64cf19d11bf3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5818 :tutorial/title "Further Properties of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y"} :step/id #uuid "fb92124a-a40c-5b95-8acb-21f039c39f10" :step/math-academy-id 35674 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180482}} {:db/id 17592186180485 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180716 :tutorial/content "Similar to line integrals of unity with respect to $x,$ the line integral of unity with respect to $y$ along a path $C$ is equal to the net change in $y$ between the terminal and initial points:\n\n$$\n\\int_C \\,\\textrm d y = y_2 - y_1,\n$$\n\nwhere $y_2$ is the $y$-coordinate of the terminal point, and $y_1$ is the $y$-coordinate of the initial point. \n\nAlso, if $C$ is a closed, positively oriented curve traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, then\n\n$$\n\\oint_C \\,\\textrm d y = 0.\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "16485104-9964-58c8-8611-2769190cbf9c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5819 :tutorial/title "Line Integrals of Unity With Respect to Y"} :step/id #uuid "e5542a0f-35f9-5d2c-a937-679f3e3b6ef6" :step/math-academy-id 35675 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180481}} {:db/id 17592186180486 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180717 :tutorial/content "![](images/c2/c2ab6be66d91822186ee94c846f8cd1a247da776b89d7d9220b836193b9b04d3.png)\n\nConsider the path $C$ above. Earlier, we showed that\n\n$$\n\\int_{C}\\,\\textrm d x = 2,\n$$\n\nWe note the following:\n\n- In the context of our usual interpretation of line integrals with respect to $x,$ this result represents the total area accumulated when the function $z=1$ is projected onto the plane $y=0$ as $C$ is traversed from the initial point $(0,2)$ to the terminal point $(2,0).$ \n\n![](images/29/297e4e302b0cec7f4448ec7e8b36ab6c1f84d79d5f71aad1c6887d86d54dc328.png)\n\nFrom the diagram, we see that this projection generates a rectangle of length $x_2 - x_1 = 2$ and height $z=1.$ Since the integral of unity with respect to $x$ along $C$ is equal to the area of this rectangle, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\int }_{C}\\,\\text{d}x & =1\\cdot ({x}_{2}-{x}_{1}) \\\\  & ={x}_{2}-{x}_{1} \\\\  & =2.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFurthermore, this result is *positive* because the rectangle is traced out in the direction of *increasing* $x.$\n\n- If we reverse the direction of the curve then we get a *negative* result. This is because the rectangle is traced out in the direction of *decreasing* $x,$ as shown below.\n\n![](images/17/179713734445f85818ef4e46cfa5948115cea936538acd3095cbfa706d381972.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "1ba2d901-3b8c-5ce9-a7bd-ace7643f3277" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5820 :tutorial/title "Intuition Behind Some of the Results"} :step/id #uuid "a896d261-9315-51e1-80bb-4191a37e68b3" :step/math-academy-id 35676}] :activity/title "Properties of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186179861} {:db/id 17592186180479 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180713 :tutorial/content "The line integral with respect to $x$ of the function $f(x,y)$ along the path $C$ can be calculated using the formula\n\n$$\n\\int_C f(x,y)\\,\\textrm d x = \\int\\limits_a^b  f(\\mathbf r(t)) \\, \\dfrac{\\text{d}x}{\\text{d}t} \\, \\textrm{d}t,\n$$\n\nwhere $\\mathbf r (t)$ for $a\\leq t\\leq b$ is a parametrization of $C.$ \n\nNow, if we set $f(x,y) = 1,$ then by the change of variables formula, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\int }_{C}\\,\\text{d}x & ={\\int }_{a}^{b}\\frac{\\text{d}x}{\\text{d}t}\\,\\text{d}t \\\\  & ={\\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={x}_{2}-{x}_{1},\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhere $x_1$ and $x_2$ are the $x$-coordinates at the initial and terminal points of $C,$ respectively. Then,*\n\n$$\n\\displaystyle\\int_{-C} f(x,y)\\,\\textrm d x = -\\int_{C} f(x,y)\\,\\textrm d x.\n$$\n\n*Similarly, *\n\n$$\n\\displaystyle\\int_{-C} f(x,y)\\,\\textrm d y = -\\int_{C} f(x,y)\\,\\textrm d y.\n$$\n\nIn other words, line integrals with respect to $x$ and $y$ are *dependent on orientation*. This is quite different from the case for line integrals with respect to arc length, which are independent of orientation." :tutorial/id #uuid "6fb52502-a498-5599-851c-64cf19d11bf3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5818 :tutorial/title "Further Properties of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y"} {:db/id 17592186180716 :tutorial/content "Similar to line integrals of unity with respect to $x,$ the line integral of unity with respect to $y$ along a path $C$ is equal to the net change in $y$ between the terminal and initial points:\n\n$$\n\\int_C \\,\\textrm d y = y_2 - y_1,\n$$\n\nwhere $y_2$ is the $y$-coordinate of the terminal point, and $y_1$ is the $y$-coordinate of the initial point. \n\nAlso, if $C$ is a closed, positively oriented curve traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, then\n\n$$\n\\oint_C \\,\\textrm d y = 0.\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "16485104-9964-58c8-8611-2769190cbf9c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5819 :tutorial/title "Line Integrals of Unity With Respect to Y"} {:db/id 17592186180717 :tutorial/content "![](images/c2/c2ab6be66d91822186ee94c846f8cd1a247da776b89d7d9220b836193b9b04d3.png)\n\nConsider the path $C$ above. Earlier, we showed that\n\n$$\n\\int_{C}\\,\\textrm d x = 2,\n$$\n\nWe note the following:\n\n- In the context of our usual interpretation of line integrals with respect to $x,$ this result represents the total area accumulated when the function $z=1$ is projected onto the plane $y=0$ as $C$ is traversed from the initial point $(0,2)$ to the terminal point $(2,0).$ \n\n![](images/29/297e4e302b0cec7f4448ec7e8b36ab6c1f84d79d5f71aad1c6887d86d54dc328.png)\n\nFrom the diagram, we see that this projection generates a rectangle of length $x_2 - x_1 = 2$ and height $z=1.$ Since the integral of unity with respect to $x$ along $C$ is equal to the area of this rectangle, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\int }_{C}\\,\\text{d}x & =1\\cdot ({x}_{2}-{x}_{1}) \\\\  & ={x}_{2}-{x}_{1} \\\\  & =2.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFurthermore, this result is *positive* because the rectangle is traced out in the direction of *increasing* $x.$\n\n- If we reverse the direction of the curve then we get a *negative* result.
