"b02a7662-acf4-57da-98d7-bae7093076f2" :step/math-academy-id 45126} {:db/id 17592186180578 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180765 :tutorial/content "The **kinetic energy** of a particle with mass $m$ and velocity $v$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\text{KE} = \\dfrac12mv^2.\n$$\n\nWhen the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms ($\\rm{kg}$) and meters per second ($\\rm{m/s}$), respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($\\rm{J}$). \n\nFor example, suppose a particle $P$ of mass $5\\,\\rm{kg}$ is moving along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of $3t^2\\,\\rm{m/s}^2,$ where $t \\geq 0$ is the time in seconds. Let's calculate the particle's kinetic energy at time $t=2\\,\\rm{s}.$\n\nFirst, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\\int a(t)\\,\\text{d}t \\\\ v(t) & =\\int 3{t}^{2}\\,\\text{d}t \\\\ v(t) & ={t}^{3}+C\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives\n\n$$\n0 = 0^3 + C\n\\qquad\\Longrightarrow\\qquad\nC = 0.\n$$\n\nHence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t) = t^3.$ In particular, its velocity at time $t=2\\,\\rm{s}$ is\n\n$$\nv=v(2) = 2^3 = 8\\,\\rm{m/s}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the kinetic energy of the particle at $t=2$ is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\text{KE} & =\\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}\\cdot 5\\cdot {8}^{2} \\\\  & =160\\,J.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNote the following:\n\n- Kinetic energy is a *scalar* quantity.\n\n- You probably noticed that kinetic energy and work have the same units. This is not a coincidence! We'll learn more about that shortly.\n\n- In practical applications, it's often more important to calculate a *change* in the kinetic energy of a particle between two points in time. \n\nThe **change in kinetic energy** of a particle with mass $m,$ **initial velocity** $v_0,$ and **final velocity** $v_1$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\Delta \\, \\text{KE} = \\dfrac12mv_1^2 - \\dfrac12mv_0^2.\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "42f83ae3-3805-546b-a5bf-264b8b56d6ef" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7811 :tutorial/title "Kinetic Energy"} :step/id #uuid "3bec1351-7ee4-5f29-8760-5dd679edda2e" :step/math-academy-id 45179 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180575}} {:db/id 17592186180579 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180766 :tutorial/content "The **work-energy principle** states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,\n\n$$\nW = \\Delta\\, \\text{KE}\n$$\n\nwhere the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by\n\n$$\n\\Delta\\, \\text{KE} = \\dfrac12 m v_1^2 - \\dfrac12 m v_0^2\n$$\n\nand $m$ is the particle's mass, $v_0$ is its initial velocity, and $v_1$ is its final velocity." :tutorial/id #uuid "e00f462b-c087-5c42-afc7-bfeffad5906b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7812 :tutorial/title "The Work-Energy Principle"} :step/id #uuid "4d3d3f00-8ddb-5882-984a-2f48d2b19da6" :step/math-academy-id 45180 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180576}}] :activity/title "The Work-Energy Principle" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186179842} {:db/id 17592186180573 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180764 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll discuss the concepts of **work** and **kinetic energy** and describe how these concepts are related. \n\nThe **work done by the force** $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from the position $x=x_1$ to the position $x=x_2$ along the $x$-axis is defined as\n\n$$\nW = \\int_{x_1}^{x_2} F(x) \\,\\textrm{d}x.\n$$\n\nWhen the force and distance are measured in Newtons ($\\textrm{N}$) and meters ($\\textrm{m}$), respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($\\rm{J}$).\n\nFor example, suppose a particle $P$ is moving along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $4x^3\\,\\textrm{N},$ acting in the direction of increasing $x,$ as shown below. Let's calculate the particle's kinetic energy at time $t=2\\,\\rm{s}.$\n\nFirst, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\\int a(t)\\,\\text{d}t \\\\ v(t) & =\\int 3{t}^{2}\\,\\text{d}t \\\\ v(t) & ={t}^{3}+C\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives\n\n$$\n0 = 0^3 + C\n\\qquad\\Longrightarrow\\qquad\nC = 0.\n$$\n\nHence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t) = t^3.$ In particular, its velocity at time $t=2\\,\\rm{s}$ is\n\n$$\nv=v(2) = 2^3 = 8\\,\\rm{m/s}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the kinetic energy of the particle at $t=2$ is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\text{KE} & =\\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}\\cdot 5\\cdot {8}^{2} \\\\  & =160\\,J.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNote the following:\n\n- Kinetic energy is a *scalar* quantity.\n\n- You probably noticed that kinetic energy and work have the same units. This is not a coincidence! We'll learn more about that shortly.\n\n- In practical applications, it's often more important to calculate a *change* in the kinetic energy of a particle between two points in time. \n\nThe **change in kinetic energy** of a particle with mass $m,$ **initial velocity** $v_0,$ and **final velocity** $v_1$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\Delta \\, \\text{KE} = \\dfrac12mv_1^2 - \\dfrac12mv_0^2.\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "42f83ae3-3805-546b-a5bf-264b8b56d6ef" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7811 :tutorial/title "Kinetic Energy"} :step/id #uuid "3bec1351-7ee4-5f29-8760-5dd679edda2e" :step/math-academy-id 45179 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180575}} {:db/id 17592186180575 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179778 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179439 :question/id #uuid "4e428ee4-0017-5e83-887c-26e723b4af08" :question/math-academy-id "e-12526"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ec390427-7510-57ea-aedf-a930284f93b5" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049947}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180101} {:db/id 17592186180102} {:db/id 17592186284412} {:db/id 17592186284413} {:db/id 17592186284414} {:db/id 17592186389463} {:db/id 17592186389470} {:db/id 17592186416258} {:db/id 17592186416259} {:db/id 17592186416264} {:db/id 17592186416270}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Kinetic Energy of a Particle"} :step/id #uuid "54dddd69-accb-5eb8-beac-e9f9dbc87bf7" :step/math-academy-id 45124 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180579}} {:db/id 17592186180579 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180766 :tutorial/content "The **work-energy principle** states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. 17592186134817 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135105 :tutorial/content "Let $V$ be an inner product space with the inner product $\\langle\\cdot, \\cdot\\rangle.$ If \n\n$$\n\\big\\{ \\mathbf{a}_1, \\mathbf{a}_2 , \\ldots, \\mathbf{a}_n \\big\\}\n$$\n\n is a set of mutually orthogonal vectors in $V,$  then the **orthogonal projection** of a vector $\\mathbf{x}\\in V$ onto the subspace \n\n$$\nS = \\textrm{Span}\\{ \\mathbf{a}_1, \\mathbf{a}_2 , \\ldots, \\mathbf{a}_n \\}\n$$\n\nwith respect to the inner product is given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\text{proj}}_{S}\\,x & ={\\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+⋯+{\\text{proj}}_{{a}_{n}}x \\\\  & =\\frac{⟨x,{a}_{1}⟩}{⟨{a}_{1},{a}_{1}⟩}{a}_{1}+\\frac{⟨x,{a}_{2}⟩}{⟨{a}_{2},{a}_{2}⟩}{a}_{2}+⋯+\\frac{⟨x,{a}_{n}⟩}{⟨{a}_{n},{a}_{n}⟩}{a}_{n}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nIn other words, the orthogonal projection of $\\mathbf{x}$ onto $S$ is the sum of the orthogonal projections of $\\mathbf{x}$ onto each one-dimensional subspace $\\textrm{Span}\\big\\{ \\mathbf{a}_i\\}$ for $i=1, 2, \\cdots, n.$ \n\nNote the following:\n\n- This is entirely analogous to the corresponding formula for Euclidean spaces.\n\n- As in Euclidean spaces, the formula works *only* when the set of vectors $\\{ \\mathbf{a}_1, \\mathbf{a}_2 , \\ldots, \\mathbf{a}_n \\}$ is orthogonal with respect to the inner product!" :tutorial/id #uuid "9b462101-527b-5e26-bcd4-89b8459552bd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5162 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $V$ is a vector space equipped with an inner product $\\left\\langle\\cdot, \\cdot\\right\\rangle$ and that $\\mathbf{v}, \\mathbf{w} \\in V.$ The **distance $d$ between $\\mathbf v$ and $\\mathbf w$ with respect to the inner product** is defined by the *norm* of $\\mathbf{v}- \\mathbf{w}.$ That is,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}d & =‖v-w‖=\\sqrt{⟨v-w,v-w⟩}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFor example, suppose that $V = \\mathcal{C}[0,1],$ the vector space of continuous functions over $[0,1],$ equipped with the inner product\n\n$$\n\\langle x(t),y(t) \\rangle = \\int_0^{1} x(t) y(t) \\, \\text{d}t.\n$$\n\nThe distance between the functions $f(t)=4t$ and $g(t)=t+1$ with respect to the given inner product is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}d & =‖f(t)-g(t)‖ \\\\  & =‖4t-(t+1)‖ \\\\  & =‖3t-1‖ \\\\  & =\\sqrt{⟨3t-1,3t-1⟩} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{{\\int }_{0}^{1}(3t-1)^{2}\\,\\text{d}t} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{{\\frac{1}{9}\\cdot (3t-1)^{3}|}_{0}^{1}} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{\\frac{1}{9}\\cdot [(8)-(-1)]} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{\\frac{1}{9}\\cdot 9} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{1} \\\\  & =1.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nMore generally, given an orthogonal set \n\n$$\n\\big\\{ \\mathbf{a}_1, \\mathbf{a}_2 , \\ldots, \\mathbf{a}_n \\big\\} \\subset  V\n$$\n\nand a vector $\\mathbf x \\in V,$  the **distance between $\\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace** \n\n$$\nS=\\textrm{Span}\\{ \\mathbf{a}_1,\\mathbf{a}_2,  \\ldots, \\mathbf{a}_n \\}\n$$\n\nis defined as\n\n$$\n\\Vert{ \\color{black} \\mathbf{x} - \\text{proj}_{S}\\,\\mathbf{x} }\\Vert.\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186134885 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135141 :tutorial/content "Consider the functions \n\n$$\nf_1(t)=t,\\qquad f_2(t)=t^2+1, \\qquad h(t)= 5t^3,\n$$\n\nin the vector space $V = \\mathcal{C}[-1,1]$ of continuous functions over $[-1,1],$ where the inner product is defined as\n\n$$\n\\langle x(t),y(t) \\rangle = \\int_{-1}^1 x(t) y(t) \\, \\text{d}t.\n$$\n\nLet's find the :tutorial/content "Suppose that $V$ is a vector space equipped with an inner product $\\left\\langle\\cdot, \\cdot\\right\\rangle$ and that $\\mathbf{v}, \\mathbf{w} \\in V.$ The **distance $d$ between $\\mathbf v$ and $\\mathbf w$ with respect to the inner product** is defined by the *norm* of $\\mathbf{v}- \\mathbf{w}.$ That is,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}d & =‖v-w‖=\\sqrt{⟨v-w,v-w⟩}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFor example, suppose that $V = \\mathcal{C}[0,1],$ the vector space of continuous functions over $[0,1],$ equipped with the inner product\n\n$$\n\\langle x(t),y(t) \\rangle = \\int_0^{1} x(t) y(t) \\, \\text{d}t.\n$$\n\nThe distance between the functions $f(t)=4t$ and $g(t)=t+1$ with respect to the given inner product is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}d & =‖f(t)-g(t)‖ \\\\  & =‖4t-(t+1)‖ \\\\  & =‖3t-1‖ \\\\  & =\\sqrt{⟨3t-1,3t-1⟩} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{{\\int }_{0}^{1}(3t-1)^{2}\\,\\text{d}t} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{{\\frac{1}{9}\\cdot (3t-1)^{3}|}_{0}^{1}} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{\\frac{1}{9}\\cdot [(8)-(-1)]} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{\\frac{1}{9}\\cdot 9} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{1} \\\\  & =1.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nMore generally, given an orthogonal set \n\n$$\n\\big\\{ \\mathbf{a}_1, \\mathbf{a}_2 , \\ldots, \\mathbf{a}_n \\big\\} \\subset  V\n$$\n\nand a vector $\\mathbf x \\in V,$  the **distance between $\\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace** \n\n$$\nS=\\textrm{Span}\\{ \\mathbf{a}_1,\\mathbf{a}_2,  \\ldots, \\mathbf{a}_n \\}\n$$\n\nis defined as\n\n$$\n\\Vert{ \\color{black} \\mathbf{x} - \\text{proj}_{S}\\,\\mathbf{x} }\\Vert.\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "$$\n{u}_{1}=[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}} \\\\ -\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{5}}\\end{aligned}],\\,{u}_{2}=[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{5}} \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}}\\end{aligned}]\n$$\n\nConsider the vectors above, and let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following statements are true?\n\nI. ${u}_{1}\\cdot {u}_{2}=0$\n\nII. $\\{Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})\\}$ is orthogonal\n\nIII. $\\{Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})\\}$ is orthonormal" :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\\cdot Q(y)=x\\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$\n\nThe linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:\n\n- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.\n\n- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$\n\n- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.\n\n- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.\n\nWith that in mind, let's examine our statements.\n\n- Statement I is true. Indeed,\n\n$$\n{u}_{1}\\cdot {u}_{2}=[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}} \\\\ -\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{5}}\\end{aligned}]\\cdot [\\begin{aligned}\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{5}} \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}}\\end{aligned}]=\\frac{2}{5}-\\frac{2}{5}=0.\n$$\n\n- Statement II is true. Indeed, $Q({u}_{1})⊥Q({u}_{2})$ since\n\n$$\nQ({u}_{1})\\cdot Q({u}_{2})={u}_{1}\\cdot {u}_{2}=0.\n$$\n\n- Statement III is true. Indeed, both $Q({u}_{1})$ and $Q({u}_{2})$ are unit vectors:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}‖Q({u}_{1})‖ & =‖{u}_{1}‖=\\sqrt{(\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}})^{2}+(-\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{5}})^{2}}=1 \\\\ ‖Q({u}_{2})‖ & =‖{u}_{2}‖=\\sqrt{(\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{5}})^{2}+(\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}})^{2}}=1\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I, II, and III.\""} :step/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties:\n\n- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\\alpha \\in C,$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\\,$ and $\\,⟨a,\\alpha b⟩=\\overset{―}{\\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$\n\n- It has conjugate symmetry. :question/problem "Given that $⟨\\,\\cdot \\,,\\,\\cdot \\,⟩$ is the standard Hermitian inner product over $C,$ find $⟨a,\\,b-(1+3\\text{i})c⟩$ if \n\n$\\,$ $⟨b,a⟩=1+\\text{i}\\,$ and $\\,⟨a,c⟩=2.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties. \n\n- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\\alpha \\in C,$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\\,$ and $\\,⟨\\alpha a,b⟩=\\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$\n\n- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\\alpha \\in C,$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\\,$ and $\\,⟨a,\\alpha b⟩=\\overset{―}{\\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$\n\n- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\\in {C}^{n},$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$\n\n- It is positive-definite. For any $a\\in {C}^{n},$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$\n\nFirst, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ is antilinear in the second argument:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}⟨a,\\,b-(1+3\\text{i})c⟩ & =⟨a,b⟩-⟨a,(1+3\\text{i})c⟩ \\\\  & =⟨a,b⟩-(\\overset{―}{1+3\\text{i}})⟨a,c⟩ \\\\  & =⟨a,b⟩-(1-3\\text{i})⟨a,c⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}⟨a,b⟩-(1-3\\text{i})⟨a,c⟩ & =\\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}-(1-3\\text{i})⟨a,c⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we substitute the values for $⟨b,a⟩$ and $⟨a,c⟩:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}-(1-3\\text{i})⟨a,c⟩ & =\\overset{―}{1+\\text{i}}-(1-3\\text{i})\\cdot 2 \\\\  & =1-\\text{i}-2+6\\text{i} \\\\  & =-1+5\\text{i}\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "ff45ad40-043f-5835-bb86-3d1e620fd852" :step/next {:db/id :question/math-academy-id "q-141160" :question/problem "Consider the standard Hermitian inner product $⟨\\,\\cdot \\,,\\,\\cdot \\,⟩$ over $C.$ \nWhich of the following statements are true?\n\nSelect all that apply.\n\n- **I.** $⟨ia,b⟩=i⟨a,b⟩$ for any $a,b\\in {C}^{n}$\n\n- **II.** $⟨a,\\overset{―}{\\alpha }b⟩=⟨\\alpha a,b⟩$ for any $a,b\\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\\alpha \\in C$\n\n- **III.** $⟨ia,a⟩\\in R$ for any $a\\in {C}^{n}$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties:\n\n- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\\alpha \\in C,$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\\,$ and $\\,⟨\\alpha a,b⟩=\\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$\n\n- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\\alpha \\in C,$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\\,$ and $\\,⟨a,\\alpha b⟩=\\overset{―}{\\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$\n\n- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\\in {C}^{n},$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$\n\n- It is positive-definite. For any $a\\in {C}^{n},$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$\n\nWith that in mind, let's examine our statements. \n\n- Statement I is true.  Indeed, the inner product in ${C}^{n}$ is linear in the first argument. So, a constant multiple from the first argument can be factored out.\n\n- Statement II is true. By the antilinearity of a complex inner product in the second argument and linearity in the first argument, we have \n\n$$\n⟨a,\\overset{―}{\\alpha }b⟩=\\overset{―}{(\\overset{―}{\\alpha })}⟨a,b⟩=\\alpha ⟨a,b⟩=⟨\\alpha a,b⟩.\n$$\n\n- Statement III is false. Notice that $⟨a,a⟩\\in R$ for any $a\\in {C}^{n}.$ Therefore, if $a\\ne 0,$ then\n\n$$\n⟨ia,a⟩=i⟨a,a⟩\\notin R.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I and II only.\""} :step/id #uuid :question/problem "Consider the region $D$ in the $xy$-plane, given by\n\n$$\nD = \\big\\{ (x,y) \\: : \\: -2 \\leq 4x+2y \\leq 2, \\:\\: 0 \\leq y-x \\leq 3 \\big\\}.\n$$\n\nBy performing the change of variables $u = 4x+2y$ and $v=y - x,$ write the following integral in terms of $u$ and $v.$ \n\n$$\n\\displaystyle \n\\iint\\limits_D \\sin \\left(3(x+y)\\right)  \\: \\mathrm{d}x \\, \\mathrm{d}y\n$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $\\mathbf{T}$ as follows:\n\n![](images/e9/e9a07b75be73621bb23edb6f4da67999c5f5ce07b8776f549cf12464e74fa702.svg)\n\nThis transformation maps some region $\\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.\n\nTo compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula\n\n$$\n\\iint\\limits_{D} f(x,y) \\, \\mathrm d x \\, \\mathrm d y = \\iint\\limits_{\\Delta} \\ f(x(u,v), y(u,v))  \\left| \\dfrac{\\partial (x, y)}{\\partial (u, v)} \\right|  \\mathrm d u \\, \\mathrm d v\n$$\n\nwhere $\\dfrac{\\partial (x, y)}{\\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\\mathbf{T}.$\n\nNote that the change of variables\n\n$$\nu = 4x + 2y, \\qquad v = y - x\n$$\n\n \n\ngives us the *inverse* function $\\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is\n\n![](images/a1/a1228e77194b92d8b2c527845273ae9f70d9b90d4c3091f5ed9dd9f8c430776c.svg)\n\nTo compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:\n\n**Step 1**: Find $\\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ \n\nOur domain in the $uv$-plane is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Δ & =\\{(u,v)\\,:\\,-2\\le u\\le 2,\\,0\\le v\\le 3\\}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\\mathbf T^{-1}.$\n\nThe Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\\mathbf T^{-1}$ is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \\frac{∂u}{∂y} \\\\ \\frac{∂v}{∂x} & \\frac{∂v}{∂y}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =|\\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\\\ -1 & \\text{ }\\text{ }1\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =6.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\\mathbf T.$\n\nThe Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\\mathbf T$ is\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\partial (x, y)}{\\partial (u, v)} = \\left( \\dfrac{\\partial (u, v)}{\\partial (x, y)} \\right)^{-1} = \\dfrac{1}{6}.\n$$\n\nNote that $\\dfrac{\\partial (x, y)}{\\partial (u, v)} \\neq 0$ everywhere inside $\\Delta.$ In other words, $\\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\\Delta.$\n\n**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables.\n\nIn this case, we first need to solve the transformation equations\n\n$$\nu = 4x+2y, \\qquad v = y-x\n$$\n\n \nfor $x$ and $y$, which gives\n\n$$\nx = \\dfrac{u-2v}6, \\qquad y =\\dfrac{u+4v}6.\n$$\n\n \n\nPerforming the change of variables, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(x+y))\\,dx\\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(\\frac{u-2v}{6}+\\frac{u+4v}{6}))|\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\\text{d}u\\,\\text{d}v \\\\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(\\frac{2u+2v}{6}))|\\frac{1}{6}|\\text{d}u\\,\\text{d}v \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{6}{\\int }_{0}^{3}{\\int }_{-2}^{2}sin\\,(u+v)\\,du\\,dv.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186120934 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121142 :tutorial/content "Finding the **cube root** of a number is the reverse of cubing a number. We express the cube root using the **radical symbol** $\\sqrt[3]{\\phantom{x}}.$\n\nFor example, the \"cube root of $8$\" equals $\\color{blue}2$ since \n\n$$\n{\\color{blue}2}^3 = {\\color{blue}2}\\cdot {\\color{blue}2}\\cdot {\\color{blue}2} = 8.\n$$\n\nSo, we write $\\sqrt[3]{8}={\\color{blue}2}.$\n\nSome basic cube roots are as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\sqrt[3]{0} & = & \\sqrt[3]{{0}^{3}} & = & 0 \\\\ \\sqrt[3]{1} & = & \\sqrt[3]{{1}^{3}} & = & 1 \\\\ \\sqrt[3]{8} & = & \\sqrt[3]{{2}^{3}} & = & 2 \\\\ \\sqrt[3]{27} & = & \\sqrt[3]{{3}^{3}} & = & 3 \\\\ \\sqrt[3]{64} & = & \\sqrt[3]{{4}^{3}} & = & 4 \\\\ \\sqrt[3]{125} & = & \\sqrt[3]{{5}^{3}} & = & 5 \\\\ \\sqrt[3]{1\\,000} & = & \\sqrt[3]{{10}^{3}} & = & 10\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nA **perfect cube** is a number whose cube root is a whole number. So, the numbers \n\n$$\n0,\\qquad 1,\\qquad  8,\\qquad  27,\\qquad  64,\\qquad 125, \\qquad 1\\,000\n$$\n\n are all perfect cubes. You need to remember them." :tutorial/id #uuid "82bf149b-fb3b-506e-9c7b-3d6716081eaa" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8377 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid basic cube roots of negative numbers are as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\sqrt[3]{-1} & = & \\sqrt[3]{(-1)^{3}} & = & -1 \\\\ \\sqrt[3]{-8} & = & \\sqrt[3]{(-2)^{3}} & = & -2 \\\\ \\sqrt[3]{-27} & = & \\sqrt[3]{(-3)^{3}} & = & -3 \\\\ \\sqrt[3]{-64} & = & \\sqrt[3]{(-4)^{3}} & = & -4 \\\\ \\sqrt[3]{-125} & = & \\sqrt[3]{(-5)^{3}} & = & -5 \\\\ \\sqrt[3]{-1\\,000} & = & \\sqrt[3]{(-10)^{3}} & = & -10\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNote that the numbers \n\n$$\n-1,\\qquad  -8,\\qquad  -27,\\qquad  -64,\\qquad -125, \\qquad -1\\,000\n$$\n\nare all perfect cubes." :tutorial/id #uuid x-y-z\n$$\n\nsubject to the constraints \n\n$$\ng(x,y,z)=x+y+z=2, \\qquad h(x,y,z)=x^2 + z^2 = 4.\n$$\n\nSince $f(x,y,z)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y,z)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. \n\nTherefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:\n\n$$\n{\\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z)=\\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\\\ g(x,y,z)=2 \\\\ h(x,y,z)=4\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe start by expanding the first equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\\\ ⟨{f}_{x},{f}_{y},{f}_{z}⟩ & =\\lambda ⟨{g}_{x},{g}_{y},{g}_{z}⟩+\\mu ⟨{h}_{x},{h}_{y},{h}_{z}⟩ \\\\ ⟨1,-1,-1⟩ & =\\lambda ⟨1,1,1⟩+\\mu ⟨2x,0,2z⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nTherefore, we have the following system:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\begin{aligned}1=\\lambda +2\\mu x \\\\ -1=\\lambda  \\\\ -1=\\lambda +2\\mu z\\end{aligned}\\,⇒\\,{\\begin{aligned}x=\\frac{1}{\\mu } \\\\ \\lambda =-1 \\\\ \\mu z=0\\end{aligned}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNotice that $\\mu$ can't be zero since this leads to a contradiction. So, from the third equation above, we must have $z=0.$\n\nNext, we substitute $z=0$  into the second constraint:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =4 \\\\ {x}^{2} & =4 \\\\ x & =\\pm 2\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nFinally, we substitute $x$ and $z$ into the first constraint:\n\n- If $x=2$ and $z= 0,$ we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}x+y+z & =2 \\\\ 2+y+0 & =2 \\\\ 2+y & =2 \\\\ y & =0.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- If $x=-2$ and $z=0,$ we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}x+y+z & =2 \\\\ -2+y+0 & =2 \\\\ -2+y & =2 \\\\ y & =4.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points\n\n$$\n(2, 0, 0), \\qquad (-2, 4, 0).\n$$\n\nWe evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:\n\n| $(x,y,z)$ | $(2, 0, 0 )$ | $(-2, 4, 0)$ |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| $f(x,y,z)$ | $2$ | $-6$ |\n\nTherefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(-2, 4, 0),$ and its minimum value is $-6.$"} {:db/id 17592186172382 :question/id #uuid "332ef138-daaa-584b-88e1-280c181c6e29" :question/math-academy-id "q-162669" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id of Lagrange multipliers.\n\nFor example, suppose that we want to find the minimum value of\n\n$$f(x,y,z) = 4xy+z^2$$\n\nsubject to the following *two* constraints:\n\n$$g(x,y,z)=x^2+y^2=1, \\qquad h(x,y,z)=2x^2 + 4y^2 - z = 0$$\n\nGeometrically, this means that we want to minimize $f(x,y,z)$ over the intersection of the cylinder $x^2+y^2=1$ and the elliptic paraboloid $2x^2 + 4y^2 - z = 0,$ as shown below.\n\n![](images/54/546d4f2fe43e27374a0e7f7c743c0d3b8a81d0d0a41ab561dec287a8af594a04.svg)\n\n![](images/0b/0b16f73e034724a9f38d91a606f627db85299507552c45192e91c39bc0c6725a.png)\n\n![](images/51/510b3b8dc8d56fe2fc20ccac08356638ee1f1c58cd2edac451b077070679c6c7.svg)\n\nThe method of Lagrange multipliers states that the extrema of the function $f(x,y,z)$ subject to constraints $g(x,y,z)=a$ and $h(x,y,z)=b$ can be found by solving the following system: $${\\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z)=\\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\\\ g(x,y,z)=a \\\\ h(x,y,z)=b\\end{aligned}$$\n\nHere, the constants $\\lambda$ and $\\mu$ are the Lagrange multipliers of this system.\n\nAs before, this method assumes that $\\nabla g \\neq \\mathbf{0}$ and $\\nabla h \\neq \\mathbf{0}$ on the curves $g(x,y,z)=a$ and $h(x,y,z)=b,$ and that the extreme values exist.\n\n**Note:** Geometrically, the condition $\\nabla f = \\lambda \\nabla g + \\mu \\nabla h$ states that\n\n- $\\nabla f$ lies in the plane spanned by $\\nabla g$ and $\\nabla h,$ or, equivalently,\n- $\\nabla f$ is perpendicular to the level surfaces $g(x,y,z) = a$ and $h(x,y,z) = b.$\n\nWe'll explore this geometric intuition further at the end of the lesson." :tutorial/id #uuid :step/math-academy-id 44841 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173091}} {:db/id 17592186173096 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173262 :tutorial/content "Let's now justify why the Lagrange multipliers method works with multiple constraints.\n\nSuppose we wish to optimize the function $f(x,y,z)$ subject to the constraints $g(x,y,z)=a$ and $h(x,y,z)=b.$\n\nNote the following:\n\n- The natural domain of $f$ is some subset of $\\mathbb R^3.$\n- If we were to impose the first constraint only, we'd restrict the domain of $f$ to points on the level surface $g(x,y,z)=a.$\n- Similarly, if we were to impose the second constraint only, we'd restrict the domain of $f$ to points on the level surface $h(x,y,z)=b.$\n- Thus, by imposing *both* constraints, we restrict the domain of $f$ to the *intersection* of these two level surfaces. The intersection of two surfaces is a curve, which we'll denote as $\\mathbf r(t)$ for some real parameter $t.$\n\nThe curve $\\mathbf r(t)$ and the level surfaces are shown below.\n\n![](images/e8/e8b1db73c9952642ba53983ffb7090ad147ae965f1b935a812811742330b4dfc.png)\n\nNow, let $P(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ be a point that lies on $\\mathbf r(t)$ for some $t = t_0$ that is an extrema (max or min) of $f.$\n\nSince $g(x,y,z)=a$ and $h(x,y,z)=b$ are level surfaces of the functions $g(x,y,z)$ and $h(x,y,z),$ we have the following:\n\n- $\\nabla g$ is perpendicular to $g(x,y,z)=a$ at $P,$ and is therefore perpendicular to $\\mathbf r(t)$ at $P.$\n- $\\nabla h$ is perpendicular to $h(x,y,z)=b$ at $P,$ and is therefore perpendicular to $\\mathbf r(t)$ at $P.$\n\nThe situation is sketched below.\n\n![](images/16/16f2f1818628d9eb12ed0f3f2834cd916101839362813afe1be3f90ea35dd104.png)\n\nLet's now compute $\\big[f(\\mathbf r(t))\\big]',$ the derivative of $f$ over the curve $\\mathbf r(t).$ By the chain rule, we get\n\n$$\\begin{aligned}[f(r(t))]^{'} & =[f(x(t),y(t),z(t))]^{'} \\\\ & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\\cdot {x}^{'}(t)+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\\cdot {y}^{'}(t)+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\\cdot {z}^{'}(t) \\\\ & =⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩\\cdot ⟨{x}^{'}(t),{y}^{'}(t),{z}^{'}(t)⟩ \\\\ & =∇f(r(t))\\cdot {r}^{'}(t).\\end{aligned}$$\n\nSince $P$ is an extremum, we must have $$\\big[f(\\mathbf{r}(t_0))\\big]' = 0 \\qquad\\Longrightarrow\\qquad \\nabla f(\\mathbf{r}(t_0)) \\cdot \\mathbf{r}'(t_0) = 0 \\qquad\\Longrightarrow\\qquad \\nabla f(\\mathbf{r}(t_0)) \\perp \\mathbf{r}'(t_0).$$\n\nSince $\\mathbf{r}'(t_0)$ is tangent to $\\mathbf r(t)$ at $P,$ we have that $\\nabla f(\\mathbf{r}(t_0))$ is perpendicular to $\\mathbf r(t)$ at $P.$\n\nSo, $\\nabla g$ and $\\nabla h$ are both perpendicular to $\\mathbf{r}(t)$ at $P$. Assuming they aren't parallel, they span the two-dimensional space perpendicular to $\\mathbf{r}(t)$. Now $\\nabla f$ is also perpendicular to $\\mathbf{r}(t)$ at $P$. This means that $\\nabla f$ lies in the plane spanned by $\\nabla g$ and $\\nabla h.$ This condition can be represented by the following equation:\n\n$$\\nabla f(x,y,z) = \\lambda \\nabla g(x,y,z) + \\mu \\nabla h(x,y,z),$$\n\nwhere the real numbers $\\lambda$ and $\\mu$ are the Lagrange multipliers.\n\n![](images/b4/b48d7973b28bbd6a99704736dd60737d2f74ebcc2ddfddb0ab6f4749002e826e.png)" }_{2}^{5}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{4}}.\n$$\n\n- The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\\in [-6,-3].$ The corresponding region is a right $x$-axis, where $x\\in (-3,0].$ The corresponding region is a rectangle, so\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =bh \\\\  & =3\\cdot 1 \\\\  & =3.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- The $3$rd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\\in (0,2].$ The corresponding region is a trapezoid, so\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}_{3} & =\\frac{1}{2}(a+b)h \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}(4+2)(2) \\\\  & =6.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- The $4$th integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\\in (2,5].$ The corresponding region is a right triangle, so\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}_{4} & =\\frac{1}{2}(bh) \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}3(6) \\\\  & =9.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\int }_{-6}^{5}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x & :question/worked-solution "The graph consists of $4$ parts: the arc of the quarter-circle for $x\\in [-3,-1],$ the line segment for $x\\in [-1,1],$ the line segment for $x\\in (1,4],$ and the arc of the quarter-circle for $x\\in [4,7].$ So, we can use the additive property of integrals to get\n\n$$\n{\\int }_{-3}^{7}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x={{{\\int }_{-3}^{-1}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{1}}+{{{\\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{2}}+{{{\\int }_{1}^{4}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{3}}+{{{\\int }_{4}^{7}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{4}}.\n$$\n\n- The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\\in [-3,-1].$ The corresponding region is a combination of a rectangle and a quarter-circle of radius $2,$ so we find the area using the formula\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =bh-\\frac{1}{4}\\pi {r}^{2} \\\\  & =(2)(3)-\\frac{1}{4}\\pi (2)^{2} \\\\  & =6-\\pi .\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have\n\n$$\n{\\int }_{-3}^{-1}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x=-{A}_{1}=\\pi -6.\n$$\n\n- The $2$nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\\in [-1,1].$ The corresponding region is a rectangle, so we find the area using the formula\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =bh \\\\  & =2\\cdot 1 \\\\  & =2.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have\n\n$$\n{\\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\\,\\text{d}x=-{A}_{2}=-2.\n$$\n\n- The $3$rd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\\in (1,4].$ The corresponding region is a trapezoid, so we find the area using the formula\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}_{3} & =\\frac{1}{2}(a+b)h \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}(1+3)\\cdot 3 \\\\  & =6.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- The $4$th integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\\in [4,7].$ The corresponding region is a quarter-circle of radius $3,$ so we find the area using the We get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X<1.07\\mu ) & =0.75 \\\\ P(Z<\\frac{0.07\\mu }{12}) & =0.75 \\\\ Φ(\\frac{0.07\\mu }{12}) & =0.75 \\\\ \\frac{0.07\\mu }{12} & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.75).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFrom the table, \n\n$$\n\\Phi^{-1}(0.75) \\approx 0.6745.\n$$\n\nTherefore, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{0.07\\mu }{12} & =0.6745 \\\\ 0.07\\mu  & =8.094 \\\\ \\mu  & =\\frac{8.094}{0.07} \\\\  & ≈115.629.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we can find $P(X <   120)$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X<120) & =P(Z<\\frac{120-115.629}{12}) \\\\  & ≈P(Z<0.36) \\\\  & =Φ(0.36) \\\\  & =0.6406 \\\\  & ≈64.1%\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, approximately $64.1\\%$ of the people have systolic blood pressure lower than patients with a fasting glucose lower than $130\\,\\text{mg/dL}.$ **Round your answer to two decimal places.**\n\n*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *\n\n| $p$ | $\\,0.75\\,$ | $\\,0.80\\,$ | $\\,0.85\\,$ | $\\,0.90\\,$ | $\\,0.95\\,$ | $\\,0.99\\,$ |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\\,0.6745\\,$ | $\\,0.8416\\,$ | $\\,1.0364\\,$ | $\\,1.2816\\,$ | $\\,1.6449\\,$ | $\\,2.3263\\,$ |\n\n$$\n\n$$\n\n*In addition, you're given the following table of values for $p=Φ(z)$*.\n\n| $z$ | $\\,0.04\\,$ | $\\,0.05\\,$ | $\\,0.06\\,$ |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| $\\,-1.9\\,$ | $\\,0.0262\\,$ | $\\,0.0256\\,$ | $\\,0.0250\\,$ |\n| $\\,-1.8\\,$ | $\\,0.0329\\,$ | $\\,0.0322\\,$ | $\\,0.0314\\,$ |\n| $\\,-1.7\\,$ | $\\,0.0409\\,$ | $\\,0.0401\\,$ | $\\,0.0392\\,$ |\n\nApproximately\n{{field-1}}$%$ of the patients have a fasting glucose lower than $130\\,\\text{mg/dL}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the fasting glucose level of a randomly selected patient. Then we have $X∼N(\\mu ,{15}^{2}),$ and we want to find $P(X<130).$ But first, we need to find the mean $\\mu .$ \n\nWe know that $P(0.92\\mu <X<1.08\\mu )=0.60.$ First, we convert this to a cumulative probability:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(0.92\\mu <X<1.08\\mu ) & =0.60 \\\\ 2P(\\mu <X<1.08\\mu ) & =0.60 \\\\ P(\\mu <X<1.08\\mu ) & =0.30 \\\\ P(X<\\mu )+P(\\mu <X<1.08\\mu ) & =0.5+0.30 \\\\ P(X<1.08\\mu ) & =0.80\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring. We get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X<1.08\\mu ) & =0.80 \\\\ P(Z<\\frac{0.08\\mu }{15}) & =0.80 \\\\ Φ(\\frac{0.08\\mu }{15}) & =0.80 \\\\ \\frac{0.08\\mu }{15} & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.80).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFrom the table, \n\n$$\n{Φ}^{-1}(0.80)=0.8416.\n$$\n\nTherefore, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{0.08\\mu }{15} & =0.8416 \\\\ 0.08\\mu  & =12.624 \\\\ \\mu  & =\\frac{12.624}{0.08} \\\\  & ≈157.80.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we can solve for $P(X<130)$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(X<130) & =P(Z<\\frac{130-157.80}{15}) \\\\  & ≈P(Z<-1.85) \\\\  & =Φ(-1.85) \\\\  & =0.0322 \\\\  & ≈3.22%\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, approximately $3.22%$ of the patients have a fasting glucose lower than $130\\,\\text{mg/dL}.$"} {:db/id 17592186083342 Moreover, it is symmetrical about the mean, median, and mode, which all equal $\\mu$.  \n\n![](images/0c/0c8951446f52cea9db6c0a2b600fc53cb564c3d64ff0afab15c9756dc0c0f29b.png)\n\nWe can use the normal distribution to model a wide range of real-life situations because many real-world distributions are roughly bell-shaped and symmetrical around a mean value. \n\nPatients' blood pressures, people's weights, measurement errors, and IQ scores are just some of the real-world examples that can be modeled as a normal distribution. \n\nTo determine whether a given data is normal, the first thing to do is to check the shape of the distribution. For example, if a data set is roughly bell-shaped, then it *might* be normally distributed. \n\nIt should be noted that, in practice, statisticians will often need to perform several tests on the data to check for normality (these are called **normality tests**). Assuming that the duration of the videos is normally distributed, find the standard deviation of the duration times, rounded to the near minute.\n\n*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*\n\n| $p$ | $\\,0.01\\,$ | $\\,0.03\\,$ | $\\,0.05\\,$ | $\\,0.10\\,$ | $\\,0.15\\,$ | $\\,0.20\\,$ | $\\,0.25\\,$ |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\\,-2.3263\\,$ | $\\,-1.8808\\,$ | $\\,-1.6449\\,$ | $\\,-1.2816\\,$ | $\\,-1.0364\\,$ | $\\,-0.8416\\,$ | $\\,-0.6745\\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the duration of a video. 17592186168143 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we will generalize Bayes' theorem to deal with situations where the sample space $\\mathcal S$ is partitioned into a disjoint union of multiple events. \n\nSuppose we have three events $A_1,A_2,$ and $A_3$ that form a disjoint union of the sample space $\\mathcal S,$ as shown below.\n\n![](images/89/89a78ef526fcd29a59bacd4d6ae1a456a596d6616af7453f1ba530a610d9a2ac.png)\n\n \n\nNow consider an event $B$ that also lies in the sample space:\n\n![](images/da/daa96423e45f9f80897e2c2d61177eab2faff77f440921866d1b81b7ef2cfe09.png)\n\n \n\nBayes' theorem states that\n\n$$\nP(A_1|B)=\\dfrac{P(B|A_1)P(A_1)}{P(B)}.\n$$\n\nNow, the law of total probability tells us that\n\n$$\nP(B)=P(B|A_1)P(A_1) + P(B|A_2)P(A_2) + P(B|A_3)P(A_3).\n$$\n\nSubstituting this into Bayes' theorem, we get\n\n$$\nP(A_1 | B) = \\dfrac{P(B|A_1) P(A_1)}{P(B|A_1)P(A_1) + P(B|A_2)P(A_2) + P(B|A_3)P(A_3)} .\n$$\n\nUsing similar arguments, we can say that for $A_k$ for $k=1,2,3,$ we have\n\n$$\nP(A_k | B) = \\dfrac{P(B|A_k) P(A_k)}{P(B|A_1)P(A_1) + P(B|A_2)P(A_2) + P(B|A_3)P(A_3)}\n$$\n\nwhich is usually written more compactly as\n\n$$\nP(A_k | B) = \\dfrac{P(B|A_k) P(A_k)}{\\sum_{i=1}^3 P(B|A_i)P(A_i)}.\n$$\n\nIt's easy to see how this generalizes. If the disjoint union $A_1 \\sqcup A_2 \\sqcup \\ldots \\sqcup A_n$ covers the entire sample space, Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability gives us the following:\n\n$$\nP(A_k | B) = \\dfrac{P(B|A_k) P(A_k)}{\\sum_{i=1}^n P(B|A_i)P(A_i)}\n$$\n\nLet's see an example of how to apply this theorem." :tutorial/id #uuid "bf17685f-9890-54cc-b8a2-15815558e87a" :tutorial/math-academy-id "To find the lowest common multiple of two numbers, we first find the prime factorization of both numbers.\n\n- We start by finding the prime factorization of $120$:![](images/fb/fb213f6ac09abbf31aacfdbfbd08b76dbea4199528abeb1c8041a73f0d7780ed.png)\nTherefore, $120 = 2^3 \\cdot 3 \\cdot 5$.\n- Next, we find the prime factorization of $90$:![](images/03/034b3fe25edb2741abb035b8ca71a3c499fe6fae1a5975b4241d6379b819f19e.png)\nTherefore, $90 = 2 \\cdot 3^2 \\cdot 5$.\n\nSo, we have the following prime factorizations:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\n120 &= 2^{3} \\cdot 3 \\cdot 5 \\\\\n90 &= 2 \\cdot 3^{2} \\cdot 5\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we write down every prime factor that is shown above, and we raise each prime factor to the highest power given in either factorization:\n\n- the highest power of $2$ is $3$\n- the highest power of $3$ is $2$\n- the highest power of $5$ is $1$\n\nTherefore, the lowest common multiple of $120$ and $90$ is\n\n$$\n\\textrm{LCM}(120, 90) = 2^3 \\cdot 3^2 \\cdot 5 = 360\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186049086} {:db/id 17592186050170} {:db/id 17592186050212} {:db/id numbers.\n\nTo find the lowest common multiple of two small numbers, we can list all multiples of the two numbers and identify the smallest multiple that they have in common.\n\nFor example, let's find the lowest common multiple of $4$ and $6$. We start by listing all multiples of $4$ and $6$:\n\n$\\begin{bmatrix}4 & → 04, 08, [math]12[/math], 16, 20, 24, … \\\\ 6 & → 06, [math]12[/math], 18, 24, 30, 36, …\\end{bmatrix}$\nThe smallest multiple in both lists is $12$ So $12$ is our answer, and we can write\n\n$$\n\\textrm{LCM}(4,6)= 12\n$$\n\n**Note:** The lowest common multiple is also sometimes called the *least* common multiple." In our case, the unique prime factors are\n\n$$\n{\\color{red}2}, \\qquad {\\color{red}3}, \\qquad {\\color{red}5}\n$$\n\nNow, for each number in our list, we look at *both* prime factorizations and we take the *largest* power shown for each prime factor:\n\n- The factors corresponding to ${\\color{red}2}$ are ${\\color{red}2}^{\\color{blue}1}$ and ${\\color{red}2}^{\\color{blue}2}$. 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1007 "Mathematics for Machine Learning" 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1008 "Our Mathematics for Machine Learning course provides a comprehensive foundation of the essential mathematical tools required to study modern machine learning.\nThis course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals.\nOn completing this course, students will be well-prepared for a university-level machine learning course that tackles concepts such as gradient descent, neural networks, backpropagation, support vector machines, naive Bayes classifiers, and Gaussian mixture models." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics in set theory and logic. Students develop a precise mathematical language for describing sets, functions, and predicates, and are introduced to key ideas such as supremum and infimum, as well as argmax and argmin notation. Logical reasoning and Boolean functions are also studied, providing important conceptual motivation for understanding the expressive limitations of some simple machine learning models, such as why certain functions (e.g. XOR) cannot be represented by a single-layer neural network.\nStudents then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.\nAs part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. They also study operations such as the Hadamard product, which appears naturally in element-wise computations in neural networks. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process.\nStudents will learn how to find eigenvectors of a matrix, compute matrix diagonalizations, and extend these ideas to orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices. These techniques underpin dimensionality reduction methods and are central to understanding the structure of data.\nThe course then develops key applications of linear algebra in machine learning. Students study singular value decomposition and its relationship to principal component analysis, and learn how these tools are used for dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and identifying structure in high-dimensional datasets. Linear least-squares problems and regression techniques are also studied as foundational methods for fitting models to data.\nA solid grasp of multivariable calculus is essential for understanding modern machine learning algorithms. In this course, students become well-versed in partial derivatives and gradient vectors (used in gradient-based optimization), the multivariable chain rule (essential for backpropagation), and vector-valued functions. Students extend differentiation to maps between multi-dimensional vector spaces and develop the tools of vector and matrix calculus used to compute gradients of loss functions in neural networks.\nStudents also study optimization of multivariable functions, including critical points, second derivative tests, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. These techniques form the mathematical foundation of algorithms such as support vector machines and constrained optimization problems in machine learning.\nStudents work with standard multivariable surfaces to build intuition for loss surfaces, and study double integrals as a tool for understanding continuous probability distributions.\nOn the probability and statistics side, students study discrete and continuous random variables, including probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, transformations, expectation, moments, variance, and Bayes' theorem. Important probability distributions are explored in detail.\nStudents extend their understanding to joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, as well as sums and products of random variables. Topics such as covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions are introduced, which are essential in probabilistic modeling.\nThe course concludes with parametric inference, focusing on point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals, which form the statistical foundation for many machine learning methods." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1012 145 "e1974a4e-dd77-5808-a604-05fb1fa36604" 17592186045417] [17592186106931 1063 17592186107084 17592186045417] [17592186107078 1064 "Geometrically, the absolute value of the scalar triple product $\\mathbf{a} \\cdot (\\mathbf{b} \\times \\mathbf{c})$ represents the volume enclosed by the parallelepiped whose sides are formed by the three vectors $\\mathbf{a},$ $\\mathbf{b},$ and $\\mathbf{c}.$\n\nTo illustrate, consider the parallelepiped shown below. The sides of this parallelepiped are formed by the vectors $\\mathbf{a},$ $\\mathbf{b},$ and $\\mathbf{c}.$\n\n![](images/25/2597b48a010607fca71c551dbce8e9e2bbeda47d0892a582347ae1cdf19f1bf6.png)\n\nThe volume of this parallelepiped is given by the absolute value of the triple product:\n\n$$\nV = |\\mathbf{a} \\cdot (\\mathbf{b} \\times \\mathbf{c})|\n$$\n\nA proof of this result will be given at the end of this lesson." 17592186045417] [17592186107078 1065 2956 17592186045417] [17592186107078 1066 #uuid "c5917536-1cb1-5fba-9f81-7d866e832dcc" 17592186045417] [17592186107078 1067 "Introduction" 17592186045417] [17592186107079 1064 "Three vectors are said to be **coplanar** if they are parallel to the same plane.\n\nWhen we have three coplanar vectors, the parallelepiped they span is *flat* on the plane, and therefore its volume is zero. Consequently, the triple product of the vectors is zero as well.\n\nSo, if three vectors are coplanar, then their triple product is zero. The converse is also true: if the triple product of three nonzero vectors is zero, then the vectors are coplanar.\n\nTherefore, we have the following statement:\n\n$\\mathbf{a}, \\mathbf{b},$ and $\\mathbf{c}$ are coplanar $\\quad\\Leftrightarrow\\quad$    $\\mathbf{a} \\cdot (\\mathbf{b} \\times \\mathbf{c}) = 0$" 17592186045417] [17592186107079 1065 2957 17592186045417] [17592186107079 1066 #uuid "e3012c88-77aa-5271-ad5f-b2176f99ba15" 17592186045417] [17592186107079 1067 "The Volume Spanned by Coplanar Vectors" 17592186045417] [17592186107084 1064 "We have been using the fact that the volume of a parallelepiped spanned by the vectors $\\mathbf{a},$ $\\mathbf{b},$ and $\\mathbf{c}$ is given by the absolute value of the triple product:\n\n$$\nV =  |\\mathbf{a} \\cdot (\\mathbf{b} \\times \\mathbf{c})|\n$$\n\nBut why is this formula true? To understand why, remember that the volume of a parallelepiped can be obtained by multiplying the area of the base by the height.\n\nAs we can see in the diagram below, \n\n- the area of the base is given by $A = | \\mathbf{b} \\times \\mathbf{c} |,$ and\n\n- the height is given by $h = |\\text{proj}_{\\mathbf{b}\\times\\mathbf{c}}\\:\\mathbf{a}|.$\n\n![](images/cf/cfc492127bed6d6929518a708288691c5fe79e1842be6ecf92666bed6b03200b.png)\n\nTo compute the volume, we will multiply the area of the base by the height. First, though, let's write down the expression for the height:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}h & =|{\\text{proj}}_{b\\times c}\\,a| \\\\  & =|\\frac{a\\cdot (b\\times c)}{|b\\times c|}| \\\\  & =\\frac{|a\\cdot (b\\times c)|}{|b\\times c|}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, multiplying the area of the base by the height, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}V & =A\\cdot h \\\\  & =|b\\times c|\\cdot \\frac{|a\\cdot (b\\times c)|}{|b\\times c|} \\\\  & =|a\\cdot (b\\times c)|.\\end{aligned}\n$$" 17592186045417] [17592186107084 1065 3309 17592186045417] [17592186107084 1066 #uuid "6b371cde-1beb-5aa2-b564-0bae79e2faf1" 17592186045417] [17592186107084 1067 "Proof That the Volume of a Parallelepiped is Given by the Absolute Value of the Triple Product" 17592186045417] [17592186107085 1064 "Sometimes, we are not given the vectors that represent the sides of a parallelepiped. Instead, we might be given the points at which the vertices lie.\n\nTo compute the volume of a parallelepiped given the vertices, we can still use a similar process as before. The only difference is that we have to start by computing the displacement vectors between the points.\n\nOnce we have the displacement vectors, then we can find the desired volume by computing the Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.\nStudents then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.\nApplications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.\nThe course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.\nStudents next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Concepts such as circulation, flux, and path independence lead to the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Green’s theorem, the divergence theorem, and Stokes’ theorem. These results form the mathematical framework underlying conservation laws and the differential and integral formulations of electromagnetic theory.\nApplications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Students analyze motion using vector-valued functions, apply Newton’s second law to systems in the plane, and study work–energy relationships. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.\nThe course then returns to differential equations, extending earlier techniques to systems of linear differential equations. Students analyze dynamical systems using eigenvalues, phase portraits, and matrix methods, which appear in models of interacting systems such as coupled oscillators or predator–prey dynamics.\nLaplace transforms are introduced as a powerful tool for solving linear differential equations with discontinuous inputs or initial conditions. Boundary value problems and Fourier series are then developed, providing mathematical techniques used to solve differential equations describing heat flow, vibrating strings, wave propagation, and other physical phenomena.\nThe course concludes with numerical methods for differential equations and advanced probability topics. Students analyze the accuracy and stability of numerical schemes used in computational physics and study multivariate probability distributions and the central limit theorem, which appear in Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems.\nStudents learn how mathematical concepts such as vector spaces, linear transformations, multivariable functions, and differential equations provide the language and computational techniques used to describe motion, fields, and dynamical processes. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.\nStudents then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.\nThe course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.\nThe course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.\nStudents then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. "In statistics, we often want to use sample data to deduce (or **infer**) the values of various **population parameters**. The two most common population parameters that we wish to find are\n\n- the **population mean** $\\mu,$ and\n\n- the **population variance** $\\sigma^2.$\n\nThe population mean is the mean of the *entire* population. Likewise, the population variance is the variance of the *entire* population. We should consider these values as *fixed* unknowns. \n\nSuppose, for example, we want to find the mean number of pages per book at a particular library. 4y^2 - z = 0$$\n\nGeometrically, this means that we want to minimize $f(x,y,z)$ over the intersection of the cylinder $x^2+y^2=1$ and the elliptic paraboloid $2x^2 + 4y^2 - z = 0,$ as shown method of Lagrange multipliers states that the extrema of the function $f(x,y,z)$ subject to constraints $g(x,y,z)=a$ and $h(x,y,z)=b$ can be found by solving the following system: $${\\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z)=\\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\\\ g(x,y,z)=a \\\\ h(x,y,z)=b\\end{aligned}$$\n\nHere, the constants $\\lambda$ and $\\mu$ are the Lagrange multipliers of this exist.\n\n**Note:** Geometrically, the condition $\\nabla f = \\lambda \\nabla g + \\mu \\nabla h$ states that\n\n- $\\nabla f$ lies in the plane spanned by $\\nabla g$ and $\\nabla h,$ or, equivalently,\n- $\\nabla f$ is perpendicular to the level surfaces $g(x,y,z) = a$ and $h(x,y,z) = b.$\n\nWe'll explore this geometric intuition further at the end of the lesson." 17592186045417] "Let's now justify why the Lagrange multipliers method works with multiple constraints.\n\nSuppose we wish to optimize the function $f(x,y,z)$ subject to the constraints $g(x,y,z)=a$ and $h(x,y,z)=b.$\n\nNote the following:\n\n- The natural domain of $f$ is some subset of $\\mathbb R^3.$\n- If we were to impose the first constraint only, we'd restrict the domain of $f$ to points on the level surface $g(x,y,z)=a.$\n- Similarly, if we were to impose the second constraint only, we'd restrict the domain of $f$ to points on the level surface $h(x,y,z)=b.$\n- Thus, by imposing *both* constraints, we restrict the domain of $f$ to the *intersection* of these two level surfaces. The intersection of two surfaces is a curve, which we'll denote as $\\mathbf r(t)$ for some real parameter $t.$\n\nThe curve $\\mathbf r(t)$ and the level surfaces are shown below.\n\n![](images/e8/e8b1db73c9952642ba53983ffb7090ad147ae965f1b935a812811742330b4dfc.png)\n\nNow, let $P(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ be a point that lies on $\\mathbf r(t)$ for some $t = t_0$ that is an extrema (max or min) of $f.$\n\nSince $g(x,y,z)=a$ and $h(x,y,z)=b$ are level surfaces of the functions $g(x,y,z)$ and $h(x,y,z),$ we have the following:\n\n- $\\nabla g$ is perpendicular to $g(x,y,z)=a$ at $P,$ and is therefore perpendicular to $\\mathbf r(t)$ at $P.$\n- $\\nabla h$ is perpendicular to $h(x,y,z)=b$ at $P,$ and is therefore perpendicular to $\\mathbf r(t)$ at $P.$\n\nThe situation is sketched below.\n\n![](images/16/16f2f1818628d9eb12ed0f3f2834cd916101839362813afe1be3f90ea35dd104.png)\n\nLet's now compute $\\big[f(\\mathbf r(t))\\big]',$ the derivative of $f$ over the curve $\\mathbf r(t).$ By the chain rule, we get\n\n$$\\begin{aligned}[f(r(t))]^{'} & =[f(x(t),y(t),z(t))]^{'} \\\\ & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\\cdot {x}^{'}(t)+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\\cdot {y}^{'}(t)+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\\cdot {z}^{'}(t) \\\\ & =⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩\\cdot ⟨{x}^{'}(t),{y}^{'}(t),{z}^{'}(t)⟩ \\\\ & =∇f(r(t))\\cdot {r}^{'}(t).\\end{aligned}$$\n\nSince $P$ is an extremum, we must have $$\\big[f(\\mathbf{r}(t_0))\\big]' = 0 \\qquad\\Longrightarrow\\qquad \\nabla f(\\mathbf{r}(t_0)) \\cdot \\mathbf{r}'(t_0) = 0 \\qquad\\Longrightarrow\\qquad \\nabla f(\\mathbf{r}(t_0)) \\perp \\mathbf{r}'(t_0).$$\n\nSince $\\mathbf{r}'(t_0)$ is tangent to $\\mathbf r(t)$ at $P,$ we have that $\\nabla f(\\mathbf{r}(t_0))$ is perpendicular to $\\mathbf r(t)$ at $P.$\n\nSo, $\\nabla g$ and $\\nabla h$ are both perpendicular to $\\mathbf{r}(t)$ at $P$. Assuming they aren't parallel, they span the two-dimensional space perpendicular to $\\mathbf{r}(t)$. Now $\\nabla f$ is also perpendicular to $\\mathbf{r}(t)$ at $P$. This means that $\\nabla f$ lies in the plane spanned by $\\nabla g$ and $\\nabla h.$ This condition can be represented by the following equation:\n\n$$\\nabla f(x,y,z) = \\lambda \\nabla g(x,y,z) + \\mu \\nabla h(x,y,z),$$\n\nwhere the real numbers $\\lambda$ and $\\mu$ are the Lagrange multipliers.\n\n![](images/b4/b48d7973b28bbd6a99704736dd60737d2f74ebcc2ddfddb0ab6f4749002e826e.png)" 17592186045417] [17592186173262 1065 7919 17592186045417] [17592186173262 1066 #uuid "669fb037-8c12-5658-a176-7753a99e8c7e" 17592186045417] [17592186173262 1067 "Justification of the Lagrange Multiplier Method With Multiple Constraints" 17592186045417] [17592186429054 1030 1.0 17592186045436] [17592186429054 1032 "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. \n\nSuppose we have three events $A_1,A_2,$ and $A_3$ that form a disjoint union of the sample space $\\mathcal S,$ as shown space:\n\n![](images/da/daa96423e45f9f80897e2c2d61177eab2faff77f440921866d1b81b7ef2cfe09.png)\n\n \n\nBayes' theorem states that\n\n$$\nP(A_1|B)=\\dfrac{P(B|A_1)P(A_1)}{P(B)}.\n$$\n\nNow, the law of total probability tells us that\n\n$$\nP(B)=P(B|A_1)P(A_1) + P(B|A_2)P(A_2) + P(B|A_3)P(A_3).\n$$\n\nSubstituting this into Bayes' theorem, we get\n\n$$\nP(A_1 | B) = \\dfrac{P(B|A_1) P(A_1)}{P(B|A_1)P(A_1) + P(B|A_2)P(A_2) + P(B|A_3)P(A_3)} .\n$$\n\nUsing similar arguments, we can say that for $A_k$ for $k=1,2,3,$ we have\n\n$$\nP(A_k | B) = \\dfrac{P(B|A_k) P(A_k)}{P(B|A_1)P(A_1) + P(B|A_2)P(A_2) + P(B|A_3)P(A_3)}\n$$\n\nwhich is usually written more compactly as\n\n$$\nP(A_k | B) = \\dfrac{P(B|A_k) P(A_k)}{\\sum_{i=1}^3 P(B|A_i)P(A_i)}.\n$$\n\nIt's easy to see how this generalizes. If the disjoint union $A_1 \\sqcup A_2 \\sqcup \\ldots \\sqcup A_n$ covers the entire sample space, Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability gives us the following:\n\n$$\nP(A_k | B) = \\dfrac{P(B|A_k) P(A_k)}{\\sum_{i=1}^n P(B|A_i)P(A_i)}\n$$\n\nLet's see an example of how to apply this theorem." 17592186045417] [17592186168143 1065 6969 17592186045417] [17592186168143 1066 #uuid 17592186045417] [17592186084281 1063 17592186084485 17592186045417] [17592186084484 1064 "The **lowest common multiple** (or $\\textrm{LCM}$) of two integers is the smallest multiple that's common to both numbers.\n\nTo find the lowest common multiple of two small numbers, we can list all multiples of the two numbers and identify the smallest multiple that they have in common.\n\nFor example, let's find the lowest common multiple of $4$ and $6$. We start by listing all multiples of $4$ and $6$:\n\n$\\begin{bmatrix}4 & → 04, 08, [math]12[/math], 16, 20, 24, … \\\\ 6 & → 06, [math]12[/math], 18, 24, 30, 36, …\\end{bmatrix}$\nThe smallest multiple in both lists is $12$ So $12$ is our answer, and we can write\n\n$$\n\\textrm{LCM}(4,6)= 12\n$$\n\n**Note:** The lowest common multiple is also sometimes called the *least* common multiple." 17592186045417] [17592186084484 1065 5301 17592186045417] [17592186084484 1066 #uuid "b16f2464-2c19-5166-bd61-97043695afcb" 17592186045417] [17592186084484 1067 "Introduction" 17592186045417] [17592186084485 1064 "Now suppose that we want to find the lowest common multiple of two larger numbers. It would take a while to make long lists of multiples. Luckily, there is a faster method.\n\nLet's demonstrate by finding $\\textrm{LCM}(10,12)$. We start by writing the prime factorization of $10$ and $12$, writing any repeating factors as powers:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\n10 &= 2 \\cdot 5 = 2^{1} \\cdot 5^{1} \\\\\n12 &= 2 \\cdot 2 \\cdot 3 = 2^{2} \\cdot 3^{1}\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThen, we write down each unique prime factor that appears in either of our decompositions. In our case, the unique prime factors are\n\n$$\n{\\color{red}2}, \\qquad {\\color{red}3}, \\qquad {\\color{red}5}\n$$\n\nNow, for each number in our list, we look at *both* prime factorizations and we take the *largest* power shown for each prime factor:\n\n- The factors corresponding to ${\\color{red}2}$ are ${\\color{red}2}^{\\color{blue}1}$ and ${\\color{red}2}^{\\color{blue}2}$. Of these, the larger power is ${\\color{red}2}^{\\color{blue}2}$.\n- There is only one factor corresponding to ${\\color{red}3}$. It is ${\\color{red}3}^{\\color{blue}1}$.\n- There is only one factor corresponding to ${\\color{red}5}$. It is ${\\color{red}5}^{\\color{blue}1}$.\n\nFinally, we multiply the largest powers of each factor together, and we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nLCM(10, 12) &= 2^{2} \\cdot 3^{1} \\cdot 5^{1} \\\\\n&= 4 \\cdot 3 \\cdot 5 \\\\\n&= 60\n\\end{aligned}\n$$" 17592186045417] [17592186084485 1065 5489 17592186045417] [17592186084485 1066 #uuid "de44c642-c9d2-5c1d-8b59-8781a99559ef" 17592186045417] [17592186084485 1067 "Finding the Lowest Common Multiple of Two Larger Numbers" 17592186045417]]}
